en: He who performs the action that must be done, without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant and a yogi; not he who merely maintains no sacred fires, nor he who merely abstains from action. (6.1)
Śrīdhara:
Even when the mind is pure, liberation does not occur through mere renunciation alone without meditation; thus, in this sixth chapter, they elaborate upon the yoga of meditation.

The sixth chapter begins in order to elaborate upon the yoga briefly stated in the preceding chapter. Therein, starting from the verse "having renounced all actions with the mind" (Gītā 5.13), there is a detailed exposition—primarily through the lens of renunciation—of steadfastness in knowledge; however, because action is of the nature of suffering, there is the danger of an excessive tendency toward sudden renunciation.
With two verses beginning with "anāśrita," He praises Karma-yoga as being superior even to renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in order to ward off what has already been attained [by those who have renounced].

One who performs the prescribed action because it is a necessary duty, while remaining unattached to—that is, regardless of—the fruit of that action, he alone is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi; but not one who is "without fire" (niragni), meaning one who has abandoned the action known as sacrifice (iṣṭi) which is accomplished by means of the sacred fires.
Nor is he one who is inactive, nor one who abandons the action known as *pūrta* (charitable works), which is not accomplished by fire. //1//
Madhusūdana: That which was stated at the end of the fifth [chapter] in three verses regarding the Yoga-sūtra,
the sixth chapter is now commenced for its detailed exposition.

In this context, intending to prescribe yoga through the renunciation of all actions, [the Lord] praises Karma-yoga with two verses beginning with "anāśrita," anticipating the objection that it is inferior because it must be abandoned.

One who, not depending on the fruit of actions— that is, being free from attachment to results— performs the obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra which are prescribed by the scriptures as duties to be done, is praised as being both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi, even while remaining an agent of action.
For renunciation (sannyāsa) is indeed relinquishment,
and yoga is the absence of distraction within the mind;
both of these exist for him because of his relinquishing of fruits and because of the absence of mental distraction in the form of craving for fruits.

In this context, the very renunciation of craving for the fruits of action is designated by the terms "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*) and "discipline" (*yoga*) in a figurative sense, for the purpose of praising it in comparison with actions performed with desire.
For indeed, renunciation and discipline are necessarily present as primary qualities in one who performs action without desire.
Therefore, although this person is not one who has abandoned the sacred fires nor one who has relinquished the Vedic rites accomplished through fire, [he is still praised].
Nor is he one who is without sacred fires, nor one who abandons the rites prescribed by the Smṛti while disregarding the fires;
nevertheless, he should be regarded as both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi.
Alternatively, it should not be thought that a renunciant and a yogi are necessarily one who is without fires and one who is without ritual action.

However, it is praised that such a person—one who possesses the sacred fire (*sāgni*) and is active (*sakriya*), yet performs action without desire—is to be considered both a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) and a yogi.

Just as in the passage, "Others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals; cows and horses are animals," the application of the negative particle (*nañ*) is possible through the figure of speech known as praise (*praśaṃsā-lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, since the term "inactive" (*akriya*) alone would already imply one who has renounced all actions, the addition of "without the sacred fire" (*niragni*) would be redundant.

Thus, by the word "fire" (agni), all ritual actions are indicated, and so the renunciant is called "without fire" (niragni); and by the word "action" (kriyā), the fluctuations of the mind are indicated, and so the yogi whose mental fluctuations are restrained is called "without action" (akriya).

Therefore, one should not think that the renunciant is merely "without fire," nor should one think that the yogi is merely "without action"; rather, the mutual exclusion of both [conditions] should be shown according to their respective order.
This being the case, it should be understood that even the pair of negations is logically consistent. //1//
Viśvanātha:
In the sixth [chapter], the means for achieving steadiness of the mind— even though it is flickering— is taught for the yogi who has conquered the self through the various methods of yoga.

Even for one engaged in the practice of the eightfold yoga, action performed without desire—which purifies the mind—must not be abandoned; thus he says: "He who performs the action prescribed by the scriptures as something that must necessarily be done, without depending on the fruit of action and without expectation, he alone is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) because of his renunciation of the fruits of action."
He alone is called a yogi because of the absence of mental attachment toward the enjoyment of sense objects.
Furthermore, one who is merely "without fire"—that is, one who has simply abandoned rituals such as the *agnihotra*—is not called a *saṃnyāsī*.
Nor is one called a yogi by being inactive, devoid of bodily movement, or with eyes half-closed. //1//
Baladeva:
In the sixth [chapter], the method of yoga for one whose actions are purified and who has conquered the self,
as well as the means for stabilizing the unsteady mind, is proclaimed.

Having taught Karma-yoga, which is headed by Aṣṭāṅga-yoga, the Blessed One now praises that Karma-yoga in two verses beginning with "anāśrita," intending to instruct them [the two sages] on it first because it is the means to that [higher yoga].

He who performs the action that must necessarily be done— without desiring the fruit of action, such as cattle, food, sons, heaven, and so forth— he is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) established in Jñāna-yoga.
And the yogi is precisely one who is established in the eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga).
The sense is that the perfection of both [the renunciant and the yogi] comes through karma-yoga alone.

One who is "without fire" is not a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) merely because he has abandoned rituals such as the Agnihotra and wears the garb of an ascetic; nor is one a yogi merely by being "actionless," having abandoned bodily actions, with eyes half-closed.
In this regard, it is the opinion of those who wish to practice the eightfold yoga that action should not be abandoned abruptly. //1//
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogi who has not renounced his purposeful intentions. 6.2.2
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry "Why?", he says "yam" (which), demonstrating that karma-yoga itself is renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
They call it "saṃnyāsa"—they say it is pre-eminently the best—because of such Vedic texts as, "Renunciation alone excelled [all else]."
Know that he is indeed a yogin solely by reason of the renunciation of fruits.
To the question "Why?", the author states the reason indicated by the word "iti" (thus), saying "for not" (*na hi*), because even in the case of yoga, this reason applies:
for one by whom the intention for fruit has not been renounced—whether he be established in action or established in knowledge—is certainly not a yogin.

Therefore, because of the commonality of abandoning the desire for fruits, he is indeed a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*); and because of that very abandonment of the desire for fruits, due to the absence of mental distraction, he is also a yogi—this is the meaning. //2//
Madhusūdana:

In order to show the connection with a quality that serves as the basis for applying the term "renunciation" even where there is no formal renunciation, he says, "That which they call renunciation," referring to the abandonment of all actions and their fruits. For the Śrutis declare: "Renunciation alone surpassed [all else]," and so forth.
"O son, having risen above the desire for progeny, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, the Brahmins then lead the life of mendicancy"—such are the scriptural passages.

Know that *yoga*—the performance of prescribed duties through the renunciation of both the thirst for fruits and the conceit of agency—is *saṃnyāsa*, O Pāṇḍava. According to the maxim, "That which is not given by Brahmā is called given by Brahmā; we consider this to be similar to being given by Brahmā," a word applied to one thing conveys similarity when used for another. Thus, *yoga* is designated as *saṃnyāsa* because it resembles true renunciation.
[It occurs] either by means of a secondary function (gauṇyā vṛttyā) or by the superimposition of that state (tad-bhāvāropeṇa). But what is the similarity in the present case?
To this he says: "For not... (na hi).
For indeed, because no one whatsoever who has not renounced their *saṃkalpa*— that is, who has not abandoned the intention for results— can be a yogi; rather,

every yogi must necessarily have abandoned the intention for results, it follows that by virtue of the commonality of having renounced results, and by virtue of the commonality of restraining the mental function (*vṛtti*) of wealth in the form of craving, the very person performing action (*karmī*) is, in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*).

And the meaning is that one becomes a yogin. For it is said: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Yoga Sūtra 1.2), and "the fluctuations are fivefold: right knowledge, misconception, conceptualization, sleep, and memory" (Yoga Sūtra 1.6).
Among these, the Vedists maintain that there are six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation, and non-existence.

The Yogas maintain that there are three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): perception, inference, and verbal testimony (Yoga Sūtra 1.7). The contraction and expansion [of these categories] should be understood through the principles of inclusion and exclusion;
it is for this very reason that there are differences of opinion among the logicians and others.

Error is false knowledge; its five varieties are ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and clinging to life (*abhiniveśa*). These alone are the afflictions (*kleśa*). Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon verbal cognition but is devoid of a real object; it is a linguistic usage regarding a non-existent thing, distinct from both valid cognition (*pramā*) and error (*bhrama*), such as "the horn of a hare" or "consciousness in a non-existent person," and so forth.
"Sleep is a mental modification (vṛtti) whose object is the notion of non-existence" (Yoga Sūtra 1.10); the meaning is that it is not merely the absence of knowledge and so forth.
"Memory is the non-losing of an experienced object" (Yoga Sūtra 1.11); the meaning is that it is a cognition produced by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of a previous experience.
It is mentioned last because it is produced by all the other mental modifications.
The functions such as shame (*lajjā*) and so forth should also be understood as being included within these very [categories].
The restraint of all such mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti*) is called both "yoga" and "samādhi.

However, the intention for results, known as passion (*rāga*), is a third type of error (*viparyaya*); the mere restraint of that is also called "yoga" and "renunciation" (*saṃnyāsa*) in a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). Thus, there is no contradiction. //2//
Viśvanātha:
The literal meaning of the word *saṃnyāsa* is indeed the renunciation of the fruits of action;
in reality, however, the meaning of the word *yoga* is the steadiness of the mind with regard to sense objects.
Therefore, he says "yam" (which) to show that the two words *saṃnyāsa* and *yoga* have indeed arrived at a single meaning:
one who is not un-renounced—that is, one by whom renunciation has been performed, by whom mental resolve, desire for results, and longing for the enjoyment of sense objects have been abandoned. //2//

Baladeva: Now, if it be objected that the word *saṃnyāsa* is used for the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) characterized by the cessation of the functions of all the senses, while the word *yoga* is used for the restraint of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*), then by what interpretation do you apply these terms to *karma-yoga*, which consists of the activity of all the senses—when you say, "He is both a renunciant and a yogi"? To this, He says: "That" and so forth.
O Pāṇḍava! Know that very *karma-yoga* which those who know the true meaning and intent call *saṃnyāsa* to be that same *yoga*, namely the eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) yoga.
[Objection: Is it not the case that in expressions such as "the boy is a lion," such usage occurs due to a similarity in qualities like bravery?
If it is asked what the similarity is in the present context, he says "for not" (na hi).

The meaning is that no one who has not renounced their intentions can be a fit vessel for knowledge or a practitioner of the eightfold yoga; rather, it is only one who has renounced their intentions who becomes so.
He is one by whom *saṅkalpa*—the desire for results—has been renounced and abandoned.

Thus, because of the similarity between the abandonment of results and the cessation of mental fluctuations in the form of craving, the application of those two terms to the practitioner of *karma-yoga* is figurative (*gauṇa-vṛtti*). //2//
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means. //3//

Śrīdhara: Then, fearing that karma-yoga alone would be required for as long as one lives, he states its limit with the words "of one who desires to ascend. For a person who wishes to ascend—that is, to attain—the yoga of knowledge, karma is said to be the means for that ascent, because it effects the purification of the mind.

But for that very person who has ascended to the yoga of knowledge and is established in meditation, tranquility and concentration—the cessation of karma that distracts the mind—are said to be the cause for the ripening of knowledge. //3//
Madhusūdana:
[Objection: "Is it then the case that because of its excellence, Karma-yoga alone is to be practiced throughout one's life? [Reply: No; he says "of one who desires to ascend" (ārurukṣoḥ).
This refers to one who desires to ascend—that is, to attain—Yoga in the form of purity of the internal organ or dispassion (*vairāgya*), but not to one who has already ascended.
For the sage who is to become [an enlightened one]— one who has abandoned craving for the fruits of action— the action prescribed by the scriptures, such as the *agnihotra* and other rites,
performed with the consciousness of offering it to the Blessed Lord, is declared by Me through the mouth of the Vedas to be the cause, the means to be practiced, for ascending to yoga.
But for that same person once he has ascended to yoga— that is, having attained yoga in the form of internal purification and dispassion— he [should perform action] as previously [stated].

Even for one who is an agent of action, tranquility—consisting precisely in the renunciation of all actions—is declared to be the means to be practiced as the instrument for the ripening of knowledge. //3//
Viśvanātha:

Now, one might object that for a practitioner of the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yogin), the yoga of action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) would thus be required for as long as one lives. Anticipating this doubt, he states its limit with the words "for the seeker" (ārurukṣoḥ).

For a sage—a practitioner of yoga—who desires to ascend to yoga, meaning the yoga of unwavering meditation (niścala-dhyāna-yoga), action is said to be the means for that ascent because it effects the purification of the mind.
Then, for one who has ascended to the yoga of meditation (dhyāna-yoga), tranquility (śama)—the cessation of all distracting activities—is the cause for attaining steadfastness in meditation.
Thus, one who desires to ascend to yoga must be devoid of such [external] purification of the mind. //3//

Baladeva: If it is argued that, in this way, the performance of ritual action would follow for one practicing the eightfold yoga as long as life lasts, he says "for one who desires to ascend" (*ārurukṣoḥ*) in response.

For a sage (*muni*), one who practices yoga, who desires to ascend to yoga—that is, to the state of steadfastness in meditation (*dhyāna-niṣṭhā*)—action is the cause, because it effects purification of the heart. For that same person once they have ascended to yoga—that is, for one steadfast in meditation—the cause for its firmness is tranquility (*śama*), which is the cessation of distracting actions. //3//
For when one is attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, having renounced all volitional thoughts, then one is said to have ascended to yoga. (6.4)
Śrīdhara: What kind of person is this "one established in yoga" (yogārūḍha) for whom tranquility (śama) is said to be the cause?
To this, he says: "When...

When one does not become attached—that is, when one does not form an attachment—to the objects of the senses, which are the things to be enjoyed by the senses such as sound and so forth, nor to the actions that are the means to those [objects].

In this regard, the cause [of being established in yoga] is as follows: he whose nature it is to renounce—that is, to abandon—all volitions concerning objects of enjoyment and objects of action, which constitute the root of attachment;
at that time, he is said to be "established in yoga" (yogārūḍha). //4//
Madhusūdana:
It is said that one becomes established in yoga when—

when, at which time of mental concentration— one [remains] with respect to the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, and with respect to actions, whether obligatory, occasional, optional, worldly, or prohibited.

He does not become attached to them; because of his vision of their false nature and his vision of his own self as non-agent, non-enjoyer, supreme, blissful, and non-dual, he possesses the realization that there is no purpose [in such attachment] and thus does not form the kind of persistent clinging characterized by the thought, "I am the doer for these people" or "these are my objects of enjoyment.
Indeed, for this reason, he is one who has renounced all volitions—that is, all thoughts of the form, "This must be done by me."

One who is habituated to the renunciation of those specific mental fluctuations in the form of "this fruit must be enjoyed," as well as the desires directed toward them and the actions that serve as their means—

then, due to the absence of attachment to sound and other objects, to actions, and to the volition that causes them (all of which obstruct the ascent to yoga), such a person is said to have ascended to yoga, being "one who has ascended to yoga" (*yogārūḍha*), meaning one established in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Viśvanātha:
But one whose mind is perfectly purified and who has ascended to yoga states the characteristic that indicates this [state], beginning with "when":
regarding the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, and regarding actions, which are the means for accomplishing those [objects]. //4//

Baladeva says: He states the sign that indicates one has ascended to yoga with the words "When... When, being a connoisseur of the nectar of the Self, one does not become attached to the objects of the senses—such as sound and so forth—nor to the actions that serve as their means, the reason for this is "all... [meaning all desires].

He is one whose nature it is to renounce—that is, to completely abandon—all objects of enjoyment and all volitions regarding the sphere of action, which have their root in the notion of "I-ness" (asmitā). //4//
One should uplift oneself by means of the self; one should not degrade the self. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. (6.5)

Śrīdhara: Therefore, having reflected that liberation results from abandoning attachment to sense objects while bondage results from attachment to them, one should abandon the nature of passion and the like; thus he says, "one should uplift.
With one's own self endowed with discernment (*viveka*), one should uplift oneself from the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*);
one should not, however, cause oneself to sink—that is, one should not lead oneself downward.

For it is the self alone that, when restrained from attachment to the mind and other such things, is the benefactor and friend of one's own self; and [the self] is the enemy and the doer of harm. //5//
Madhusūdana:
When one has thus become established in yoga, then by that very self one has been uplifted from the multitude of evils of saṃsāra;
therefore, [the Lord says] "one should uplift oneself."
With one's own mind endowed with discernment (*viveka*), one should lift up— that is, draw upward— one's own self, the individual soul (*jīva*) submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
The meaning is that, by abandoning attachment to sense objects, one should bring about the state of being established in yoga (*yogārūḍhatā*).
But one should not let oneself be exhausted by attachment to sense objects, nor cause oneself to sink into the ocean of saṃsāra;

for it is the self alone that is the friend of the self—the benefactor and the cause of liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra—and no other whatsoever. This is because even a worldly kinsman, due to the persistence of affection, becomes a cause of bondage;
therefore, the self alone is [the friend], and no other.
A certain enemy is one who, by causing entry into the prison of sense objects—which are devoid of true enemies—acts like a silkworm for oneself;
because even an external enemy is employed by oneself, the restriction is appropriate: "The self alone is the enemy of the self. //5//
Viśvanātha:
Since the self has fallen into the well of saṃsāra solely through attachment to the objects of the senses, one should lift it up with effort;
that is, one should uplift the self—the living soul—with a mind that is free from attachment to sense-objects.
One should not cause oneself to sink—that is, one should not cast oneself into the well of saṃsāra—with a mind attached to sense objects;
therefore, the self is indeed the friend, and the mind itself is the enemy. //5//
Baladeva: He says "one should lift up" (*uddharet*) as the reason for non-attachment to the objects of the senses and so forth.

One should lift up—that is, draw upward—one's own self, which is the living soul (*jīva*), that has sunk into the well of *saṃsāra* due to the mind being attached to sense-objects; one should do so by means of the self, that is, by means of a mind free from attachment to sense-objects.
One should not cause the self to perish—that is, one should not cause it to sink—by means of a mind attached to sense-objects.
Indeed, as a certainty, it is not thus: the self alone, the mind alone, is the kinsman of the self; that very same [mind] is its enemy. And the Smṛti says:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, the mind leads to bondage; free from sense objects, the mind leads to liberation. (5)
The self is the kinsman of that person by whom the self has been conquered by the self; but for one who has not conquered the self, the self would act as an enemy, like an actual foe. (6)
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "Of what kind of person is the self alone the friend, and of what kind of person is the self alone the enemy?", he says: "The friend...
For one by whom the self—consisting of the aggregate of causes and effects—is conquered and brought under control, for such a self, the self alone is the friend.
But for one who is not self-controlled and lacks self-mastery, the very self acts as an enemy toward itself, like an enemy, by causing harm. //6//
Madhusūdana:
Now, it is said that "the self is the friend" and "of what characteristics is the enemy of the self?

By whom has the self—the aggregate of the body and the instruments of action—been conquered and brought under its own control? It is by the self alone, through a mind endowed with discrimination, and not by means of weapons or the like.
One's own self is one's own friend because, by refraining from unrestrained activity, it brings about one's own welfare;
however, for one who has not conquered the self— that is, for one whose self is unsubdued—
one's very self would behave like an enemy in its state of enmity.
Because, through unrestrained activity, one performs for oneself what is undesirable by means of oneself, just like an external enemy. //6//
Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry, "Whose friend is he? Whose enemy is he? he says, "A friend... and so forth.
By whatever self—that is, by whatever living being—the self has conquered the mind, for that living being, that self is a friend to the mind.

But for one who is not a self—that is, for one who has not conquered the mind—the self, which is the mind itself, would act like an enemy, existing as an adversary in its capacity to cause harm. //6//
Baladeva: In response to the inquiry, "Of what kind is he a friend? Of what kind is he an enemy?", he says, "A friend.
For one by whom the self—the mind itself—has been conquered through the individual soul (jīva), that self, the mind, is the friend of that soul, acting for its benefit.
But for the soul that lacks self-mastery and has not conquered its mind, the mind itself acts as an enemy—just like an external foe—in terms of hostility, that is, in causing harm. //6//
For one who has conquered the self and is serene, the Supreme Self is fully concentrated amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor. (6.7)
Śrīdhara: He clarifies the state of being a kinsman to one who has conquered the self by saying "of the one who has conquered the self" (*jitātmanaḥ*).

For one by whom the self is conquered—that is, for one who is tranquil and free from passion and the like—it is only that supreme Self which remains composed and established in its own nature even when cold, heat, and other such conditions exist; this is not the case for anyone else.
Or rather, the Supreme Self remains concentrated and established within his heart. //7//

Madhusūdana explains the state of one who has conquered the self (*jitātman*) as being a true kinsman through the words "of one who has conquered the self. This refers to one who maintains equanimity even when cold and heat, pleasure and pain—factors that cause distraction of the mind—are present, as well as when honor and dishonor, or respect and contempt, which are causes of mental distraction, occur. It means remaining equal amidst these.
Or rather:

for one who has conquered the self as previously described, who has mastered the senses, who is tranquil, whose intellect is equal toward all things and who is free from attachment and aversion, the Supreme Self—the Self whose nature is self-luminous knowledge—becomes concentrated;
that is, it becomes the object of samādhi for him who is established in yoga.
Alternatively, there is a division [of the compound] as "param" (supreme).
Only for one who has conquered the self and is tranquil does the supreme, absolute Self become concentrated, and not for anyone else.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should become both self-conquered and tranquil. //7//
Viśvanātha:
Now, he shows the signs of one who has ascended to yoga through three verses.

For the yogi who has conquered the self—that is, whose mind is mastered—and who is tranquil, being free from passion and other such afflictions, the self becomes supremely, that is, exceedingly, composed and established in samādhi.
Even when cold and other such conditions are present, and even when honor and dishonor are encountered. //7//
Baladeva: With three verses beginning with "jita," he describes the state suitable for the commencement of yoga.

For one who has conquered the self—that is, whose mind is unchanging—toward cold, heat, and so forth, as well as toward honor and dishonor; who is tranquil and free from passion and other such afflictions; his *ātman* becomes exceedingly well-composed, established in *samādhi*. //7//

One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realized wisdom, who is steadfast, has conquered the senses, and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same, is called a yogi who is disciplined. //8//

Śrīdhara: Having established the characteristics and the excellence of one who has ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*), he concludes with the verse beginning "jñāna-". One whose self—that is, the mind—is satisfied by and free from further longing for both *jñāna* (knowledge acquired through instruction) and *vijñāna* (direct, immediate experience), is therefore *kūṭastha*, meaning changeless.
Therefore, he is one by whom the senses have been conquered;
therefore, he is one for whom clods of earth and other such things are equal.
He is devoid of the notion of what is to be rejected or accepted regarding lumps of clay, stones, and gold.
He is called one who is disciplined and established in yoga. //8//
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth:

"knowledge" is the instructional knowledge of the categories of reality as taught in the scriptures; "realized knowledge" (*vijñāna*) is that which has as its fruit the removal of doubts concerning the invalidity of that [instructional] knowledge.

Likewise, by means of reflection (*vicāra*) and through their own direct experience (*svānubhava*), one makes them manifest; he whose self (*ātman*) and mind (*citta*) have become satisfied by these two and have developed the conviction of "enoughness" (*ālamb-pratyaya*) is such [a person].
He is the immutable (*kūṭastha*), devoid of modification even in the presence of objects.
Therefore, he is one by whom the senses have been conquered, having been turned away from the grasping of sense objects preceded by attachment and aversion.

For that very reason, because he is devoid of the notion of what is to be rejected or accepted, he for whom a lump of clay, a stone, and gold are equal is called a yogi, a wandering mendicant of the highest order (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka), one endowed with supreme dispassion, and one who has ascended to yoga. //8//
Viśvanātha:
He whose self (ātman)—that is, his mind—is satisfied by and free from desire for both knowledge (*jñāna*), which is instructional, and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), which is immediate experience;
who is immutable (*kūṭastha*), remaining pervasively at all times through a single nature because of non-attachment to all things.
He for whom clods of earth and other such things are equal;
a *loṣṭa* is a lump of clay. //8//
Baladeva: "By knowledge," etc.

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is that which arises from the scriptures; realized knowledge (*vijñāna*) is the experience of the distinct Self. One whose self is satisfied by these two is one whose mind is full.
"Immovable" (*kūṭastha*) means established at all times through a single, unchanging nature.

Therefore, one who has conquered the senses, because he is established solely in the Self which is by nature secluded from the material world, [views] common objects such as clods of earth; "loṣṭa" means a lump of clay.
Such a yogi, a performer of action free from desire, is said to be "yukta," fit for the practice of yoga consisting in the realization of the Self. //8//
One who possesses an even mind toward friends, companions, enemies, the indifferent, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen, as well as toward the virtuous and the sinful, is preeminent. (6.9)
Śrīdhara: But one who possesses an even-mindedness toward friends, enemies, and others is superior even to that; thus he says, "A friend" (*suhṛd*).
A friend is one who by his very nature desires one's welfare;
a well-wisher (*mitra*) is one who renders assistance through the power of affection.
An enemy is a killer;
a neutral person is one who remains indifferent even toward two parties in conflict;
a mediator is one who desires the welfare of both parties in their dispute.
One who is detested is the object of hatred;
a kinsman is a relative;
the virtuous are those of noble conduct.
They are evil and of wicked conduct;
however, he whose intellect is equal toward them—being devoid of attachment, aversion, and the like—is indeed distinguished. //9//
Madhusūdana:
He says "a friend" (*suhṛt*) to show that one who possesses equal intelligence toward friends, enemies, and others is the best among all yogis.
A "friend" (*suhṛt*) is one who benefits others without regard for a return favor, and without prior affection or a [specific] relationship.
A friend is one who benefits out of affection;
an enemy is one who inflicts harm through natural cruelty, regardless of any harm he himself has suffered;
and a neutral person is one who remains indifferent toward both parties engaged in a dispute.
One who stands in the middle is a seeker of the welfare of both disputing parties.
An enemy is one who inflicts harm in consideration of a wrong done by oneself.
A kinsman is one who renders assistance by virtue of a relationship.

Among these—among the virtuous who perform what is enjoined by the scriptures, among the sinful who perform what is prohibited by the scriptures, and by the word "and" (ca), among all others as well—one who possesses an even mind, whose intellect is not preoccupied with the question of who is doing what kind of action, and who is free from attachment and aversion toward everything, is distinguished; he becomes superior in all respects.
Alternatively, the reading is "he is liberated" (vimucyate). //9//
Viśvanātha:
A *suhṛt* (well-wisher) is one who desires one's welfare by his very nature;
a *mitra* (friend) is one who acts for one's benefit through some form of affection.
An enemy is one who kills;
a neutral person is one who remains indifferent toward two contending parties;
a mediator is one who desires to resolve the dispute between two contending parties.
One who is hateful is so because of being a wrongdoer and thus deserving of hatred;
a kinsman is one who is related;
the virtuous are those who possess righteousness.
The wicked are unrighteous;
however, one who maintains an even mind toward them is distinguished.
Indeed, he is superior even to one who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal. //9//
Baladeva says: "A friend" refers to one who possesses an equal mind toward friends and others;
such a person is distinguished from, and indeed superior to, even a yogi who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
In this context, a "well-wisher" (suhṛt) is one who desires one's welfare by their very nature;
a "friend" (mitra) is one who acts for one's benefit out of some affection; and an "enemy" (ari) is one who, due to the absence of friendship, desires one's harm.
One who is indifferent and impartial toward two disputing parties is a mediator, seeking to resolve their dispute. One who acts with hostility is "deserving of hatred" because of his harmful intent.
A kinsman is one who desires one's welfare through their relationship;
the virtuous are those who are righteous, while the wicked are those who are unrighteous. //9//
The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline the self. (6.10)

Śrīdhara: Having thus stated the characteristics of one who has ascended to yoga (*yogārūḍha*), he now prescribes the yoga along with its ancillaries for that person, by means of the text beginning with "The yogi" and ending with "that yogi is considered supreme.
Here, "the yogi" refers to one who has ascended to yoga;
"himself" refers to the mind (*manas*).
One should apply oneself; that is, one should practice with concentration, constantly and without interruption,
while remaining in a secret, solitary place.
Solitary and free from attachment,
whose mind, self, and body are restrained and controlled,
he is without desire and without longing.
Non-grasping is also empty of grasping. //10//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus described the characteristics and the fruit of one who has ascended to yoga, [the Lord] prescribes the yoga with its constituent parts through twenty-three verses beginning with "The yogi... and ending with "...he is considered the supreme yogi.
In that context, the word "yogi" is used for the attainment of such a supreme fruit.

The yogi who has ascended to yoga should constantly and uninterruptedly yoke the self—that is, the mind—by abandoning the states of the distracted (*kṣipta*) and the agitated-distracted (*ūḍha-vikṣipta*), and instead making it concentrated through the states of one-pointedness (*ekāgra*) and restraint (*nirodha*).
Remaining alone in a secluded place such as a mountain cave, free from wicked people and other obstacles to yoga, having renounced all household ties and attendants, he is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*).
He is one whose mind and body (*yata-cittātmā*) are restrained, meaning his internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) and physical frame are devoid of activities that obstruct yoga.

Since he is free from longing due to the firmness of his dispassion (*vairāgya*), he is likewise without possessions; that is, he is devoid of even those objects permitted by the scriptures which would otherwise obstruct his yoga. //10//
Viśvanātha:
Now, with the verse beginning "The yogi," he prescribes Yoga along with its ancillaries. From the words "that yogi is considered supreme" onwards, [it is said]:
the yogi, one who has ascended to Yoga, should yoke the self—the mind—meaning he should make it endowed with meditative absorption (samādhi). //10//
Baladeva: Now, with twenty-three verses beginning with "The yogi," he teaches him yoga along with its ancillaries.
A "yogi" is one who performs actions free from desire.
He should constantly, day after day, "yoke" the self—that is, the mind—meaning he should bring it into union through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He stands in a secret, solitary, and noiseless place;
even there, he is alone, devoid of a second; even there, his mind and body are restrained—that is, his mind and body are controlled and free from activities unfavorable to yoga;
and because he is free from desire, through firm dispassion, he is without longing for anything else.
Non-possessiveness is the absence of food. //10//
Having established a firm seat for himself in a clean place— neither too high nor too low, covered with kusha grass, a deerskin, and a cloth, each placed over the one before it (6.11).
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, let him sit upon his seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self. //12//
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the rule for the seat, he says with two verses beginning with "In a pure place" (*śucau*).
Having established his own seat in a clean location, what kind [of seat]? Firm, meaning immovable.
Neither too high— that is, not excessively elevated— nor too low;
[this refers to] *cela*, meaning a garment.
*Ajina* refers to the skin of a tiger or similar animal. Regarding the phrase "when *cela* (cloth) and *ajina* (skin) follow after *kuśa* (grass)":
the meaning is that one should spread the skin upon the *kuśa* grass, and then spread the cloth upon that [skin]. //11//
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): having sat down there on that seat, one should practice yoga—that is, one should train—having made the mind one-pointed and free from distraction.
One whose activities of the mind and the senses are restrained or controlled (*yatāḥ*) [should do so] for the purification and pacification of the self, which is the mind. (12)
Madhusūdana:
Regarding that, showing the rule for the seat (*āsana*), he says in two verses beginning with "in a pure place" (*śucau deśe*).
"Pure" means naturally or through refinement (*saṃskāra*) clean, devoid of crowds of people, and free from fear—such as on the banks of the Gaṅgā, in caves, and so forth.

Having established it in a suitable place, steady and motionless—neither too high, nor too tall, nor too low—covered with cloth, antelope skin, and kusha grass: "cloth" (*caila*) means soft fabric; "antelope skin" (*ajina*) means the soft hide of a tiger or similar animal; "and those [skins] are above the kusha grass" (*kuśottara*) means that which has them as its uppermost layer. It is called a "seat" (*āsana*) because one sits upon it; the meaning is that there is a soft hide upon a mat made of kusha grass, and upon that, a soft garment.
And thus the Blessed Patañjali said: "Posture is that which is steady and comfortable.
The word "of the self" is intended to exclude other seats, because even those are subject to the will of others and are therefore conducive to the distraction of yoga. //11//
Having thus established the seat, what should one do? To this he says: "There, with one-pointed [mind].
There, having sat down upon that very seat—and not lying down or standing—because of the principle that "one who is seated is capable."

One whose activities of the mind and senses are restrained—meaning one by whom the functions and fluctuations of the mind and the senses have been controlled—being thus one whose mental and sensory activities are restrained (*yata-cittendriya-kriya*), should practice (*yuñjīta*) yoga, that is, meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For what purpose? For the purification of the self (*ātma-viśuddhaye*), so that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) may become fit for the direct realization of Brahman through its extreme subtlety when it is free from all distractions.
As the Śruti says: "But it is seen by those who perceive the subtle with a sharp and subtle intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12).

Having done what should one practice yoga? To this he says: having made the mind—one-pointed, meaning endowed with a continuous stream of multiple mental modifications directed toward a single object by abandoning the three previously mentioned stages known as the rajasic, tāmasa, and vyutthāna, and consisting of intensified *sattva*—and having accomplished this through effort established on a firm ground, one should practice yoga, that is, *samprajñāta-samādhi*, for the sake of increasing one-pointedness.
And that very stream of mental modification (mano-vṛtti) in the form of Brahman is what is called nididhyāsana. As it has been said:
"The stream of mental modification in the form of Brahman, devoid of egoity (ahaṅkṛti), becomes samprajñāta-samādhi through the excellence of the practice of meditation (dhyāna)."

Intending this very point, the Blessed One prescribed the excellence of the practice of meditation many times, saying: "The yogi should constantly apply himself" (Gītā 6.10), "One should practice yoga for the purification of the self" (Gītā 6.12), "Being disciplined, one should sit with me as the supreme goal" (Gītā 6.14), and so forth. //12//
Viśvanātha:
*Pratiṣṭhāpya* means having established or placed;
*celājina-kuśottaram* means a deer-skin seat upon a seat of *kuśa* grass.
The meaning is that one should place a cloth seat upon that.

This is because when one's own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is purified—being free from distraction and exceedingly subtle—it becomes fit for the direct realization of Brahman, according to the Vedic scripture: "But it is seen by the highest intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12). //11–12//
Baladeva says: He describes the seat with two verses beginning with "In a pure place" (*śucau*).
In a pure place—pure both by its own nature and through refinement—such as on the bank of the Ganges, on a mountain, or in a cave; it should be firm and motionless, neither too high nor too low.

Having established and settled a seat made of wood or similar materials that is not too low— wherein the cloth, the deerskin, and the kusha grass are placed in ascending order; "cloth" (caila) refers to a soft garment.
*Ajina* refers to the skin of a soft deer or similar animal;
the meaning is that one should spread a cloth over the *kuśa* grass.
The use of the word "one's own" (*ātmanaḥ*) is to exclude a seat belonging to another, because a seat intended for someone else is indeterminate [in its purpose] and thus unfavorable to yoga.
"In that place" means having sat down upon that established seat, and not while standing or lying down; this is the meaning.
Thus the author of the Sūtra says: "He should be seated, because it is possible" (VS 4.1.7).

He whose mental activities, such as thought and so forth, have been restrained—having made his mind one-pointed and undisturbed—should practice yoga; he should cultivate meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for the purification of the self, that is, the internal organ. This is for the sake of attaining the fitness for the vision of the Self through extreme clarity and subtlety, according to the scriptural teaching: "But it is seen by those who perceive the subtle with a sharp and subtle intellect" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12). //11-12//
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the quarters; 13.
With a tranquil self, free from fear, established in the vow of celibacy, having restrained the mind, with his thoughts fixed on Me, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me as the supreme goal. 14.
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the practice of one-pointedness of mind for those who possess a body, he says "evenly" in two verses.
By "kāya," the middle part of the body is intended.
"Kāya-śiro-grīvam" is a compound meaning the body, the head, and the neck.
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending to the tip of the head, holding [the breath] evenly, descending,
immovable,
and steady.
The meaning is: "having become firm and resolute in effort.
"Gazing at the tip of one's own nose" means with eyes half-closed.
The connection with the following verse is: "one should sit without looking here and there toward the various directions. //13//
"Tranquil" means one whose self and mind are tranquil; one from whom fear and dread have departed.
Abiding in the vow of celibacy— that is, established in the practice of brahmacarya—
having restrained the mind, that is, having withdrawn it,
he whose consciousness is fixed on Me alone.
He for whom I alone am the supreme goal of human endeavor is "one who has Me as the supreme" (mat-paraḥ).
Having become thus disciplined, he should sit—that is, remain—steadfast. //14//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus described the external seat for that purpose, it is now stated how the body is to be maintained therein, beginning with the words "samaṃ" (even).
"Kāya" refers to the middle of the body, and together with the head and neck, this constitutes "kāya-śiro-grīvam"; [this posture] begins from the *mūlādhāra*.

Holding [the body] level, straight, motionless, and unwavering up to the very top of the head, one should— by means of the practice of a single reality (eka-tattvābhyāsa)— bring about the absence of one-pointedness (ekāgratā) which is a limb characterized by the coexistence with distraction; having become steady and firm in effort,

furthermore, one should gaze at the tip of one's own nose for the sake of being free from lethargy and distraction, meaning that one is devoid of engagement with sense objects and has eyes that are not closed.

Not looking at the directions, yet occasionally casting glances toward the quarters because that would be an obstacle to yoga—being thus situated, he sat; this is the connection with what follows. //13//

Furthermore, regarding the term *praśāntātmā*: he whose inner organ (*ātman*), which is the mind, is profoundly tranquil—meaning it is free from defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like by way of the cessation of their causes—is one whose self is tranquil. Because of the firmness of his scriptural certainty, fear has departed;
he whose suspicion regarding what is appropriate or inappropriate has vanished through the renunciation of all actions is one who is "free from fear" (*vigatabhīḥ*).

Remaining established in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), such as in the service of the guru and the eating of alms-food; having restrained the mind by making it devoid of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) directed toward sense objects;

one whose mind is fixed on Me—the Supreme Lord, the inward-facing Consciousness, whether with attributes (*saguṇa*) or without attributes (*nirguṇa*)—is "one whose mind is fixed on Me" (*mac-citta*), possessing a continuous stream of mental modifications directed toward Me.

If one were to think of a son or other such beloved objects, how could this state be achieved? To answer this, he says "devoted to Me" (*mat-paraḥ*). Because I am the supreme bliss, I am the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) who is dear; one for whom I am thus dear is so designated.

This is in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal than all else" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.8).
Thus, by means of the cessation of all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) that take the form of sense objects,
one who possesses the cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) characterized by a mental fluctuation focused solely on the Blessed One should sit or remain seated according to his capacity;
the meaning is that he should not rise at his own will.
There may be someone who is full of passion and whose mind is fixed on a woman, yet he does not perceive her alone as the supreme object of worship;
rather, he perceives a king or a god as such.
However, this person—one whose mind is fixed on Me and who regards Me as the supreme—considers Me alone to be the object of all worship. This is the explanation of the authors of the Bhāṣya.
Even though I am a commentator, I cannot be equated here with the author of the Bhāṣya;
for can a guñjā seed ever be equal to gold, even when both are placed on the same scale? (14)
Viśvanātha:

Holding the body—the middle part of the torso—straight, level, and motionless, having restrained and withdrawn the mind, with his thoughts fixed on Me, contemplating Me as the four-armed one of beautiful form, he is intent on Me, being devoted to My bhakti. //13-14//
Baladeva says: He describes the method for maintaining the body of one seated upon that seat with the word "evenly" (*samam*).
"The body" (*kāya*) refers to the middle portion of the trunk;
and "body," "head," and "neck"—the collection of these three forms a compound because they are parts of a living being.
Maintaining [the body] evenly, straight, immovable, and unshaking;

becoming steady with firm effort, one should gaze at the tip of one's own nose— meaning that, for the sake of ceasing mental dissolution and distraction, one should have one's vision fixed between the eyebrows.
Without looking around at the directions from time to time—being thus situated—he sat; this is to be connected with what follows. "With a tranquil self" means one whose mind is undisturbed.
Free from fear, he is fearless; established in the vow of celibacy, he remains steadfast in the practice of brahmacarya;
having restrained his mind, he has withdrawn it from sense objects.
With his mind fixed on Me, meditating upon Me as four-armed and of beautiful limbs, intent on Me alone with Me as his sole goal, he is a disciplined yogi. (13–14)
Thus constantly yoking the self, the yogi of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in nirvāṇa and is established in Me. 15.
Śrīdhara: He states the fruit of the practice of yoga with the words "yuñjann evam" (thus practicing).
Thus, in the manner described, one who is always practicing yoga—that is, making the mind (*ātman*) concentrated—possesses a restrained and controlled mental faculty (*mānasa-citta*).
One attains peace, which is the cessation of saṃsāra;
of what nature is it?
It is that in which the supreme goal, nirvāṇa, is attained.
Established in me, abiding in my own form.
Madhusūdana:
It is now stated what happens for one who sits in this way through *samprajñāta-samādhi*, beginning with the words "yuñjan" (while joining).
Thus, while joining the self—that is, the mind—in accordance with the previously mentioned rules such as staying in solitude, by means of both practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Making the mind concentrated, the yogi who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga— being one whose mind is restrained by means of an excellence of non-existence (*abhāva-atiśaya*), or rather, being one whose mental fluctuations in the form of modifications are restrained and controlled— attains peace, which consists in the cessation of all fluctuations, a state of tranquil flow culminating in *nirvāṇa*, by way of the arising of the direct realization of reality.

He attains the final state established in Me— which culminates in liberation consisting of the cessation of ignorance along with its effects— and which is of the nature of the supreme bliss that is My own essence;
he does not, however, attain worldly powers, which are the fruits of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) directed toward objects other than the Self.

Because these are obstacles (*upasarga*) to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that leads to liberation (*apavarga*). Accordingly, after describing the various fruits of those respective absorptions, the Blessed Patañjali said: "These are obstacles in absorption, but they are accomplishments (*siddhi*) in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)" (Yoga Sūtra 3.37), and also: "Upon being invited by celestial beings dwelling in their respective stations, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest undesirable consequences follow" (Yoga Sūtra 3.51).
The gods are the presiding deities (*sthāninaḥ*).

Thus, although Uddālaka was invited by the gods, he did not show them respect, nor did he feel attachment, pride, or arrogance; instead, disregarding the gods, he entered a state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpaka-samādhi*) once more in order to prevent the recurrence of undesirable circumstances—so it is related by Vasiṣṭha.

And this samādhi, which is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), was aphorized by Patañjali: "Cognitive (*samprajñāta*) samādhi follows upon the forms of coarse discernment (*vitarka*), subtle discernment (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*)" (Yoga Sūtra 1.17). That by which the nature of the object of meditation is correctly (*samyak*)—that is, free from doubt, error, and indecision—known thoroughly (*prakarṣeṇa*) in its specific form, is cognitive samādhi.
For meditation (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated placement of the mind upon the object of meditation by means of abandoning other objects.
The object of cultivation (*bhāvya*) is threefold, distinguished as the grasped (*grāhya*), the grasping (*grahaṇa*), and the grasper (*grahītṛ*).
The grasped is also twofold, distinguished as gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*).

As it has been said: "For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) consisting of the identification with that [object], and the absence of its own nature, within the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped—just like a gem of pure birth" (Yoga Sūtra 1.41).

For that mind whose Rajasic and Tamasic fluctuations have been exhausted, "steadfastness" (tat-sthatā) refers to one-pointedness upon those very objects— the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped— which are the self, the senses, and their objects.
This means being colored by them (tad-añjanatā), becoming absorbed in them (tan-mayatā), and the excellence of that which is being cultivated once the mind has become subsided.
A meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of such a kind;
just as a noble, stainless crystal gem assumes various forms by virtue of its proximity to various objects,
so too the mind, being stainless, assumes various forms through its coloring by various objects of meditation— this assuming of various forms is meditative attainment.
"Samādhi" is also a synonym.

Although it was stated [in the verse] as "regarding the censurer, the grasping, and the graspable," nevertheless, by virtue of the sequence of stages (*bhūmikā-krama*), it should be understood as "regarding the graspable, the grasping, and the grasper.
For concentration first becomes established upon the graspable, then upon the grasping, and finally upon the grasper.
The sequence beginning with the grasper (grahītṛ) will also be explained further on.

In that regard, when meditation is performed by taking as its object a gross thing consisting of the sixteen transformations— the great elements and the sense organs— and by means of connecting the preceding and following [moments] and by the mental articulation of words and their meanings, then that is *samādhi* with deliberation (*savitarka*).

When meditation proceeds by resting upon this very [object], being devoid of the mental verbalization of words and meanings through the synthesis of the preceding and the succeeding, then it is *nirvitarka* (without coarse discrimination).
Both of these are designated here by the term *vitarka*.
Having taken as its object a subtle domain characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consisting of that [subtle element] alone—its...
When meditative cultivation proceeds with the delimitation of place, time, and attributes, it is "with deliberation" (savicāra).

When meditative cultivation proceeds upon that very same object without the delimitation of place, time, and attributes, appearing as the mere substrate (dharmin) alone, it is "without deliberation" (nirvicāra).
Both of these states are here designated by the term "deliberation" (vicāra).
And thus the Bhāṣya states: "Vitarka is the coarse application of the mind toward an object; vicāra is [the application] toward a subtle [object].
This is designated as the meditative attainment of the grasped (grāhya-samāpatti).
When the sattva of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is permeated by even slight traces of rajas and tamas...

When that [sattva] is cultivated, because the power of consciousness (cic-chakti) has become subordinate, there arises for the one cultivating it a samādhi characterized by the predominance of sattva—which consists of bliss and light—and which bestows self-bliss.

Those whose fortitude is fixed in this very samādhi do not perceive any other principle in the form of *pradhāna* or *puruṣa*; because they are free from the ego-identification with the body, they are called "bodiless" (*videha*).
This is the perfection of apprehension (*grahaṇa-sampatti*).

Thereafter, when meditation proceeds by taking as its object pure *sattva*— which is not overwhelmed by even a trace of *rajas* or *tamas*— that *samādhi* is called "with self-consciousness" (*sāsmita*), because in that state the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), which is *sattva*, has become subordinate, while the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) predominates, leaving only pure existence.
Nor should one suspect that there is no difference between *ahaṅkāra* (egoism) and *asmitā* (I-am-ness).
For where the internal organ perceives objects through the manifestation "I am this," that is *ahaṅkāra*.
But where, due to an inward-turning and inverse transformation, mere existence alone shines forth in the mind as it dissolves into *prakṛti*, that is *asmitā*.
Those who find satisfaction in this very samādhi, not seeing the Supreme Person because their minds have dissolved into *prakṛti*, are called "those absorbed in *prakṛti*" (*prakṛti-laya*).
This is the attainment of the grasper (*grahītṛ-samāpatti*), because it culminates in the grasper whose nature is pure egoity (*asmitā-mātra*).

However, for those who, having discriminated the Supreme Puruṣa, proceed toward meditative cultivation, their discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) which has the isolated Puruṣa as its object is indeed a "grasping attainment" (*grahītṛ-samāpatti*), yet it is not a "I-am-ness" (*sāsmita*) samādhi,
because through discrimination, *asmitā* is abandoned.

In that state, the manifestation of the instrument of perception (*grahaṇa*) is preceded by the manifestation of the perceiver (*grahītṛ*), and the manifestation of the subtle objects of perception is preceded by that.
And preceded by that, there is the appearance of the gross object of apprehension; thus, the first type of vitarka, having a gross object, is accompanied by all four [mental factors].
The second type of vitarka, being devoid of vicāra, is accompanied by three.
The third type, being devoid of both vitarka and vicāra, is accompanied by two.
The fourth [stage] is devoid of vitarka, vicāra, and ānanda, and consists of asmitā alone; thus, this samprajñāta [samādhi] has four stages.

In this way, samādhi accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, and asmitā—being the cause of powers such as invisibility—is contrary to the samādhi that is the cause of liberation, and therefore it should be abandoned by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu).

Furthermore, since the subject (grahītṛ) and the instrument of perception (grahaṇa), at the time they are objects of mental modification (citta-vṛtti), are included within the category of the object (grāhya), the author of the Sūtras has explained only the "object-samāpatti" (grāhya-samāpatti) in order to describe the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.
For the attainment of the apprehended object (*grāhya-samāpatti*) is fourfold: that which has the gross apprehended object as its domain is twofold—namely, with vitarka and without vitarka;
and that which has the subtle apprehended object as its domain is also twofold—namely, with vicāra and without vicāra.

In that regard, "the meditative attainment mixed with conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge" (Yoga Sūtra 1.42) means that the *savitarka* attainment is one in which there is an appearance of a gross object, being permeated by conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge; its meaning is that it is a determinate mental modification (*savikalpaka-vṛtti*) having a gross thing as its domain. "When memory is purified, [the mind], as if empty of its own form, has the appearance of the object alone—this is the *nirvitarka* [attainment]" (Yoga Sūtra 1.43). In that [state]:

Thus, when the recollection of the word and its meaning has dissolved regarding a gross object, there arises the *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), which has as its field the gross; this means it is a non-conceptual mental mode (*nirvikalpa-vṛtti*) whose essence is as if empty because the aspect of knowledge is subordinated by the manifestation of a clearly arisen form of the perceived object. By this very [attainment], the *savicāra* (discursive) and *nirvicāra* (non-discursive) attainments having subtle objects are explained [Yoga Sūtra 1.44]; "subtle" refers to the *tanmātras* and so forth.

That meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which has a subtle object is of two kinds: with deliberation (*savicārā*) and without deliberation (*nirvicārā*), distinguished by being conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
By this very [explanation] of the gross-object attainment—both with and without discursive thought—it is explained.

That attainment in which a subtle object appears, accompanied by the conceptualization of word, meaning, and knowledge, and delimited by place, time, qualities, and so forth, is "with deliberation" (*savicārā*).

By specifying that the states with subtle objects (*sūkṣma-viṣayatva*) pertain to those with and without subtle reflection (*sa-vicāra* and *nirvicāra*), it is implied that the states with gross objects (*sthūla-viṣayatva*) pertain to those with and without discursive thought (*sa-vitarka* and *nirvitarka*). Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the state of having subtle objects culminates in the unmanifest" (*Yoga Sūtra* 1.45), the subtle objectivity described for both the *sa-vicāra* and *nirvicāra* attainments extends as far as the unmanifest (*aliṅga*).
This must be understood.

Therefore, the meaning is that the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) of the "with-joy" (*sānanda*) and "with-I-am-ness" (*sāsmitā*) stages are also included within the absorption of the "object" (*grāhya-samāpatti*).
For instance, the subtle object of the earthly atom (*pārthiva-aṇu*) is the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*).
From water comes the subtle element of taste; from fire, the subtle element of form;
and from air, the subtle element of touch.

From space arises the subtle element of sound; from these [subtle elements] arises the ego (ahaṅkāra); from that arises the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), which is the mere indicator (liṅga-mātra); and from that too arises the Unmanifest (aliṅga), the Pradhāna, which is the subtle object.
Since the state of subtlety for all seven constituent natures (prakṛtis) finds its ultimate rest in the Pradhāna alone, it is said that the range of subtle objects extends only as far as that.

Although the *puruṣa* is subtler even than the *pradhāna*, nevertheless, because it lacks the status of being an inherent cause (*anvayi-kāraṇa*), its unsurpassed subtlety is explained as residing only in the *pradhāna*, which is the inherent cause of all things.
The *puruṣa*, however, even though it is an instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), does not deserve to be considered subtle by virtue of being a non-inherent cause.

However, when one intends to express that [the self] is a concomitant cause (*anvayi-kāraṇa*), it should be understood that the person (*puruṣa*) also indeed becomes subtle. "Those very [attainments] are seeded concentration" (Yoga Sūtra 1.46). These four attainments (*samāpatti*) exist together with the seed which is the object of perception; thus, they are "seeded concentration. As was stated previously, this is called "cognitive concentration" (*samprajñāta*) because it is accompanied by coarse reflection (*vitarka*), subtle reflection (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*).
With regard to a gross object, there is *savitarka* and *nirvitarka*;
with regard to a subtle object, there is *savicāra* and *nirvicāra*.
Among these, the fruit of the last is stated: "When there is lucidity (*vaiśāradya*) in *nirvicāra*, there is inner serenity (*adhyātma-prasāda*)" (Yoga Sūtra 1.47).

Although they are equal in having gross objects as their domain, the *nirvitarka* [samādhi], which is free from the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of words, meanings, and cognitions, is primary compared to the *savitarka*, which is intermingled with them.
Following that is the *savicāra*, which has subtle objects as its domain and consists of the appearance of conceptual construction (*savikalpaka-pratibhāsa*).
Even more than that, there is the predominance of the non-discursive [samādhi], which has a subtle object and consists of non-conceptual appearance.
In that regard, because the first three have non-discursiveness as their goal, they possess fruit only through the fruit of non-discursiveness.
But for non-discursiveness itself, when there is proficiency through the power of intense practice, there is an increase of *sattva* unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*.

When there is inner clarity (*adhyātma-prasāda*), for a mind free from the latencies of the afflictions (*kleśa-vāsanā*), there arises a clear light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*) that has the true nature of reality as its object and does not follow a gradual sequence.
And so it is said in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*):

"Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, free from sorrow, looks down upon all grieving people as one standing on a mountain peak looks upon those on the ground. Thus it is said: "In that state, wisdom bears the truth" (Yoga Sūtra 1.48). In that state—when that clarity of wisdom has arisen—the wisdom that is born for the yogi whose mind is concentrated is called "bearing the truth" (*ṛtambharā*).
It sustains only the *ṛta* and the *satya*; since there is not even a trace of error therein, this is designated as "yogic.
And that is the supreme yoga.
Thus says the Bhāṣya:
"By means of scripture, inference, and the savor of the practice of meditation, one who cultivates wisdom in these three ways attains the supreme yoga.
This [wisdom], however, has a different object from the wisdoms of hearing and inference, because it pertains to specific particulars (viśeṣa). [Yoga Sūtra 1.49]
Scriptural knowledge (*śruta*), which consists of the cognition of traditional authority (*āgama*), has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object;
for it is impossible to grasp the connection of any word with a particular (*viśeṣa*).
Likewise, inference (*anumāna*) has only the universal as its object.
For it is not possible to apprehend the pervasion (vyāpti) of anything with a particular (viśeṣa).
Therefore, no particular exists as an object of either perception or inference.
Nor is there the apprehension of such an entity—subtle, concealed, or remote—by means of worldly perception (loka-pratyakṣa).
However, that distinction— whether pertaining to the subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma*) or to the *puruṣa*— is to be grasped only by concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the yogi must exert great effort toward that very wisdom known as "truth-bearing" (*ṛtambharā*), which arises from proficiency in the state beyond deliberation (*nirvicāra-vaiśāradya*), which is distinct from what is heard or inferred, and which has as its object all distinctions, whether subtle, concealed, or remote.

[Objection: But surely, since the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the emergent states known as the "distracted," "infatuated," and "occasionally distracted" exist even during one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*), and since there also exist the latent impressions produced by "with-discursive-thought" (*savitarka*) and "without-discursive-thought" (*nirvitarka*) and "with-deliberation" (*savicāra") states, how could the "truth-bearing" wisdom (*ṛtambharā prajñā*)—which is attained through internal clarity preceded by the "mastery of deliberation-free" state—be established in a mind that is being agitated by those impressions? To this, he says: "The impression born from that [wisdom] obstructs other impressions. (Yoga Sūtra 1.50)

The impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that *ṛtambharā* wisdom— being powerful due to its being generated by wisdom whose object is reality— obstructs other impressions born of the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) as well as those born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because they are weak, being generated by wisdom whose object is not reality; it renders them incapable of their own effects, or rather, destroys them.
Through the overcoming of those formative forces (saṃskāra), the conditions arising from them no longer occur;
from that, concentration (samādhi) is established,
and from that, wisdom born of concentration (prajñā).

Then, because the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are produced by wisdom (*prajñā*), the accumulation of formative forces increases ever anew; and from that, wisdom arises; and from that, the formative forces arise once more.

Now, it may be granted that there is an obstruction of the *saṃskāras* of emergence—which are produced by the wisdom (*prajñā*) whose object is not reality—by the *saṃskāras* arising from *samprajñāta-samādhi*, whose object is reality alone; however, since there would be no such obstructing factor for those [other] *saṃskāras*, there would be only seeded (*sabīja*) samādhi on the level of one-pointedness (*ekāgra-bhūmi*), and not seedless (*nirbīja*) samādhi on the level of cessation (*nirodha-bhūmi*). To this, he says: "Upon the cessation of even that... (*tasyāpi nirodhe*).

"From the cessation of all [modifications], there is seedless concentration" (Yoga Sūtra 1.51). This refers to that cognitive (*samprajñāta*) concentration which belongs to the stage of one-pointedness.

By the force of the word "also," when even the distracted, infatuated, and occasionally distracted states are ceased—that is, dissolved—through a specific effort of the yogi, then from the cessation of all [mental modifications], because even the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of concentration is ceased, there arises the seedless, objectless *asaṃprajñāta* concentration.

And that [samādhi], along with its means, was previously aphorized: "The other [samādhi] is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation (virāma-pratyaya) and consists of residual latent impressions" (Yoga Sūtra 1.18).
"Cessation" (virāma) is so called because one ceases by means of it; it is the abandonment of thought characterized by reasoning, reflection, bliss, and egoism.
Its "cognition" (pratyaya) is its cause, which is to say, supreme detachment (para-vairāgya).

Or, it is that which is both a cessation (*virāma*) and a mental modification (*pratyaya*), meaning a specific state of the mind's fluctuations. Its practice is the repeated instillation [of this state] into the consciousness. That whose primary cause is precisely this is such [a state]; it remains as mere latent impression (*saṃskāra-mātra-śeṣa*). It is entirely free from fluctuations and is different from the previously mentioned "seeded" (*sabīja*) state; it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*).
This means "cognitive absorption" (*samprajñāta-samādhi*).

For it has been stated that there are two means for the non-cognitive absorption (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*): practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). Since practice possesses an objective support (*sālambanatva*), it cannot logically serve as the cause for an objectless absorption; therefore, only supreme dispassion, which is itself objectless, is declared to be the cause.
Practice, however, is useful by way of the indirect path through *samprajñāta-samādhi*.
As it has been said: "The triad is internal compared to the preceding ones" (Yoga Sūtra 3.7).

This triad of means consisting of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* is internal to the seeded (*sabīja*) samādhi when compared to the fivefold set of means consisting of *yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, and *pratyāhāra*.
The means of accomplishment;
and within the category of the means of accomplishment, it is practice alone that is expressed by the word "concentration" (samādhi),
because concentration in its primary sense is that which is to be accomplished.
Even that is external to the seedless [samādhi] (Yoga Sūtra 3.8).
However, for the seedless samādhi, even those three are external, assisting only indirectly; the meaning is that for it, supreme detachment alone is internal.
This [seedless samādhi] is also of two kinds: that which has existence as its cause and that which has means as its cause.
"Existence is the cause for those who are merged in the bodyless and in primordial nature" (Yoga Sūtra 1.19).

For the "bodyless" (*videha*), who are accompanied by bliss (*sānanda*), and for those "merged in primordial nature" (*prakṛtilaya*), who are accompanied by the sense of "I" (*sāsmita*)— as previously explained— the concentration (*samādhi*) that arises from a particular birth, a particular herb, a particular mantra, or a particular austerity is "caused by existence" (*bhavapratyaya*).
"Bhava" refers to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); it is that whose cause is a cognition (*pratyaya*) consisting in the absence of discrimination between the self and the non-self.
Alternatively, it may mean that which has mere birth as its cause, like the flight of birds through the sky.
The meaning is that, because it is the cause of further cyclic existence, it is to be abandoned by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
[The samādhi] of others is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom (Yogasūtra 1.20).
For those who perceive the distinction between the self and the non-self—excluding those perfected through birth, herbs, mantras, or austerity—their samādhi is preceded by faith.
That is to say, it is that for which faith and the other qualities are the preliminary means.
The meaning is "the condition of skillful means.
Faith in those [means], regarding the object of yoga, is clarity of mind;
for she protects the practitioner like a mother.
Then, for one who possesses faith and seeks discernment, vigor—enthusiasm—is born.
For one in whom vigor has arisen, mindfulness emerges regarding the subsequent stages.
And through that mindfulness, the mind, being undisturbed, becomes concentrated.
In this context, *samādhi* is one-pointedness of mind.
For one whose mind is concentrated, wisdom arises through discernment, having the objects of cultivation as its domain.
Through the practice of that, and subsequently through dispassion, the *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive) *samādhi* occurs for those seeking liberation; such is the meaning.

According to the principle that "all entities undergo transformation at every moment except for the power of consciousness," even during that state where all mental modifications (*vṛtti*) have ceased, there continues to exist a flow of mental transformations and a flow of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by them; with this in mind, the term "specific latent impression" was used. Furthermore, the purpose of that latent impression has been stated: "From that latent impression comes the flow of tranquility" (Yoga Sūtra 3.10).

The state called "tranquil flow" (*praśāntavāhitā*) is the subsiding of the non-returning mind through a reverse transformation, like a fire without fuel. Just as a fire blazes up with ever-increasing intensity when offerings of wood, clarified butter, and so forth are cast into it, yet subsides slightly in its very first moment upon the exhaustion of that wood and other materials; so too does the mind subside.
However, in each successive moment, [the afflictions] subside more and more; thus, tranquility increases by degrees.
Likewise, for one whose mind has been suppressed, an ever-increasing calm flows forth.
In this regard, the very formation (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding calm is the cause of each subsequent calm.

And then, like a fire without fuel, the mind gradually subsides and dissolves into its own primordial nature along with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence, meditative absorption, and cessation. At that time, when ignorance has ceased through right vision (*samyag-darśana*) born from the Vedāntic statements—which arises from the ripening of meditative absorption—the conjunction between the seer and the seen, which is caused by that ignorance, no longer exists. Consequently, when even the fivefold activity of the mind has ceased, the person, established in his own true nature, is called pure, solitary, and liberated.
Thus it has been said: "Then there is the establishment of the seer in its own nature" (Yoga Sūtra 1.3).
This refers to the state when all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) have ceased.
