However, during the state of fluctuation, although the self is eternally pure by virtue of its nature as consciousness—which is permanent and unchanging—it is nonetheless [associated with impurity] due to beginningless [ignorance].

Through association with the visible object, which arises from ignorance, there occurs an illusory identification (adhyāsa) of the Self with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); thereby attaining a conformity with the modifications (vṛtti) of the internal organ, the Self, though not an actual enjoyer, becomes as if an enjoyer of sufferings.
As it has been said: "There is a conformity with the modification in the other [the Self]" (Yogasūtra 4.22).
In other cases, when its activity manifests;

this very point is explained in detail: "The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object" (Yoga Sūtra 4.23). The mind itself, colored by the seer and the seen, appearing as both subject and object, having assumed the nature of both conscious and unconscious, becomes identical with the objects.
Although its nature is objectless, as if insentient, and though it is insentient, it is said to be like a crystal gem, capable of all objects.
Because of this similarity to the mind, some are deluded and say that this [Buddhi] itself is sentient.
Although variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another, because it functions through combination [Yoga Sūtra 4.24].

That for whose sake there is enjoyment and liberation is that very Supreme Conscious Being (*cetana*), the uncomposite *puruṣa*; the meaning is that the mind (*citta*) is not conscious, as it acts through composite aggregation like a jar or other objects.

And thus, for one who perceives this distinction, there is the cessation of the identification with the self-nature [of the internal organ], according to Yoga Sūtra 4.25: "Thus, for one who perceives the distinction between the internal organ and the *puruṣa*, that identification with the self-nature which previously existed in the internal organ due to the power of non-discrimination ceases. Thus, for him who perceives the distinction between the internal organ and the *puruṣa*, whatever identification with the self-nature had previously existed in the internal organ by virtue of non-discrimination...
That [ignorance] ceases,
because when difference is perceived, the delusion of non-difference cannot arise;
and the perception of the distinction between the *sattva* (the intellect) and the *puruṣa* (the self) is accomplished through desireless action dedicated to the Lord.
And that mark has been shown in the *Yoga-bhāṣya*:

"Just as the existence of a seed is inferred by the sprouting of a blade of grass during the rainy season, so too, when the bristling of hair and the shedding of tears are observed in someone upon hearing the path to liberation due to an inclination toward the established doctrine, there exists therein the seed of the vision of reality."
It is inferred that [such a person] has brought into effect karma pertaining to the path of liberation (*apavarga*).

However, for one who lacks such a seed of karma, upon hearing about the path to liberation, there arises an attraction toward the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and a lack of attraction toward the arguments of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
In such a person, the natural contemplation of the nature of the self—such as "Who was I? How was I?"—proceeds spontaneously.

"But that [mind] ceases for one who perceives the distinction. To the question "What would happen if this were so?", he says: "At that time, the mind is inclined toward discernment and weighted toward isolation" (Yoga Sūtra 4.26). "Inclined" (*nimna*) refers to a low-lying place suitable for the flow of water.
The "pre-disposition" (*prāg-bhāra*) is an elevated region unsuitable for that [flow].

And the mind, like flowing water, always moves in a continuous stream of evolving fluctuations; previously it flowed toward the enjoyment of objects along a wrong path consisting of the non-discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, but now it becomes directed toward the path of discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, culminating in absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).

And regarding this mind flowing toward discernment (*viveka*), those obstacles along with their causes must be removed; thus he says in two sūtras: "In the gaps of that [mind], other cognitions arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Their abandonment is said to be like that of the afflictions" (YS 4.27–28).

In that mind flowing toward discernment, during the gaps or intervals, other cognitions in the form of emergence—such as "I" and "mine"—arise from the latent impressions born of the experience of emergence.
They manifest even while [the aggregates] are decaying;
and for these conditioned phenomena, a process of abandonment has been taught, just as there is for the afflictions.

Just as the afflictions such as ignorance, once their seed-nature has been burnt by the fire of knowledge, do not sprout again upon the ground of the mind, so too the formative predispositions (saṃskāra), their seed-nature having been burnt by the fire of knowledge,
are no longer capable of sprouting through other conditions;
for the predispositions, once consumed by the fire of knowledge, persist only as long as the mind itself endures.

And thus, when the mind has become stabilized, flowing in discernment due to the non-arising of other conditions, there arises for one who is no longer desirous even of *prasaṃkhyāna* the *dharmamegha* samādhi, because of the complete manifestation of discernment (*sarvathā-viveka-khyāti*).
*Prasaṃkhyāna* is the manifestation of the distinctness between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa; that is to say, it is the knowledge of the pure Self.

In that regard, for one who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the sattvic transformation of the intellect, there arises the mastery over all transformations of the *guṇas*, like a sovereign; and the knowledge of them exactly as they are— as they abide in their states of being past (*śānta*), present (*udita*), or unmanifest (*avyapadeśya*)— is the omniscience called "the sorrowless" (*viśokā*), which is the fruit of that [mastery], and from dispassion toward that [fruit]...

And isolation (*kaivalya*) has been described by the two sūtras: "For one whose nature consists solely in the discernment of the difference between *sattva* and the Puruṣa, there arises sovereignty over all states and omniscience" (YS 3.49), and "When the purity of *sattva* and the Puruṣa is equal, there is isolation" (YS 3.55).

This is what is being stated here: even when that higher discriminative discernment (*prasaṅkhyāna*) exists, for one who is not indolent and does not desire its fruit, other mental modifications arise.

When the discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) has reached its full development through every means so that no further [impurities] arise, the "Cloud of Virtue" (*dharma-megha*) concentration occurs.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "Of sacrifices, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts—this is the supreme dharma: the perception of the Self through yoga."

"Dharma-megha" means that which rains or pours down the *dharma*—the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the identity of the individual self and Brahman; the meaning is that it is the cause for the direct realization of reality.
From that follows the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma.

Then, from that "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharma-megha*) samādhi, or from that *dharma*, there is the cessation of the fivefold afflictions: ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to cling to life (*abhiniveśa*).

Furthermore, regarding actions—which are of three kinds, namely black, white-black, and white—since they are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), their absolute cessation occurs through the destruction of ignorance, which is like the destruction of a seed; this results in isolation (*kaivalya*).
The meaning is that the absolute cessation of the effect is appropriate once the cause has ceased.
This being the case, by the phrase "constantly yoking the self," *samprajñāta* (cognitive) samādhi is described as occurring on the stage of one-pointedness (*ekāgra-bhūmi*).
By the phrase "with the mind restrained," its result, *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive) samādhi, is described as occurring on the stage of cessation (*nirodha-bhūmi*).
By the word "peace" (*śāntim*), the state of tranquil flow (*praśānta-vāhitā*)—which is the fruit of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born of the samādhi of cessation—is indicated.

"Having Nirvana as the supreme goal" indicates that the Samādhi of the Cloud of Dharma (dharma-megha) is the cause of absolute liberation (kaivalya) by means of the knowledge of reality; by the phrase "established in Me," the absolute liberation favored by the Upaniṣads is shown.
Since Yoga thus yields such a great fruit, the intention is that one should accomplish it with great effort. //15//
Viśvanātha:
"Yoking the self" means making the mind engaged in the yoga of meditation;
for this reason, one whose mind is restrained is one whose consciousness has withdrawn from sense objects.

One attains that peace, which is the cessation of saṃsāra, in which there is perfect abiding in me alone—the non-differentiated Brahman—wherein Nirvāṇa, liberation itself as the supreme goal, is attained. //15//
Baladeva: To explain what happens for one who remains thus seated, he says "yuñjan" (while engaging).
The yogi, constantly—that is, every day—engaging or offering himself [to Me];
"niyata-mānasaḥ": one whose mind (*mānasa*), that is, whose consciousness (*citta*), is restrained or steady due to being purified by contact with Me.
One attains—that is, obtains—peace whose highest point is *nirvāṇa* and which is dependent on me, under my control;
for it is heard in such passages as: "Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death" (ŚvetU 3.8).
Since it is said that even the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are fruits of yoga, [this peace] is characterized as having *nirvāṇa* as its ultimate limit, meaning it culminates in liberation. //15//
But yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all; nor for him who is habituated to excessive sleep, O Arjuna, nor for him who is ever awake. 6.16
Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "Not by overeating," he states the rules regarding food and so forth for one intent on the practice of yoga.
Yoga, which is samādhi, does not occur for one who eats excessively, nor for one who abstains from eating entirely.
Likewise, yoga does not exist for one who is habitually over-sleeping or over-wakeful. (16)
Madhusūdana:
Thus, with two verses beginning with "Not by overeating" (*nātyaśanataḥ*), he states the rules regarding food and so forth for one who is steadfast in the practice of yoga.

That food which, when eaten, is digested and brings about the body's capacity for action is "food measured to one's own self" (*ātma-saṃmitam annam*). For one who, transgressing that limit out of greed, eats excessively, there is no yoga due to the defect of indigestion (*ajīrṇa-doṣa*).
Because one is afflicted by disease;
and for one who does not eat at all, yoga is not possible,
because through lack of food or from eating too little, the body becomes incapable of its functions due to the absence of nourishment from the bodily fluids (*rasa*).

"Indeed, that food which is commensurate with one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more harms; and that food which is less does not protect," according to the Śatapatha-śruti (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 9.2.1.2).
Therefore, the meaning is that the yogi should not eat more or less than food commensurate with his own self.
Alternatively—
One should fill half [the stomach] with food, but a third with water;
however, one should leave the fourth part empty for the movement of the wind (vāyu).
The meaning is that for one who eats more or less than the quantity prescribed in the Yoga scriptures and so forth, yoga is not accomplished.
Likewise, for one who is excessively prone to sleep or excessively wakeful, there is no yoga at all, O Arjuna; the intention is that you must be heedful.
As it is said in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
O King of kings, a yogi seeking his own perfection should practice yoga when he is neither bloated with food, nor hungry, nor exhausted, nor of distracted mind.
"One intent on meditation should not practice yoga at times that are too cold, nor too hot, nor when there are dualities [of heat and cold], nor when accompanied by wind," and so forth. //16//
Viśvanātha:

He states the rule for one devoted to the practice of yoga in two verses beginning with "not from over-eating" (*nātyaśanataḥ*). For one who eats excessively—that is, one who consumes more than is proper—as it has been said:
"One should fill half [the stomach] with food, but one-third with water;
however, one should leave the fourth part remaining for the movement of the vital air. //16//
Baladeva says: With two verses beginning with "Not too much," he states the rules for eating and so forth for one practicing yoga:
namely, overeating and not eating enough, as well as excessive sleep and excessive wakefulness.
And excessive wandering about and so forth, which are contrary to yoga, [are abandoned] by means of the subsequent [limb]. //16//
For one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in performing actions, and moderate in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering. (6.17)

Śrīdhara: If so, for one of what nature does yoga arise? To this he says: "yuktāhāra" (one whose food and recreation are regulated). One whose food (*āhāra*) and recreation (*vihāra*), which is movement (*gati*), are regulated (*yukta*)—that is, disciplined (*niyata*).

He whose activity in actions and duties is disciplined and regulated, and whose sleep and waking are likewise disciplined and regulated—for him, yoga becomes the remover of suffering; it succeeds. //17//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus stated the absence of yoga for one who lacks the regulation of diet and so forth, he states the presence of yoga for one who possesses that regulation, beginning with "yuktāhāra" (one whose food is regulated).
That which is brought in is "āhāra," meaning food.
*Vihāra* is wandering, which is the movement of the feet; he is one for whom those two are disciplined and of fixed measure.
Likewise, he is one whose activity in other rites—such as the chanting of the *praṇava*, the recitation of the *upaniṣads*, and so forth—is disciplined and performed at fixed times.
Likewise, for one in whom sleep and waking—dreaming and consciousness—are both regulated by fixed times, yoga occurs.
Through proficiency in the means of practice, self-concentration (*ātma-samādhi*) is accomplished, but not for anyone else.
To the question of what the fruit of yoga is when it has been thus perfected through specific methods of application, he says: "It is the cause of the destruction of suffering."

The meaning is that, because it generates the knowledge of Brahman (brahma-vidyā), which is the cause for uprooting the ignorance that is the cause of all the sufferings of saṃsāra, it is the cause for the cessation of all suffering along with its root.
In this regard, there is a fixed rule for food:
one half for solid food with its condiments, and a third for water.
However, one should leave the fourth [channel] remaining for the purpose of the movement of the vital air (vāyu).
This and more was stated previously.

Regarding the fixed nature of one’s dwelling, it means one should not go elsewhere due to the practice of yoga, and so forth. Regarding the fixed nature of activity in ritual actions, it means the abandonment of fickleness of speech and other such behaviors.
Having divided the night into three parts, one should remain awake during the first and last portions and sleep in the middle; thus, there is a fixed time for sleeping and waking.
In this same manner, other rules mentioned in the Yoga-shastra are to be observed. //17//
Viśvanātha:

For one whose food—eating—is disciplined and regulated, and whose movement—walking—and whose activities—both worldly transactions and ultimate spiritual duties—are likewise disciplined and regulated, as are his physical exertions and verbal operations;
for such a person [the following applies]. //17//
Baladeva: It is appropriate.

For one who is moderate in diet and recreation, whose speech and other activities are moderate in worldly and transcendental duties, and whose sleep and wakefulness are moderate, yoga becomes the destroyer of all suffering;
therefore, the yogi conducts himself in such a manner. //17//
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone,
free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be "yoked" (in yoga). //18//
Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "When does a person become one whose yoga is perfected?", he says, "When...
When the mind, being thoroughly restrained and specifically stilled, remains motionless within the Self alone;
and furthermore, when one becomes free from longing—that is, devoid of thirst—for all desires, meaning for enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next.
Then, being liberated, he is said to have attained yoga. //18//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus described *samprajñāta-samādhi* on the stage of one-pointedness (*ekāgra-bhūmi*), he begins to explain *asamprajñāta-samādhi* on the stage of cessation (*nirodha-bhūmi*) with the words "when" (*yadā*).

When—at which time—by the power of supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*), [the mind] becomes specifically restrained, that is, thoroughly controlled, such that it is devoid of all mental fluctuations (*sarva-vṛtti-śūnyatām*).

The mind, having been brought to a state free from passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), consists of the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-sattva*). Although it is capable of assuming the forms of all objects due to its transparency, because its mental modifications (*vṛtti*) have been restrained on all sides, it remains directed toward the Self alone—that is, toward the directly perceived consciousness (*pratyak-citi*) which is uncolored by the non-Self. Even in the absence of mental modification, the form of the Self, being self-established, cannot be removed; therefore, due to the primacy of consciousness itself, the mind becomes subservient.
It remains steady and becomes motionless.
At that time, during the cessation of all mental fluctuations, one is said to be "yoked" or "concentrated.
Who is this? It is he who is free from longing for all desires.

One whose longing and thirst for all objects of sense—whether seen or unseen—have departed through the perception of their defects is said to possess supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*), which is the internal means for *asamprajñāta-samādhi*.
This has been explained previously. (18)
Viśvanātha:
In response to the inquiry as to when a yogi becomes one whose yoga is perfected, he says, "When...
The meaning is that the mind, being thoroughly restrained and suppressed, abides in the Self—that is, in itself alone—and becomes motionless. //18//
Baladeva: In response to the inquiry as to when a yogi becomes one whose yoga is perfected (*niṣpanna-yoga*), he says, "When...

When the mind of the yogi practicing yoga is thoroughly restrained—that is, when being suppressed, it becomes steady, remaining fixed solely within itself, the Self—then, being devoid of all longing for anything other than that Self, he is called "yoked" (*yukta*), meaning one whose yoga is perfected. //18//
As a lamp placed in a windless spot does not flicker— this is the simile remembered for the yogi of restrained mind who practices the yoga of the Self. (6.19)
Śrīdhara: He provides an analogy for the mind that abides in the form of identity with the Self, beginning with "yathā" (just as).
Just as a lamp placed in a windless place does not flicker—that is, it does not waver—that is the simile, the illustrative example.
Of whom? Of the yogin who is practicing, who is applying yoga directed toward the Self.
He whose mind is restrained—that is, controlled—and is unwavering due to its steadiness and luminosity; the meaning is that his mind remains established in that state. //19//
Madhusūdana:
He provides a simile for the mind that has attained cessation (*nivṛtti*) in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), saying "just as":
just as a lamp situated in a place free from wind—the cause of flickering—does not waver or move due to the absence of any cause for movement; so too [the mind].
That is considered a simile; it is conceived as an illustration by those who know yoga.

Of whom? Of the yogi who possesses the cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) on the stage of one-pointedness, whose mind is restrained through proficiency in practice, and who applies himself to yoga—characterized by non-cognitive concentration (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*)—on the stage of cessation, wherein all mental fluctuations have been suppressed.

The meaning is that for one who practices [yoga], the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is the self (*ātman*)—is like a steady lamp because of its immobility, its predominance of *sattva*, and its luminosity.

In the alternative explanation, "one who joins the self in yoga" (*ātmano yogaṃ yuñjate*), there is no obtainment of the illustrandum (*dārṣṭāntika*); furthermore, since the mind would always have the form of the self in every state, the word "self" (*ātma-pada*) would be redundant.
For it is not that the mind’s state of having the self as its form is produced by yoga;
rather, the state of having the non-self as its form is simply removed from that which already exists naturally with the self as its form.
Therefore, the word "self" is used solely for the purpose of establishing the point of the analogy.
"Of one whose mind is restrained" (*yata-cittasya*) is an expression referring to the state [of being restrained] or a *karmadhāraya* compound; the meaning is "of a restrained mind. //19//
Viśvanātha:

A lamp situated in a windless place—that is, standing in a sheltered spot—does not flicker; it does not move. That very lamp is the simile (*upamā*), meaning "exactly as it is. The sandhi here is according to *so 'ci lope cet pāda-pūraṇam* [Pāṇini 6.1.134].
To the question "Of what is this a simile?", he says: "of the yogin.
Baladeva comments: In response to the inquiry as to what kind of yogin he becomes at that time, he says "as follows":
"Just as a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker, does not move, but remains steady with its light—just so is the simile remembered and contemplated by those who know yoga."
Regarding the word *sopamā* here, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) is derived from the rule *so 'ci lope cet pāda-pūraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.134).
By the term *upamā*, the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is to be understood.
To the question "Of what?", he says: "Of the yogin."

For one whose mind is restrained and all mental fluctuations have ceased, who is engaged in and practicing the yoga of meditation upon the Self—such a yogin of awakened knowledge, with all other mental fluctuations stilled, becomes like a steady lamp in a windless place. //19//
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, finds rest;
and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction in the Self alone. //20//
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; //21//
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. //22//
One should know that disjunction from the conjunction with suffering is designated as Yoga;
that Yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency. (23)
Śrīdhara: In passages such as, "That which they call renunciation (saṃnyāsa), know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava" (Gītā 6.2), it is action itself that is expressed by the word *yoga*.
However, in passages such as, "But for one who eats too much, there is no yoga" (Gītā 6.16), it is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is expressed by the word *yoga*.

In response to the inquiry as to which among these is the primary *yoga*, [the Lord], defining meditative absorption itself both in terms of its essential nature and its fruit, states in the three and a half verses beginning with "Where... that this alone is the primary *yoga*.
In that particular state wherein the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, becomes quiescent—this is stated as the essential definition of yoga.
Accordingly, the Pātañjala Sūtra states: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (YS 1.2).
Furthermore, it defines that very same yoga by means of its result, characterized by the attainment of the desired goal.
And in which specific state,
with a pure mind, he sees only the Self and not the body and so forth;
and seeing [the Self] in the Self alone, he finds contentment.
But not toward sense objects.
The connection with the fourth verse—"one should know that [state] designated as yoga"—is made through the relative pronouns beginning with "where" (*yatra*).
He states the reason for contentment within the Self alone by saying "happiness" (*sukham*).

In which particular state one experiences that certain, unsurpassed, absolute, and eternal bliss—surely, since there is then no connection between the sense objects and the senses, how could there be bliss? To this he replies: it is "beyond the senses," meaning it transcends the connection between the sense objects and the senses.
It is to be grasped solely by the intellect itself in the form of the Self;
and for this very reason, wherever it may abide, it does not deviate from the true nature of the Self in reality. //21//
He establishes its very immovability with the words "yam" and so forth:
having obtained that gain which consists of the bliss of the self, one does not consider any other gain to be superior to it,
because that alone is unsurpassed bliss.
And established in which [state], one is not shaken nor overcome even by great suffering such as cold, heat, and so forth;
by this, the characteristic of yoga should be understood as having the cessation of the undesirable as its fruit. //22//
"Tam" (that) refers to that particular state which is such; one should know that separation from the conjunction with suffering, designated as "yoga," [is what is meant].
By the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*), even sensual pleasure mixed with suffering is included.
One should understand that particular state, designated as "yoga"—that is, denoted by the word "yoga"—in which there is a separation from the conjunction with suffering, even by its mere touch.
Yoga is the union of the individual soul (kṣetrajña) with the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Alternatively, it is called "yoga" by means of a contradictory indication (viruddha-lakṣaṇā)—just as the word "coward" might be applied to a hero—referring specifically to the dissociation from the conjunction of suffering.
The intention is that the word "yoga," when applied to action (karman), is merely figurative (aupacārika), because such action is a means to that [union].
Since yoga is thus of such great fruit, it must therefore be practiced with diligent effort; this is stated in the verse beginning with "that" (tam).
That yoga is to be joined with a mind that is characterized by certainty born from the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, and is free from despondency (*nirveda*).
Despondency is the slackening of effort due to the perception of [practice] as suffering. //23//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus described samādhi in general, he begins to explain *nirodha-samādhi* in detail with the words "wherein" (*yatra*).
"Wherein" means when a particular transformation has arisen through the practice of yoga—that is, through proficiency in the cultivation of yoga—the [mind] is restrained.

Having abandoned one-pointedness, which consists of a continuous flow of mental modifications directed toward a single object, it becomes tranquil like a fire without fuel; through the cessation of all modifications, it undergoes a transformation into a state devoid of activity.
And in that transformation, by means of the internal organ—which consists solely of pure *sattva* unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*—one perceives the Self.
Perceiving the inner consciousness as non-different from the Supreme Self— dense with existence, consciousness, and bliss, infinite and non-dual—
and realizing it through a mental modification born of the authority of Vedanta, one finds satisfaction in the Self alone, which is dense with supreme bliss,
and not in the aggregate of the body and senses.
Or rather, it does not [occur] elsewhere in that which is to be experienced;
for when the vision of the Supreme Self exists, because there is an absence of any cause for dissatisfaction, one indeed becomes satisfied.
That transformation of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-pariṇāma) consists in the cessation of all mental fluctuations (sarva-citta-vṛtti-nirodha).
The connection with the subsequent [phrase] is "one should know yoga";
however, the explanation "wherein the time" is incorrect because of the lack of syntactic connection with that word (*tat*). //20//

He states the reason for contentment in the Self alone with the word "happiness" (*sukham*). In which particular state? In that state where there is the nature of Brahman—absolute, infinite, unsurpassed, beyond the senses, not manifested by the contact of objects and the senses, and graspable by the intellect alone, that is, by an intellect free from the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*.
The yogi knows—that is, experiences—the bliss carried by the flow of pure *sattva* alone;
and established therein, this wise one does not at all deviate from the true nature of the Self.
"One should know that [state] as designated 'yoga'"—the connection with the subsequent clause is the same.
In this context, "absolute" refers to the statement of the essential nature of the bliss of Brahman;
"beyond the senses" serves to exclude sensory pleasure,
because that depends upon the conjunction of objects and the sense organs.

The phrase "to be grasped by the intellect" (buddhi-grāhya) excludes the bliss of deep sleep, because in deep sleep the intellect is dissolved; whereas in meditative absorption (samādhi), that intellect exists in a state free from mental modifications (nirvṛttika). As Gauḍapāda has said: "In deep sleep it is dissolved, but when restrained, it is not dissolved."
And so it is heard:
"The bliss that arises when the mind, its impurities shaken off by meditative concentration, is established within the Self."
"At that time, that which is grasped by the internal organ cannot be described by speech"—
this means [it is grasped] by the internal organ when all its fluctuations have been restrained.

However, the Gauḍācāryas have prohibited the tasting of pleasure through mental activity (*vṛtti*) therein: "One should not taste pleasure there; one should be free from attachment through wisdom (*prajñā*).
This "tasting of pleasure" is wisdom in the form of a conceptual mental activity (*savikalpa-vṛtti*), such as thinking, "I am experiencing this great bliss in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Because it takes the form of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and is thus an obstacle to meditative absorption, the yogi should not perform it.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should abandon attachment to such a form of discernment and restrain it.

However, the experience of the bliss of one's own true nature by means of a mind free from mental activity has been demonstrated by them [the Buddhists] through the statement: "The supreme bliss is established in itself, peaceful, and is called Nirvana. This will be made clear further below. //21//
He provides the justification for what was stated— that "he who is established therein does not waver from reality"— with the verse beginning with "having obtained which":

having obtained that particular state of the mind characterized by cessation (*nirvṛtti*) which manifests unsurpassed spiritual bliss, and having brought it to perfection through the ripening of continuous practice, he considers no other gain to be superior to it.
"Whatever was to be done has been done; that which was to be attained has been attained"—for according to the Smṛti, there exists nothing higher than the attainment of the Self.

Having thus stated that there is no wavering from samādhi due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoying sense objects, he says that even for the purpose of warding off disturbances such as cold, wind, and mosquitoes, there is none, because he is established in that particular state of the mind devoid of activity (*nirvṛttika*), which consists of the bliss of the Supreme Self.
The meaning is that the yogi is not shaken even by great suffering, such as the falling of weapons, caused by a powerful enemy; how much less so by a trivial one? //22//

That specific state of the mind, characterized by many qualifiers beginning with "wherein [the mind] comes to rest," which is quiescent and manifests supreme bliss, is called *yoga*. Since this cessation of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*) is opposed to all suffering consisting of mental fluctuations, it is indeed a separation from suffering; thus, even though the word "separation" (*viyoga*) primarily denotes a lack of connection, it is used here through the figure of *virodhi-lakṣaṇā* (indication based on opposition) to signify this very state.
The meaning is that one should know—that is, understand—that which is denoted by the word "yoga," and one should apprehend some kind of relationship in accordance with the term "yoga.
And thus the venerable Patañjali formulated the aphorism: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Yoga Sūtra 1.2).
This concludes what was previously stated in the verse, "Yoga is the destroyer of suffering" (6.17).

In order to prescribe certainty and lack of despondency as the means for such a yoga, he says: "That [yoga] by means of certainty. That yoga, which has the aforementioned fruit, is to be practiced—that is, cultivated—by means of certainty, which is the conviction that the object intended by the words of the scriptures and the teacher is indeed true. It is to be practiced with a mind free from despondency; *nirveda* is the regret [expressed as]: "Even after all this time, the yoga has not been perfected; what could be more painful than this? One should practice with a mind devoid of that.
The meaning is that one should maintain composure with a mind that thinks, "He will attain perfection either in this life or in another birth; why such haste?
Regarding this, the Gauḍapādas have cited: "Just as the overflowing of the ocean [is prevented] by a single drop on the tip of a blade of kusha grass..."
"Likewise, the restraint of the mind should be practiced without weariness.
Here, "utseka" means pouring out or draining; that is to say, the removal of water by means of a channel for drying up.
Regarding this, those who know the tradition relate a narrative.
It is said that the eggs of a certain bird, situated on the shore, were carried away by the force of the waves into the great ocean.
Thereupon, the bird set out with the intent, "I shall surely dry up the ocean," and began tossing up individual drops of water with the tip of his beak.
At that time, although he was being restrained by many birds who were his kinsmen, he did not desist at all.
Although he was dissuaded by Nārada, who had arrived there by chance, he vowed: "In this birth or in another, I shall certainly dry up the ocean by whatever means possible.
Then, through the favor of destiny, the compassionate Nārada sent Garuḍa to assist him, with these words:
"The ocean despises you because of his malice toward your kinsmen."
Then, as the ocean dried up from the wind of Garuḍa’s wings, it became terrified and surrendered those eggs to that bird.
In the same way, when a yogin proceeds toward the supreme dharma through the effortless restraint of the mind, the Lord bestows his grace upon him.
And thus, the sense is that his desired object is accomplished, just like [the movement of] birds. //23//
Viśvanātha:
In the passage beginning with "But for one who eats too much, there is no yoga," the word *yoga* refers to *samādhi*.
And that [samādhi] is both *samprajñāta* (cognitive) and *asamprajñāta* (non-cognitive).
Cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration is of many kinds due to its divisions into those with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
In response to the inquiry as to what the nature of yoga in the form of non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) concentration is, he says "wherein," etc., in three and a half verses.
The meaning is that when this concentration exists, the mind comes to rest; it does not even touch upon the mere object.
In this context, the reason is "ceased" (*niruddham*).
Accordingly, the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ*, YS 1.2).
The connection of the words beginning with "wherein" (*yatra*) and so forth with the fourth [sūtra], "one should know that which is designated as yoga," is as follows.
Seeing the Self by means of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which has taken the form of the Supreme Self (paramātman), one finds contentment in that [Self] and attains the bliss found therein—
that which is known as ultimate bliss.
It is beyond the senses, being devoid of contact with objects and the sense organs.
Therefore, remaining established therein, one does not deviate from the true nature of the Self. Consequently, having attained that gain, one seeks no other gain beyond it.
One does not consider [anything] superior.

One should know that concentration (samādhi) which has attained the designation of "yoga"—that is, the designation of yoga—in which there is separation from even the mere touch of the conjunction with suffering.
Even if it is not accomplished quickly, one should proceed with the certainty: "This yoga of mine will certainly succeed."

With a mind free from despondency—that is, with a mind devoid of the regret that "yoga has not been perfected even after all this time; what more can be gained through further hardship"—[one should practice], thinking:
"May it be perfected in this life or in another birth."
"What haste have I?"—this means with a mind endowed with fortitude.
Regarding this, the Gauḍapādas cited: "Just as the overflowing of the ocean [is caused] by a single drop on the tip of a blade of kuśa grass..."
"Likewise, the restraint of the mind should be carried out without weariness.
Here, "utseka" means pouring out;
that is to say, the extraction of water through the determination to dry it up.
In this regard, there is a certain narrative:
it is said that the eggs of a certain bird, situated on the shore, were carried away by the force of the waves into the great ocean.
Having made the vow, "I shall dry up the ocean," he began to cast up one drop of water at a time with the tip of his beak.
Although he was restrained by many birds who were his kinsmen through various means, he did not desist at all.

Even when forbidden by Nārada, who had arrived there by chance, he renewed his vow before him, declaring, "In this life or in another, I shall surely dry up the ocean. Then, through the favor of destiny, the compassionate Nārada dispatched Garuḍa to assist him.
By the statement, "The ocean despises you because of your hostility toward your kinsmen," the ocean, withering from the wind of Garuḍa’s wings, became terrified and gave those eggs to that bird.

In this very same way, it should be understood that the Blessed Lord alone bestows grace upon a person who is zealous and resolute, engaging in yoga, knowledge, or devotion through faith in the words of the scriptures. (20–23)

Baladeva: In the passage beginning with "Not for one who eats too much," he defines *samādhi*—which was mentioned by the word "yoga"—both in its essential nature and its result, through the three and a half verses beginning with "Wherein" (*yatra*).
The relative pronouns (*yat*) are to be construed with the subsequent phrase, "one should know that to be designated as yoga.

Through the service of yoga—that is, by practice—the mind, whose other fluctuations have been restrained and ceased, comes to rest wherein; it becomes attached to this great bliss, thinking, "This is it."

But it is not by seeing the body and so forth in objects that yoga is shown; rather, through the cessation of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*), yoga is characterized by its own essential nature and by its fruit, which is the attainment of the desired goal.
Regarding the word "happiness" (*sukham*):
in that state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one knows—that is, experiences—that well-known, ultimate, and eternal happiness.
That which is beyond the senses is devoid of the connection between object and sense-faculty; it is to be grasped by the intellect through its own form.
Therefore, wherever it abides, it does not truly deviate from the essential nature of the Self.
That yoga which, once attained, one does not consider any other gain to be superior;
which is not disturbed by the teacher’s loss of virtuous sons and so forth;
and wherein there is the separation—that is, the destruction—of the conjunction with suffering: that is designated as *yoga*.
Samādhi //20-23//

Having completely renounced all desires born of volitional thought without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses from all sides by the mind alone, [he remains established in yoga]. //24//
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word *saṅkalpa*:

having completely abandoned all desires—which arise from mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—that are adverse to yoga, along with their latent impressions (*savāsanā*), and having especially restrained the entire collection of senses that are spreading in every direction by means of the mind alone which perceives the defects in sense-objects; [one should remain].
The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "Yoga is to be practiced. //24//
Madhusūdana:
Furthermore, having done what should yoga be practiced?
Saṅkalpa is the superimposition of attractiveness upon even wicked objects by failing to perceive their lack of beauty.
And from that volition (*saṅkalpa*), desires arise in the form of "May this be mine, may that be mine.

These longings for sense-objects, which originate from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of beauty, are sublated by the ascertainment of their lack of beauty produced through discernment (*vicāra*). Thus, they are like dog-vomited milk-porridge with respect to both seen objects—such as garlands, sandalwood, and women—and unseen objects—such as the world of Indra, the *pārijāta* tree, and the *apsarases*.

Having abandoned by his own effort alone, completely and without remainder, all things including their latent impressions (vāsanās) up to the world of Brahmā; and because the activity of the senses is preceded by desire, when that [desire] has ceased, having restrained with a mind endowed with discernment the entire collection of instruments— the eyes and so forth— that have reached the senses, and having withdrawn them from all objects on every side.
The grammatical construction is: "one should gradually come to rest. //24//
Viśvanātha:
He states the initial and final duties for one engaged in such practice of yoga in two verses beginning with "saṅkalpa.
"Having abandoned desires" refers to the initial duty.
"One should not think of anything at all"—this is the final duty. //24-25//
Baladeva: That yoga should be applied—that is, practiced—with the firm resolve that "if effort is made, it will certainly succeed in its initial stage.
It should be performed with a mind free from despondency—the thought of one's own lack of fitness for yoga—and with enthusiasm, like the bird that dried up the ocean of the cosmic egg.
Regarding one who begins such yoga, he states the first duty: "with resolve," and so forth.
Having completely abandoned those desires for sense objects—which arise from volitional construction and are antagonistic to yoga—along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
the rest is clear:
[he abandons them] by means of the mind that perceives the defects of sense objects. //24//
Gradually, by means of the intellect held with firmness, one should attain cessation;
having established the mind in the Self, one should not think of anything at all. (6.25)
Śrīdhara: But if the mind should waver due to the impressions of past karma, then one should steady it through concentration (*dhāraṇā*); thus he says "gradually" (*śanaiḥ*).
*Dhṛti* means concentration;
by means of that intellect which has been grasped and brought under control by such concentration.
Having made the mind steady and properly established within the Self alone— remaining fixed in the Self— one should come to rest;
and that should be done gradually through the process of practice,
not all at once.
He states the nature of cessation: "One should not think of anything at all.
The meaning is that when the mind is motionless, having become the very nature of supreme bliss shining forth by itself, one should even withdraw from the meditation on the Self. //25//
Madhusūdana says:
One should gradually withdraw [the mind] through the successive stages of victory;
by means of fortitude, steadfastness, and tirelessness—that intellect which consists of the determination that something must necessarily be done—one should grasp it.
Thinking, "Yoga will certainly come about sooner or later; what is the hurry?", one should gradually restrain the mind according to the path taught by the guru.
By this, the previously mentioned non-despair and firm resolve are demonstrated.
And so says the Śruti:
"The wise man should restrain speech and mind; he should restrain those two in the self of knowledge."
"One should restrain knowledge in the Great Self;
one should restrain that in the peaceful Self" (KaṭhU 1.3.13). Thus, one should restrain speech—both worldly and Vedic—in the mind, which is possessed of activity.
"One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech" (BAU 4.4.21); such is the Vedic scripture.
The meaning is that by the cessation of the activity of speech, there should remain only the activity of the mind.
In this state, the cessation of the eyes and other senses is also to be understood.
The lengthening [of the vowel] in *manasi* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage.

That mind (*manas*), which is the instrument (*karaṇa*) that effects the ninefold conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by acting as an auxiliary to both the organs of action and the organs of knowledge, one should restrain within the Knower— the Self (*ātman*)— which, according to the etymology "that which knows in the act of knowing" (*jānāti iti jñānam*), is the locus of the attribute of being a knower (*jñātṛtva-upādhi*), namely,
the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).
Having abandoned the activities of the mind, one should leave behind only the ego (ahaṅkāra).
And that knowledge should be withdrawn into the Great Self—the all-pervading principle of Mahat—which is the ego characterized by the attribute of being a knower.
For the ego is of two kinds: the specific form and the universal form.

The individual ego (vyaṣṭy-ahaṅkāra) is that which conceives itself distinctly, thinking, "I am the son of this person"; the universal ego (samaṣṭy-ahaṅkāra) is that which conceives itself merely as "I am," in its general form.
And that Hiraṇyagarbha is called the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā) because it is woven through all things.

One should restrain the Great Self—the collective intellect (samaṣṭi-buddhi)—within that Peaceful Self which is distinct from those two forms of ego, free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), and whose sole essence is pure consciousness (cid-eka-rasa) dwelling within all.
In this way, one should also restrain its cause, the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Thereupon, the pure Self—the referent of the term "thou" (tvaṃ-pada-lakṣya) free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika)—becomes directly realized.

For when the inner Self (pratyag-ātman), whose sole essence is consciousness, is pure, its limiting adjunct (upādhi) is primordial matter (prakṛti), which is of the nature of an insentient power (jaḍa-śakti), indefinable (anirvācya), and unmanifest (avyakta).
And that [primordial matter], having first assumed the form of the principle called Mahat—which is the universal ego (sāmānyāhaṅkāra)—becomes manifest.
Beyond that, in the form of the specific ego (viśeṣāhaṃkāra); beyond that, in the form of the mind (manas);
and beyond that, in the form of the sense organs, such as speech and the rest.
This very point has been declared by the Śruti: "The objects are indeed superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects;
the intellect is superior to the mind, and the Great Self is superior to the intellect."
"From the Great [Mahat] comes the Unmanifest (avyakta); from the Unmanifest, the Puruṣa is superior.
There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal. (KaṭhU 1.3.10–11).
In this context, the first stage is the restraint of speech, as in the case of [the vow of silence observed by those carrying] cows and so forth.
The second [state] is the absence of mind, as in the case of a child or a simpleton;
the third is the absence of ego, as in the state of lassitude.

Just as in deep sleep, the scripture has cited that principle called the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), which is the material cause of the Great Principle (mahat-tattva) situated between the Great Principle and the peaceful Self.
Nevertheless, the subjugation of the *mahat*-principle (*mahat-tattva*) was not prescribed therein,
because there would be the undesirable consequence of its dissolution into its own nature, as in deep sleep;
and because, upon the exhaustion of karma, that [subjugation] is accomplished by itself without human effort, and thus it would be useless for the vision of reality (*tattva-darśana*).

Having previously stated, "But you are seen by those of subtle vision through a subtle and supreme intellect," [the author] subsequently mentions *nirodha-samādhi* (the samādhi of cessation) in order to establish that subtlety.

This [samādhi] is required as a means of perception for one who desires to see reality (*tattva*), and for one who has already perceived reality, it is required for the destruction of afflictions (*kleśa*) in the form of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
If it is objected: "Since the mind restrained within the peaceful Self is devoid of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), it cannot be a cause of perception, just like deep sleep (*suṣupti*)," we reply: No.
Because it is impossible to negate a perception that is established by its own nature, it has been said:
"The mind, which by its very nature always abides in the forms of both self and non-self,
should be made to establish the view of non-self by means of the singular form of the self."
Just as a jar, while being produced, arises already full of space by its own nature;

whereas the filling with water, rice, and so forth occurs only after the jar has been produced, through the effort of a person. Even when that water and such are removed, it is impossible to remove the space.
Even when the mouth [of a mold] is covered, the space remains within; likewise, the mind, as it arises, arises already filled with consciousness (*caitanya*).

Once it has arisen, however, its form as a jar, suffering, or the like occurs by the power of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) assisted by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes of experience—just like molten copper poured into a mold.

In that regard, even if the non-self-forms such as jars and suffering are warded off through the practice of the cognition of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*), the causeless aspect of consciousness (*cid-ākāra*) cannot be warded off.

Then, by means of the cessation-concentration (*nirodha-samādhi*), through a mind that has ceased its activity and in which only the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) remain, the Self is experienced without obstacle and even without mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), because—due to extreme subtlety—it is directed solely toward the unconditioned nature of consciousness (*cid-ātman*). This is what is meant by the statement: "Having made the mind abide in the Self, one should not think of anything at all. [This refers to] in the Self.

Having made the mind established in the Self— that is, having brought it to rest in the unconditioned inner witness (pratīc) so that it is devoid of all modes of activity and characterized solely by the form of the Self which is established by its own nature— one should, abiding in asamprajñāta-samādhi achieved through the intellect of discrimination held by fortitude,
not think of anything whatsoever, whether non-self or self.

One should not make [the mind] an object through a mental modification (*vṛtti*). For if there were a modification in the form of "non-self," there would be mere emergence from meditation; and if there were a modification in the form of "self," it would be cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*). Therefore, the meaning is that one should not produce any mental modification whatsoever for the sake of stabilizing non-cognitive concentration (*asamprajñāta-samādhi*). //25//
Viśvanātha: See BhG 6.24.

Baladeva: He states the final duty: having made the mind established in the Self by means of an intellect held with fortitude—that is, brought under control through concentration—and having meditated upon the Self, one should cease from activity and remain in samādhi;
one should not think of anything other than the Self.
And this occurs gradually through the process of practice, but not by force. //25//
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. (6.26)

Śrīdhara: Even so, if the mind should waver under the influence of the quality of *rajas*, then one should again bring it under control through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); thus he says, "from whatever [object]...

The mind, by its very nature restless and unstable even when being held steady, goes toward this or that object; from each and every such [object], having withdrawn it, one should make it steady within the Self alone. //26//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, while practicing the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), the yogi— whenever, from whichever cause, such as sound or other objects, or from attachment, aversion, and so forth, his flickering mind is directed toward distraction— [should restrain it].

When the mind wanders outward, being distracted, it produces any one of the fluctuations— right cognition, misconception, conceptualization, or memory— that are contrary to samādhi and directed toward sense objects;

likewise, from whichever among the causes of dullness— such as the remnants of sleep, overeating, fatigue, and so forth— the mind wanders outward, becoming unstable and inclined toward dullness, and once it has become dull, it produces a fluctuation contrary to samādhi.
It produces the mental modification known as sleep;

therefore, having restrained this mind from those various causes of distraction and causes of dissolution, and having rendered it free from modifications, one should bring it under control within the Self alone— which is a mass of self-luminous supreme bliss—
and restrain it so that it is neither distracted nor dissolved.
The word "eva" (only) excludes the possibility that the object of concentration is anything other than the selfless (anātman).
And this has been explained by the venerable Gauḍācārya:
"One should restrain the distracted mind from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures by means of skillful methods."
It is perfectly serene even in dissolution; as is one's desire, so is the dissolution.
Recalling that all is suffering, one should turn away from the enjoyment of sensual desires;
by recollecting that all is unborn, one does not perceive anything as born at all.
One should uplift the mind when it is sluggish and calm it again when it is distracted;
one should recognize it as being affected by passion when it is so, and once equanimity is attained, one should not disturb it.
One should not relish the pleasure therein; being free from attachment, one should become possessed of wisdom.
With effort, one should unify the mind, making it motionless and free from outflow.
When the mind neither dissolves nor is distracted again, being unshakable and free from appearances, then that is the perfected Brahman.
Thus, by means of these five verses:

by the method to be described—namely, through the practice of dispassion—one should restrain the mind that is distracted by the enjoyment of desires and transformed by any one of the mental modifications (vṛtti), such as valid cognition, error, conceptualization, or memory;
the meaning is that one should suppress it within the Self alone.
Regarding "desires and enjoyments," the dual number is used due to the distinction between the state of being contemplated and the state of being experienced.
Likewise, "laya" (dissolution) is deep sleep, because one dissolves into it; even if the mind is very serene and free from exertion therein, one must certainly restrain it.
If it is already very serene, why is it restrained?

Regarding this, he says: Just as desire is an obstacle to samādhi by producing mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as those directed toward sense objects, their magnitude, and so forth, so too is lethargy (*laya*), which is called sleep, an obstacle to samādhi by producing a modification [of that nature].

For samādhi is indeed the cessation of all mental modifications. Therefore, the meaning is that the mind must be restrained from lethargy caused by fatigue and the like, just as it must be restrained from distractions caused by desire and the like.
By what means should one restrain [the mind]?
It is said: by recollecting that all duality is a manifestation of ignorance and is merely a small amount of suffering—[for] "that which is the Infinite (bhūman) is bliss;
there is no bliss in the finite (alpa)."
Now, having reflected upon the meaning of the Vedic scripture— that "what is small is mortal" and "that is suffering"—
following the instruction of the teacher, one should turn away from objects of desire in their state of being contemplated and from objects of enjoyment in their state of being experienced.
The word "from" (*sakāśāt*) is to be understood as "from the mind.
Alternatively, *kāma-bhoga* means desire and enjoyment; one should withdraw the mind from that.
Thus, the meaning is that this is the method for cultivating detachment at the time of recollecting duality.

He states that the forgetting of duality is the supreme means: having immediately after [receiving] the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher recollected that "Brahman is unborn and all; there is nothing whatsoever beyond it," one simply does not perceive the collection of dualities which is its opposite, because that which is imagined in the substratum ceases to exist once the substratum is known.
The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate a distinction from the previously mentioned means.

Thus, if the mind— being turned away from sense objects through both the cultivation of dispassion and the vision of reality— is [distracted] by the force of the habitual practice of daily dissolution (*laya*), [it must be restrained].

When the mind becomes inclined toward dissolution (*laya*), one should properly awaken it through the effort of arousal by means of suppressing the causes of dissolution— namely, sleep, indigestion, overeating, and fatigue.

If, however, while being thus awakened, the mind remains distracted by sensual enjoyments due to the force of its habitual daily practice of awakening, then one should employ the cultivation of detachment (*vairāgya*) and the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).

One should pacify it again. Thus, for one who practices repeatedly, the mind— which has been awakened from lethargy and turned away from sense objects— neither attains equanimity nor remains in a state of intermediate tension, but becomes steady.

One should recognize it as "with impurity" (sa-kaṣāya), meaning it is joined with the defect known as stagnation (stabdhībhāva) caused by the powerful latent impressions (vāsanā) of passion, hatred, and so forth; one should know this through discrimination from the concentrated mind.
Then, having understood that "this is not concentrated," one should restrain the mind from impurity just as one does from lethargy (laya) and distraction (vikṣepa).
And thus, when lethargy, distraction, and impurity have been eliminated, Brahman is attained equally by the mind through what remains.
And one should not disturb that mind which has attained equanimity through the errors of dullness (*kaṣāya*) or lethargy (*laya*),
nor should one direct it toward sense objects.
Rather, with an intellect held by steadfastness, having distinguished [the mind] from the occurrence of lethargy and dullness, one should settle it with great effort in that very state of equanimity.
In that meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even though it manifests supreme bliss, one should not relish that bliss.

One should not produce a mental state consisting of the relishing of bliss—thinking, "I have been happy for this long"—because that would lead to the destruction of the concentration; this has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, the bliss that is perceived by wisdom is also merely false, being conceptually constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*); through such cultivation, one should become free from attachment and desire regarding all forms of pleasure.
Alternatively, one should abandon attachment to wisdom in its form of mental activity consisting of conceptualized pleasure;
however, one should not fail to experience even the bliss of one's own true nature with a mind free from such activity, because that which is attained by its very nature cannot be prevented.

Having thus withdrawn [the mind] from everything and rendered it motionless through the power of effort, one should, as it tends to issue outward toward objects due to its inherent restlessness, unify it with effort as it flows out externally.
Through the effort of cessation, one should lead [the mind] to oneness in the equanimous Brahman.
What is the nature of the mind that has attained equanimity?
It is said: when it neither sinks nor becomes rigid—since the state of rigidity is indicated by the very term "sinking" (laya) due to its similarity to the quality of darkness (tāmasatva).
Furthermore, it is not distracted;
it does not experience the functioning of forms such as sound and so forth,
nor does it relish pleasure.

Because even the tasting of pleasure (*sukhāsvāda*) is characterized by the term "distraction" (*vikṣepa*) due to its similarity to the quality of passion (*rājasatva*), the previous mention of it as a distinct category was for the sake of prescribing a separate effort [to avoid it]. Thus, that which is free from lethargy (*laya*) and turbidity (*kaṣāya*), as well as from distraction and the tasting of pleasure, is "unwavering" (*aniṅgana*). "Wavering" (*iṅgana*) means movement; like a lamp in a windy place, it takes the form of being inclined toward lethargy. That which is free from this is like a lamp in a windless place.
"Non-manifestation" (anābhāsa) means that it does not manifest by way of any objective form whatsoever.
It has already been stated that both "passion" (kaṣāya) and "tasting pleasure" (sukhāsvāda) are included within these two extremes.
When the mind is thus free from the four defects, then that mind becomes the perfected Brahman; the meaning is that it attains the equanimous Brahman.
And such a yoga has been taught by the Śruti:
"When the five [senses] of knowledge stand still together with the mind,
and the intellect does not stir— that they call the supreme goal."
"They consider that steady control of the senses to be yoga;
for at that time one becomes vigilant, since yoga is both the origin and the dissolution.
This very passage is the root of the aphorism: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (Yogasūtra 1.2).
Therefore, it is logical that one should thus bring this [mind] under control within oneself alone, having restrained it from here and there. //27//
Viśvanātha:

Furthermore, if the mind should become restless due to being touched by the quality of *rajas* because of the emergence of past defects, then one should practice yoga once again; thus he says, "From whatever [object]... (26).
Baladeva: He says "yataḥ" (whence) to mean that if the mind should ever waver due to subtle past defects, one should then withdraw it.

Whichever object toward which the mind goes out, from each of those one should restrain and withdraw this mind, and bring it under control within the Self alone through the contemplation of unsurpassed bliss. //26//
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is tranquil, who is pacified of passion, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from taint. (6.27)

Śrīdhara: Thus, by repeatedly bringing the mind under control through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and other means, when the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*) has been exhausted, one attains the bliss of yoga; this is stated in the verse beginning with "praśānta.

In this manner, he whose passion is stilled—that is, he whose mind is perfectly tranquil—and who is thus stainless and has attained the state of Brahman—to such a supreme yogin, the highest bliss, which is the bliss of *samādhi*, comes of its own accord. //27//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, by the power of the practice of yoga, the mind of the yogi becomes tranquil within the Self alone;
and therefore, it is said to be "tranquil."

One whose mind is profoundly stilled—that is, ceased through the absence of active functioning and remains as mere latent disposition (*saṃskāra*)—is one of "calmed mind. Due to the emptiness of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), such a person is "mindless" (*nirmanaska*). Regarding this state of mindlessness, there are two qualifying attributes containing the underlying cause: "one whose passion is stilled" and "stainless.
One whose disturbing passion (*rajas*) has been stilled is one who is empty of distraction.
Likewise, he for whom there is no stain—that is, no darkness (*tamas*) which is the cause of dissolution—is "stainless" (*akalmaṣa*), meaning devoid of dissolution.

By the very phrase "one whose *rajas* has been stilled," *tamas* is also indicated; or alternatively, "stainless" means he is free from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) and so forth, which are the causes of saṃsāra.
Having become Brahman—having attained the equal Brahman through the certainty that "all is indeed Brahman"—this yogi is one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
Śrīdhara explains that "in this manner" means as previously stated;
one attains—that is, approaches—the supreme, unsurpassed bliss.
This refers to the well-known manifestation of the bliss of one's own true nature during deep sleep, when both the mind and its fluctuations are absent.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) serves to illuminate this;
and thus it was explained previously in the passage: "That which is absolute happiness... //27//
Viśvanātha:
And therefore, he says "praśānta" (tranquil) to show that his meditative bliss (*samādhisukha*) shall arise exactly as before;
the bliss, acting as the agent, approaches—that is, reaches—the yogin.
Baladeva: He says "praśānta" (tranquil) to show that for one who strives in this manner, there will be the bliss of samādhi just as before:
"one whose mind is tranquil and unshakable within the Self";
and for that very reason, "stainless," meaning one whose subtle past defects have been burnt away.
Therefore,

the Agent himself approaches the supreme bliss, which consists of the direct experience of the Self, for the yogin who has become tranquil in passion, who has become Brahman, and who has directly realized his own essential nature as manifested with its eightfold qualities (BhG 6.28).
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taint, easily attains the infinite bliss that is the touch of Brahman. 28.

Śrīdhara: And then, he says "yuñjan" (while engaging) to show that one becomes one who has accomplished the goal. In this manner, always engaging—that is, bringing under control—the self, which is the mind, especially with one's whole being.

He whose impurity has departed is a yogi; through ease—that is, without effort—he experiences the contact with Brahman, which is the direct realization that removes ignorance. That itself is absolute bliss; the meaning is that he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta). //28//
Madhusūdana:
The verse beginning with "yuñjan" clarifies the happiness mentioned [previously] for the yogi.
Thus, by the sequence stated in the passage beginning with "manasaivendriya-grāmam," he who always joins—that is, concentrates—his mind upon the Self.

The yogī, through yoga, is eternally connected [to the goal], free from defilement—that is, free from impurity—and devoid of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes of *saṃsāra*.
By means of effortless ease (*sukha*) arising from devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*), and through the cessation of all obstacles, he attains contact with Brahman.

"Contact with Brahman" refers to identity (*tādātmya*) with Brahman, characterized by the absence of contact with sense objects; that is to say, his essential nature is Brahman itself, untouched by external objects.
He enjoys— that is, pervades— an unsurpassed bliss (*ānanda*) that has completely transcended all infinite limitations;

he experiences it with a mind entirely free from activity, which is distinct from both lethargy (*laya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*), because in the state of distraction there is still the existence of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*).
And because even the mind (*manas*) lacks existence by its own nature when withdrawn,

the meaning is that the experience of bliss in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) occurs only through the subtle mind, which is devoid of all mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, by the phrase "without effort" (*anāyāsena*), the cessation of obstacles (*antarāya*) is indicated.

And these obstacles have been shown by the Yoga Sūtra: "Disease, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of dispassion, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these distractions of the mind are the obstacles" (Yoga Sūtra 1.30). They distract the mind, drawing it away from yoga; thus, these distractions of the mind are the adversaries of yoga.
Regarding doubt and erroneous perception, these are the direct adversaries of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*) by virtue of being fluctuations themselves.
As for the seven [afflictions] beginning with disease, however, they are adversaries [of that cessation] because they accompany those fluctuations; this is the meaning.
Disease (*vyādhi*) is a disorder caused by an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), such as fever and the like.
*Styāna* (sloth) is a state of unfitness; it means that even when being instructed by a teacher, one is incapable of performing actions such as sitting and so forth.
*Yoga* refers to the cognition that touches upon both alternatives—whether a practice is to be undertaken or not—which is doubt (*saṃśaya*).

Although this [doubt] is included within error (*viparyaya*) because it is established upon what is not that [true object], it is here distinguished from error by the intention to specify its internal particularity: namely, the quality of touching both alternatives versus touching only one alternative.

Negligence (*pramāda*) is the habit of non-performance despite having the capacity for the performance of the means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); that is to say, indifference toward the practices of yoga due to being occupied with other objects.
Laziness (*ālasya*) is the heaviness of body and mind caused by phlegm and so forth, as well as by the quality of darkness (*tamas*), even when indifference has been overcome;
and although this is not commonly known as a disease, it is an obstacle to engagement in the domain of yoga.

Non-restraint is the mind's exclusive longing for a particular object. Erroneous perception is the notion that something is a means of yoga even when it is not, as well as the notion that something is not a means of yoga even when it is. Not having attained the stage refers to the failure to obtain one-pointedness within the stage of meditative concentration.
This refers, in short, to the states of being distracted, stupefied, and scattered.
Instability is the mind’s failure to remain established even when the stage of meditative concentration has been attained, due to a slackening of effort.
These mental distractions are designated as the nine impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, and the obstacles to yoga.

Pain, mental distress, trembling, and inhalation and exhalation are co-existent with distraction (Yoga Sūtra 1.31). Pain is a transformation of the mind characterized by agitation and belonging to the quality of rajas; it consists of affliction.
This occurs internally, whether physical or mental, due to disease or the influence of desire and so forth.
External pain arises from the oppression of spirits and the like; because it is caused by the misconception known as hatred, it is an obstacle to samādhi.

Mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is a specific tamasic transformation of the mind produced by the experience of powerful suffering, such as the frustration of one's desires; it is a state of rigidity synonymous with agitation (*kṣobha*).
Because it is a form of impurity (*kaṣāya*), like lethargy (*laya*), it is an obstacle to *samādhi*.
Trembling of the limbs (*aṅga-ejaya*) is the shaking of the body parts, which is an obstacle to stability in posture (*āsana-sthairya*).

Inhalation (*śvāsa*) is the entry of external air into the interior by means of *prāṇa*; it is opposed to *recaka*, a limb of *samādhi*. Exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is the exit of the abdominal air to the exterior by means of *apāna*; it is opposed to *pūraka*, a limb of *samādhi*.
These two do not occur for one whose mind is concentrated; they belong only to one whose mind is distracted.
These arise as obstacles that coexist with distraction;
they are to be suppressed through practice and dispassion,
or by means of devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna).

Having stated the alternative view that for those with intense spiritual urgency (*tīvra-saṃvega*), the attainment of *samādhi* is near— either through the practice of *yama* and *niyama* (YS 1.21) or through devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*) (YS 1.23)— the author defines the Lord who is to be the object of devotion as "the Supreme Person (*puruṣa-viśeṣa*) untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions."

In that regard, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed. Having established this through three sūtras—beginning with "He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time" (Yoga Sūtra 1.26)—he set forth its meditative devotion (*praṇidhāna*) in two [subsequent] sūtras: "The syllable *praṇava* is its designator;
its repetition and the contemplation of its meaning" (Yoga Sūtra 1.27–28).

"Then there is the attainment of the inward-turned consciousness and the absence of obstacles" (Yoga Sūtra 1.29). From that devotion to Īśvara, consisting of the repetition (*japa*) of the *praṇava* and meditation upon its meaning, there arises the attainment—that is, the direct realization—of the inward-turned consciousness, the *puruṣa*, through its discrimination from *prakṛti*. Of those mentioned...
The meaning is that there is also an absence of obstacles.

Since the cessation of obstacles must be accomplished through both practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), he says—[for the sake of strengthening practice]—"For the purpose of preventing those, practice on a single principle" (YS 1.32).
For the purpose of preventing those obstacles, one should perform the repeated fixing of the mind upon some intended single principle; this is practice.

Likewise: "The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity toward those who are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous" (Yoga Sūtra 1.33). Friendliness is benevolence;
compassion is pity.
Sympathetic joy is gladness, and equanimity is indifference; by words such as "happiness" and so forth, those possessing such qualities are indicated.

Toward all living beings who have attained the enjoyment of happiness, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*), thinking, "How excellent is this state of happiness for my friends," and not envy.
Toward those who are suffering, one should cultivate compassion (*kṛpā*) alone, thinking, "How indeed might this cessation of suffering come about for them?"
Neither indifference nor joy:
toward those possessing merit, one should feel joy by means of rejoicing in their merit, but not hatred nor indifference.
Toward those lacking merit, one should cultivate only equanimity—neither rejoicing nor aversion. As he cultivates this, pure qualities arise within him;
consequently, his mind, freed from the stains of passion, hatred, and the like, becomes serene and fit for one-pointed concentration.

The fourfold set beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is an illustration for [the other virtues] such as fearlessness and purity of being, as well as for the qualities beginning with humility and freedom from hypocrisy; for all these, being of the nature of pure latent impressions (*śubha-vāsanā*), serve to remove impure latent impressions (*malina-vāsanā*).
The meaning of this aphorism is that passion and hatred are great enemies, obstacles to all human goals, and must therefore be abandoned with great effort.

In this way, other means such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth have also been shown for the purpose of clarifying the mind. This statement—"with ease"—is addressed specifically to one in whom this clarification of the mind has arisen through the grace of the Blessed One; otherwise, the pacification of the mind would be impossible. //28//
Viśvanātha:
And therefore, he says "yuñjan" (while practicing) to show that one indeed becomes one who has accomplished the goal;
the meaning is that one attains happiness and becomes truly liberated while living. //28//

Baladeva: Thus, he says "yuñjan" (while practicing yoga) to show that after the direct realization of one's own self (*svātma-sākṣātkāra*), one also attains the direct realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-sākṣātkāra*).

Practicing yoga—that is, experiencing through yoga—one's own self in the manner described, the yogi, by that very means, becomes free from stain, with all defects burnt away, and easily—that is, without effort—attains the touch of Brahman, the experience of the Supreme Self, which is ultimate and immeasurable bliss.
