He enjoys; he attains. //28//
One whose self is disciplined by yoga perceives the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he sees the same everywhere. (6.29)
Śrīdhara: He demonstrates the very direct realization of Brahman with the words "abiding in all beings.
One whose self is disciplined by practiced yoga is one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita-citta*).
One who sees Brahman alone as equal everywhere is one of "equal vision" (*sama-darśana*).
Likewise, he perceives his own self as devoid of the limitations of the body and so forth created by ignorance, abiding within all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects;
and he perceives those beings as non-different from himself. //29//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, when the pure referents of the words "thou" (tvaṃ-pada) and "that" (tat-pada) have been directly realized through the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samādhi), there arises a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of non-conceptual direct intuition, produced by Vedāntic statements such as "That thou art" (tattvam asi), which has their identity as its object.
The knowledge called *brahmavidyā* arises;
and then, through the cessation of all ignorance and its effects, one enjoys the bliss of Brahman absolutely—this he establishes with three verses.
Among these, first he states the presentation of the referent (*lakṣya*) of the term "Thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*) in the verse beginning with "all."

One perceives— that is, directly realizes— through discrimination, the one omnipresent Self alone as the inner conscious witness, the ultimate reality, a mass of bliss, which abides as the enjoyer within all beings, both stationary and moving, throughout all bodies; [one realizes it] by distinguishing it from the objects of witnessing, which are unreal, insentient, limited, and of the nature of suffering.

And within that Self who is the witness (*sākṣin*), all beings— being objects of experience through the relation of superimposition— are perceived by the witness as distinct from itself, through discrimination, as being false, limited, insentient, and consisting of suffering, since no other relation between the witness and the witnessed is logically possible.

Who? One whose self (ātman)—that is, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—is joined with yoga; that is, one who has attained clarity (prasāda) through yoga in the form of proficiency in the state beyond discursive thought (nirvicāra).

And so it was stated previously: "When there is proficiency in the state beyond discursive thought, there is internal clarity" (Yoga Sūtra 1.47); "In that state, wisdom (prajñā) bears the truth" (Yoga Sūtra 1.48); "That wisdom has a different object from the wisdom derived from scripture and inference, because it pertains to specific details" (Yoga Sūtra 1.49).
And thus, by means of that yogic perception known as *ṛtambhara*— which has as its object specific real entities that lie beyond the scope of verbal testimony and inference—

one simultaneously perceives everything, whether subtle, concealed, or distant, all equally; being one who possesses such equal vision regarding all things (*sarvatrasamadarsana*), it is logical that the yogi whose self is disciplined in yoga beholds both the Self and the non-Self exactly as they exist.

Alternatively, it has been stated that the one whose self is disciplined through yoga (*yoga-yuktātmā*) and the one who perceives equality everywhere (*sarvatra-sama-darśanaḥ*) are both qualified for the vision of the Self (*ātma-īkṣaṇa*), as they are both "yogis" and "seers of equality.

For just as the cessation of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*) is a cause for the direct realization of the Witness (*sākṣi-sākṣātkāra*), so too is the separation of consciousness—which is the thread running through all things—from the insentient (*jaḍa*) by means of discernment;
yoga itself is not necessarily required.
Therefore Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāghava, there are two methods for the dissolution of the mind: yoga and knowledge.
Yoga is indeed the cessation of mental fluctuations, while knowledge is right discernment."
"For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of reality.
Therefore, the supreme deity Śiva spoke of two methods. Thus [it is said].
This refers to the non-perception [of the mind] resulting from the separation of the mind—which serves as its own limiting adjunct—from the Witness who is the observer of the mind's destruction.
Its means are twofold: one is asamprajñāta-samādhi (non-cognitive absorption).

For in samprajñāta-samādhi (cognitive absorption), the sattva of the internal organ, joined with a continuous flow of mental modifications having the single form of the Self, is experienced by the witness; however, when all modifications are restrained, it is not experienced because of its state of complete tranquility—this is the distinction.

The second [view], however, is the inquiry that the testimony attributed to the witness (*sākṣin*) does not exist at all because it is unreal; rather, only the witness himself exists as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*).
Regarding this, first, the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who maintain that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the ultimate reality, adopted this [first] means.
For them, since the ultimate reality is the non-perception of the mind, there is the possibility of a means other than cessation (*nirodha*) through the perception of the witness.

However, those who follow the venerable Śrīmac-Chaṅkara-Bhagavat-Pūjya-pāda, being followers of the Upaniṣads and proponents of the unreality of the phenomenal world (prapañca-anṛtatva-vādins), resort to the second means alone.
For them, when there is firmness in the knowledge of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna),
the non-perception of the mind— which is superimposed upon it— and of its objects, which have been sublated, occurs effortlessly.
For this very reason, the venerable Bhagavat-pūjyapāda nowhere established a requirement for yoga on the part of those who know Brahman.
Consequently, the Upaniṣadic Paramahaṃsas proceed toward the direct realization of Brahman by approaching a teacher solely for the inquiry into the Vedāntic statements of the Śruti, and not for yoga.
This is because [realization] is otherwise accomplished through inquiry alone by means of the removal of defects of the mind; thus, enough of further elaboration. //29//
Viśvanātha:
He shows the direct realization of Brahman by that one liberated while living through the verse beginning with "the Self abiding in all beings.

By the word "in the Self" (*ātmani*), he indicates the Supreme Self's status as the presiding controller of all beings; and by [the phrase] "and the abiding of the Supreme Self in all beings," he indicates the locus of the Supreme Self within all beings.
He beholds—that is, he experiences through direct perception—the Self whose mind is disciplined by yoga and whose internal organ has taken the form of Brahman;
he is one who possesses equal vision, seeing all as the same, namely Brahman itself. //29//

Baladeva: Thus, one whose samādhi has been perfected and who has directly perceived the yoga of his own self with the Supreme Self experiences the omnipresence of the Supreme Self, the fact that all other selves—beginning with Druhiṇa—are dependent upon Him, and His state of being beyond the reach of the senses; this he expresses with the word "sarva" (all).
One whose self is joined in yoga is one who has attained samādhi; for it is stated in the Smṛti: "Because He is all-pervading and because He is the Knower, Hari is indeed the Supreme Self."
And because of the explanation "he who [sees] Me," he beholds the Supreme Self abiding in all beings as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all individual souls;
and in that very Self, which serves as the substratum, he beholds all beings and that same Self as the substratum of all individual souls—
this is what he says with the word "everywhere."
He is so called because he perceives the Supreme Self as equal—devoid of partiality—in all living beings, who have been created in high and low states according to their respective karmas. //29//
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me— for him I am never lost, and he is never lost to Me. (6.30)

Śrīdhara: And regarding such self-knowledge, he says "He who [sees] me," etc., to show that meditation upon Me is the primary cause. He who sees Me, the Supreme Lord, everywhere in every mere being, and he who sees every mere living being in Me.
I am not lost to him, nor do I become invisible; and he does not become invisible to me.
The meaning is that, having become manifest and beholding him with a compassionate gaze, I bestow grace upon him. //30//
Madhusūdana:
Having thus defined the pure meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (you), he defines the pure meaning of the term *tat* (That) with the words "He who [knows] Me.

That yogi who, through the discernment of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), [knows] Me—the Lord, the referent of the term *tat*, whose limiting adjunct is *māyā*, the cause of the entire phenomenal world—[attains liberation].

He perceives— through the direct perception born of yoga— the ultimate reality, which is blissful, infinite, and free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as being woven through all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) both as its essence and as its manifestation;
and likewise, he sees the entire collection of phenomena as superimposed upon Me by *māyā*, and perceives them as false precisely because they are distinct from Me.
For one who perceives such discrimination, I— the Blessed One, the referent of that word "That"— do not perish;
I do not become an object of indirect knowledge as some Lord distinct from me, but rather I become an object of direct knowledge born of yoga.

Although the state of being the object of the immediate knowledge born of the sentence occurs only through non-difference from the referent of the word *tvam*, nevertheless, it is indeed possible for the referent of the word *tat* alone to be the object of the immediate knowledge born of yoga (*yogaja*).
Thus, by making Me immediate through yogic perception, he does not perish; that is, he does not become remote.
For that wise one is indeed my own self; because of his extreme dearness to me, he is always within the range of my direct perception (*aparokṣa-jñāna*).
This is because it has been said: "In whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).
Likewise, the Blessed One spoke thus to Yudhiṣṭhira regarding the meditation upon Bhīṣma as he lay upon his bed of arrows.
But the ignorant person does not perceive the Blessed One, who is his very own self, even though he exists;
therefore, the Blessed One, although seeing him, does not see him, according to the Vedic revelation: "He, being unknown, does not benefit him" (BAU 1.4.15).
But the wise man is always present as a recipient of the Blessed One’s grace; this is the meaning. //30//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, he states the fruit for one who possesses direct experience (aparokṣānubhava) in the words "He who [knows] Me. For him, I—the Brahman—do not perish; that is, I do not cease to be directly perceived.
Thus, while my eternal direct perception remains true, that yogi—my devotee—does not perish; he never falls away at any time. //30//
Baladeva, explaining this, states the fruit for one who perceives things as they truly are with the words "He who [knows Me]":
for such a yogi, I, the Supreme Self, do not perish— that is, I do not become invisible—
and that yogi does not perish— that is, he does not become invisible— to Me.
The meaning is that there is a mutual direct perception between us at all times. //30//
He who, established in unity, worships Me as dwelling in all beings— that yogi, even while engaged in any manner of conduct, abides in Me. (6.31)
Śrīdhara: Nor would one who is thus become a servant of ritual injunction; therefore, he says, "abiding in all beings.

He who worships Me—who am situated in all beings—having resorted to and established himself in non-duality, that yogi, that man of knowledge, even while existing through the total renunciation of action, exists in Me alone and is liberated.
The meaning is that he does not fall away. //31//
Madhusūdana:

Having thus defined the pure meaning of the word *tvaṃ* (thou) and the meaning of the word *tat* (that), he defines the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" with the words "in all beings. Me, the Lord, who am the referent of the word *tat*, who abides as the substratum in all beings, and who am pure Being (*sanmātra*) pervading everything—[know me as such].

He who, establishing absolute non-difference and oneness with the indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*), ascertains— just as one ascertains that the space within a jar is the great space (*mahākāśa*) by removing the distinction created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)— worships through the direct realization born from Vedāntic statements, thinking "I am Brahman," becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) through the cessation of ignorance and its effects, having indeed accomplished all that was to be done.

However, as long as the perception of the body and so forth continues through the persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), for that long— due to the predominance of *prārabdha* karma— one may either abandon all actions like Yājñavalkya and others,
or engage in prescribed action like Janaka and others, or even perform prohibited action like Dattātreya and others.
In every way, even while existing and acting in whatever form, that yogi who knows "I am Brahman" exists non-differently within Me alone, the Supreme Self.

In every respect, there is no suspicion of an obstacle to his liberation, according to the Śruti: "Neither the gods nor anything else can prevail against his failure; for he becomes their very self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
The meaning is that even the gods, despite their great power, are not able to prevent his liberation, let alone others who are insignificant.

Although prohibited action is impossible for one who knows Brahman because of the impossibility of passion and hatred— which incite one toward prohibited action— this was said, "even while acting in every way" and "even having killed," by accepting such action for the sake of praising knowledge.
"He does not destroy these worlds, nor is he bound," as it is said in Gītā 18.17. //31//
Viśvanātha:

Thus, even in the stage prior to direct realization of Me, for the yogin who worships everywhere with the contemplation of the Supreme Self, there is no ritualistic service (*vidhi-kaṅkarya*); this he states with the word "sarva" (all).
He who worships while established in oneness—the conviction that the Supreme Self alone exists as the one [cause] because It is the instrument of all—[for him there is no ritualistic service].
One who is engaged in worship through hearing, remembering, and so forth,
exists in Me— whether performing or not performing the actions prescribed by the scriptures— in every way,
and not in saṃsāra. //31//
Baladeva: With the intention that "the yogī who experiences my inconceivable essential nature and power becomes exceedingly dear to me," he says "sarve" (all).

I, possessing four arms, the luster of an *atasī* flower, and bearing the discus and other weapons, dwell individually within the hearts of all living beings as one whose size is the measure of a span (*prādeśa-mātra*).
He who, resorting to the oneness—that is, the non-difference—of my many forms within them, worships and meditates upon me; [he becomes very dear].
Thus, that yogi, existing in every way—even when engaged in worldly activity—whether performing his prescribed duties or not, exists in Me;

by the power of experiencing My nature as possessing inconceivable potency, having burnt away the defects of acting according to one's own desires, he attains liberation characterized by proximity to Me, and not the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra); this is the meaning.
And the Śruti declares Hari’s inconceivable sixfold power (ṣaṭ-kauśalya), saying: "Though being one, he appears as many. And the Smṛti says:
"The supreme Viṣṇu is indeed one and all-pervading, there is no doubt;
yet by his sovereignty, though his form is one, it is manifested as many, like the sun. //31//
O Arjuna, he who, by means of comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere— whether it be happiness or suffering— that yogi is considered the most excellent. 6.32

Śrīdhara: And thus, he says "by way of comparison with oneself" (*ātmaupamyena*) to show that among the yogins who worship him in this manner, he is the best because he is compassionate toward all beings.
"By way of comparison with oneself" means by way of similarity to oneself.
Just as happiness is dear to me and suffering is not dear to me, so it is for others as well; seeing thus equally in all cases, he is one who desires only the happiness of everyone.
But there is no suffering for anyone;
the meaning is that such a yogi is the best and is my preferred one. //32//
Madhusūdana:

Even when such realization of reality has arisen, some person—due to the absence of the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā)—does not experience the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and through mental distraction, experiences visible suffering; such a one is an inferior yogi at the fall of the body.
Because of being a partaker of isolation (*kaivalya*),
and because of the experience of perceived suffering as long as the body exists,

one experiences the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), preceded by the cessation of perceived suffering through the simultaneous practice of the knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), yet remaining under the influence of *prārabdha* karma.
What might occur at the time of emerging from meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
It is said: "by way of comparison with oneself" (*ātmaupamyena*).
Self alone is the comparison (*aupamya*); by that analogy of oneself (*ātma-dṛṣṭāntena*), [one considers] pleasure or pain throughout the entire range of living beings.

O Arjuna, that yogi who perceives all as equal— who, being free from malice, does not bring about what is undesirable for another just as he would not do so for himself— and whose mind is thus tranquil through the absence of latent tendencies, is considered the supreme and most excellent knower of Brahman compared to the former.

Therefore, the meaning is that a great effort must be exerted for the practice of the sequence consisting of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*), and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*).

In this regard, all this world of duality is merely false because it is imagined through *māyā* within the non-dual Self which is consciousness-bliss (*cid-ānanda*); the Self alone is the ultimate truth.
The knowledge that "I am the one, non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss" is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), like the continuous stream of a lamp's flame.

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which undergoes transformation in the form of a stream of mental modifications (*vṛtti-santāna*), is called the "mind" (*manas*) because its nature is cogitation. Its destruction consists in abandoning transformation into the form of mental modifications and transforming instead in the form of cessation, which suppresses all modifications. Furthermore, *vāsanā* is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) residing in the consciousness (*citta*) that serves as the cause for specific modifications such as anger, which arise suddenly without prior reflection; this [impression] is deposited in the consciousness through repeated practice in the past.
Because it is being cultivated,

its destruction consists in the non-arising of anger and other passions even when external objects are present, provided that the firm latent impression (*vāsanā*) of mental tranquility born of discernment has been established.

In that regard, when there is knowledge of reality, because no mental modification arises toward the falsely existent world— just as one does not perceive a human horn and the like— the [non-existence] of the self...
Furthermore, because there is no further utility for its recurrence once it has been seen [as it truly is], the mind perishes like a fire without fuel.
When the mind has perished, and external causes that awaken latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are no longer perceived, the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted.
Once the latent tendencies are exhausted, the mind perishes due to the absence of a cause, as there is no arising of mental modifications such as anger.
When the mind has been destroyed through the perfection of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, the knowledge of reality arises.
Thus, when the knowledge of reality has arisen, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of passion, aversion, and the like are exhausted.
And when the latent impressions have been exhausted, because there is no longer any obstruction, the knowledge of reality arises; thus, their state of mutual causality should be demonstrated.
Therefore, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"The knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the destruction of latent impressions—
having become mutual causes for one another, these indeed remain difficult to accomplish."
"Therefore, O Rāghava, having abandoned the desire for enjoyment from afar, rely with effort upon these three through discerning human exertion.
Human exertion (*pauruṣa-yatna*) is the persistence in the form of such enthusiasm as "I shall certainly accomplish [my goal] by some means or other."
Discrimination (*viveka*) means the determination arrived at through discernment.

It consists of hearing and so forth as the means for the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), yoga as the means for the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*), and the generation of counter-vāsanās as the means for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*).

By human effort endowed with such discrimination, even a slight desire for enjoyment is said to be "far away," because—according to the maxim that "even a small amount of sacrificial butter [increases] the fire"—it serves as a cause for the increase of latent impressions.
For there are two types of persons qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*): those who have performed the meditative practice (*upāsti*) and those who have not.

Among them, for one who has performed the practice up to the point of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the object of worship and then proceeds toward the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), liberation while living (*jīvan-mukti*) is established by itself after that knowledge, due to the extreme firmness of the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*) and the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*).
However, the seeker of liberation nowadays generally fails to perform any formal worship; instead, out of mere eagerness, he suddenly engages in knowledge (*vidyā*).

Without *yoga*, and by means of the mere discrimination between consciousness and the insentient (*cij-jaḍa-viveka*), he accomplishes the temporary dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*). Then, through the perfection of tranquility, self-control, and other virtues, he performs hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*).
When these are practiced with firmness, the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) arises, which severs all bonds.
The knot of ignorance, the state of being [limited by] Brahman, the knot of the heart, doubts, actions, the lack of all-desire, death, and rebirth—this manifold bondage ceases through knowledge.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "O gentle one, he who knows that which is hidden in the cave scatters the knot of ignorance here;
he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
[Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8] "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite."

He who knows that which is hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven—he attains all desires together with him (the Creator). Having known Him alone, one passes beyond death. But he who possesses true discernment, who is self-possessed and ever pure—
"He attains that state from which he is not born again" (KaṭhU 1.3.8);

"He who knows thus, 'I am Brahman,' becomes this all" (BAU 1.4.10)—such passages should be cited as having the cessation of non-universality as their fruit. This is liberation while disembodied (*videha-mukti*), which should be understood as occurring at the very moment knowledge arises, even while the body still exists.
Since these bonds, which have been superimposed upon Brahman through ignorance (*avidyā*), cannot arise again once they have ceased upon the destruction of that ignorance,
the knowledge of reality persists because the cause for its weakening no longer exists.

However, the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*) and the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*) both turn back suddenly— like a lamp in a windy place— due to the absence of firm practice and because they are obstructed by *prārabdha* karma, which provides the experience [of the body].
Therefore, for a knower of reality in the present, there is no need for effort regarding the realization of reality that was already established previously;
rather, the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*) and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*) are to be accomplished through effort.
Among these, the dissolution of the mind has been previously described by means of the definition of *asamprajñāta-samādhi*.
Now, the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is being examined.
Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha has stated the nature of latent impressions:
"Through firm contemplation, one abandons all prior and subsequent deliberation."
That grasping of an object is proclaimed to be its latent impression (vāsanā).

And in this regard, the attachment of living beings toward the specific differences in their own respective regional customs, family traditions, and inherent natures—including the corrupt words and elegant words found therein—is the general example.
That latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is of two kinds: defiled and pure.
The pure is the divine fortune (*daivī saṃpat*).
Due to the predominance of training in the scriptures, it is of a single form as a means for attaining the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*).
However, the impure [impurity] is threefold: the worldly tendency (*loka-vāsanā*), the scriptural tendency (*śāstra-vāsanā*), and the bodily tendency (*deha-vāsanā*).
The worldly tendency is the attachment to an unattainable object, such as thinking, "I shall act in such a way that no one at all censures me."
Furthermore, because it is impossible to fulfill [the desire] according to the maxim "who is capable of pleasing the world? and because it is of no use for human goals (*puruṣārtha*), it is impure.

The impression of the scriptures (*śāstra-vāsanā*) is threefold: addiction to recitation, addiction to many scriptures, and addiction to ritual performance; these are well known respectively in the cases of Bharadvāja, Durvāsas, and Nidāgha.
Its impurity arises from its being a source of affliction (*kleśa*), its lack of utility for human goals, its being a cause of pride, and its being a cause of rebirth.
The latent impression of the body (*deha-vāsanā*) is also threefold:
the delusion of selfhood, the delusion of attributing qualities, and the delusion of removing defects.
Among these, the delusion of selfhood is well known among Virocana and others, and is universal throughout the world.

The instilling of qualities is twofold: worldly and scriptural. The accomplishment of objects such as excellent sounds and so forth is worldly; the accomplishment of bathing in the Gaṅgā, visiting the Śālagrāma, sacred fords (tīrtha), and so forth is scriptural.
The removal of defects is also twofold: worldly and scriptural.

The removal of diseases and the like by means of medicines prescribed by physicians is worldly; the removal of impurity and the like by means of Vedic bathing, sipping water, and so forth is scriptural.

And this [worldly life] is impure in every respect because it lacks authoritative foundation, because it is impossible to master, because it is useless for the goals of human life, and because it is the cause of rebirth.

Thus, these three—worldly impressions (*loka-vāsanā*), scriptural impressions (*śāstra-vāsanā*), and bodily impressions (*deha-vāsanā*)—though appearing as things to be accepted by those lacking discrimination, must be abandoned by the discerning; for they obstruct the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) in the seeker, and they obstruct steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) in the knower.
Thus, the threefold external objective impression (*vāsanā*) has been described.
Internal impression, however, consists of the demoniacal qualities such as lust, anger, deceit, and pride; it is called mental impression, the root of all misfortune.
In this way, the destruction of the fourfold set of external and internal impressions must be accomplished through pure impression.
Thus it was said by Vasiṣṭha: "O Rāma, first abandon mental impressions and impressions of sense-objects; then adopt the impressions of friendliness and so forth—these are the stainless impressions."
In this context, by the term "impressions of objects" (*viṣaya-vāsanā*), the three previously mentioned impressions—of the world, of secular treatises, and of the Vedas—are intended.
By the term "mental impressions" (*mānasa-vāsanā*), the demonic endowments such as desire, anger, deceit, and arrogance are intended;
alternatively, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects.
The impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the state of being experienced is the objective impression (*viṣaya-vāsanā*);
the impression produced by the state of being desired is the mental impression (*mānasa-vāsanā*).
In this view, the four previously mentioned [types of impressions] are included within these two alone.

Since no other latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are possible apart from external and internal ones, the abandonment of those latent impressions consists in the production of latent impressions of friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth that are opposed to them. Those latent impressions of friendliness and so forth were formulated as *sūtras* by the Blessed Patañjali; although they have already been explained briefly, they are now explained once again.

For the mind is defiled by passion, hatred, merit, and demerit. Among these, passion is that which underlies pleasure (Yoga Sūtra 2.7). Due to delusion, a certain specific modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) of a rajasic nature underlies the pleasure being experienced, thinking, "May all that belongs to the class of pleasure be mine."
And because that [state] cannot be accomplished due to the absence of the necessary conditions— both seen and unseen—
that passion defiles the mind.

However, when one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward happy beings, thinking, "All these happy ones are mine," then for one who contemplates that their happiness has indeed become one's own, passion toward them [no longer arises].
It ceases;
just as when one's own kingdom has ceased, the kingdom of one's son and so forth is still considered one's own kingdom, so it is here.
And when passion has ceased, the mind becomes serene, like water at the end of the rainy season.

Likewise, hatred is that which lies latent within suffering (Yoga Sūtra 2.8). A certain specific modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) follows along with *tamas*—a transformation of *rajas*—and thinks: "May all such suffering never be mine at any time. And that [suffering], when present in enemies, tigers, and so forth, cannot be prevented.
Furthermore, it is not possible to destroy all those causes of suffering;
therefore, that hatred constantly burns the heart.

However, when one cultivates compassion toward those who suffer, thinking, "May there be no suffering for others just as there is none for myself," then, upon the cessation of hatred such as enmity and the like, the mind becomes serene.
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"As one's own life-breaths are dear to oneself, so are they to all beings;
therefore, the virtuous show compassion toward all beings by treating them as they would themselves."
This very point has been stated here as well: "By comparison with oneself, in all cases," and so forth.
Likewise, living beings by their very nature do not practice merit, but rather practice evil. As they say:
"Human beings desire the fruit of merit, yet they do not desire merit itself."
“They do not desire the fruit of evil, yet they commit evil with effort.
And those merits and evils, when left undone or committed, produce remorse;
and that is expressed in the Veda: “Why did I not do what is good? Why did I do what is evil?”

If he should cultivate sympathetic joy (*muditā*) toward virtuous persons, then, imbued with that latent impression (*vāsanā*), he himself will spontaneously and vigilantly engage in non-white, non-black merit.

As it has been said: "The karma of the yogi is of three kinds—non-white and non-black; for others who are not yogis, it is of three kinds: white which is auspicious, black which is inauspicious, and white-black which is both auspicious and inauspicious.
Likewise, by cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward sinful persons, he himself, imbued with that latent impression, turns away from evil.
Consequently, in the absence of remorse caused by the failure to perform merit or the commission of evil, the mind becomes serene.
Thus, for one who cultivates loving-kindness toward those who are happy, not only does attachment cease, but malice, envy, and so forth also cease.
Malice (*asūyā*) is the exposing of faults in the virtues of others.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is the inability to endure the virtues of others.
When, through the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the happiness of others has become one's own, how could resentment or the like possibly arise toward their virtues?

Likewise, for one cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those who suffer, when hatred—which causes the killing of enemies and so forth—is eliminated, then pride (*darpa*) induced by one's own happiness in contrast to the suffering of others is also eliminated.
In this way, the cessation of other defects should also be inferred from the *Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa* and similar works.

Thus, these three—knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*), and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā-kṣaya*)—must be practiced. Among them, the practice of knowledge of reality consists in the repeated recollection of reality by whatever means possible. As it has been said:
Reflecting upon that, speaking of that, mutually awakening one another to that,
and being solely intent upon that— the wise know this to be the practice of Brahman.
"The visible world was never produced even at the beginning of creation; it does not exist at all, always.
'This world' and 'I'—the wise know that the supreme practice is the cultivation of awakening regarding these.
Thus, the practice of yoga that opposes the appearance of the visible is the practice of restraining the mind. As it has been said:
"Those who strive by means of reasoning and scriptures for the attainment of the absolute non-existence of both the knower and the object known— they too are established here as practitioners. Thus,
the "attainment of non-existence" refers to the realization of the falsity of both the knower and the known.
The non-perception even of its own nature constitutes the attainment of absolute non-existence; for that purpose,
through reasoning (*yukti*) and yoga,
by means of the realization of the impossibility of the object of perception, there is the attenuation of passion, hatred, and the like.
That intense delight which has arisen is called the practice of Brahman.
Thus, the practice for the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), characterized by the destruction of passion, hatred, and so forth, has been described.
Therefore, it is established that he who, through the practice of the knowledge of reality, the practice of the dissolution of the mind, and the practice of the exhaustion of latent impressions,
is free from passion and hatred and possesses an equal vision toward his own and others' happiness and suffering, is the supreme yogin.
But he who possesses a biased vision is considered dead, even if he possesses knowledge of reality; such a one is not a supreme yogin. //32//

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, it was stated that during the stage of practice (*sādhana-daśā*), the yogi should be equanimous toward all things. In that regard, he explains the primary form of equanimity with the words "by comparison with oneself" (*ātmaupamyena*).

Regarding "happiness or suffering," just as happiness is dear to me and suffering is not dear to me, so it is for others as well; seeing this equally in all cases, he who desires only happiness for everyone and not suffering for anyone at all—
That yogi is the best, and he is my preferred one. //32//
Baladeva: He clarifies what was previously stated—that he is "intent on the welfare of all beings"—with the words "by comparison with himself.

In the state of worldly activity (*vyutthāna*), he who perceives pleasure and pain everywhere equally by comparison with himself, that is, through his own likeness; [he is one whose mind is established in yoga].
He who desires only the happiness of others just as he does his own,
and not their suffering— he, the yogi who views the happiness and suffering of himself and others as equal and who is compassionate toward all, is my supreme and most excellent favorite.
The meaning is that one who possesses such uneven vision, even if they know reality, is not a supreme yogin. //32//
BhG 6.33 Arjuna said:
O Madhusūdana, this yoga which has been taught by You as equanimity—
Because of its flickering nature, I do not perceive its stable persistence. //33//
Śrīdhara: Thinking that the yoga characterized as previously described is impossible to achieve, Arjuna said, "This which...
[referring to] this yoga which has been taught by You through equanimity—that is, by the mind's abiding solely in the form of the Self, being devoid of both dissolution and distraction.
I do not see its stability as firm or long-lasting, because of the flickering nature of the mind. //33//
Madhusūdana:
Arjuna spoke, beginning with the words "This which... (yo 'yam), while challenging the meaning that had been stated.

This supreme yoga, characterized as a universal totality (*sarvatra samaṣṭi-lakṣaṇaḥ*), was taught by you—the omniscient Lord—through equanimity (*sāmyena*), that is, through equality (*samatvena*), by means of removing the causes of partial vision such as attachment, aversion, and so forth, which reside within the mind.
O Madhusūdana,
O initiator of all Vedic traditions,
[please explain] the stability— the actual existence— of this yoga described by You, which is characterized by the cessation of all mental fluctuations.

I do not see, nor do I conceive of, a steady [state] that persists for a long time—neither myself nor anyone else like me who is skilled in the practice of yoga. Why do you not conceive of it? To this he replies: "Because of its restlessness."
The word "by the mind" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. //33//
Viśvanātha:
Observing the difficulty of attaining the equanimity characterized by the Blessed One, he said, "This which...
[referring to the verse]. I do not see a steady, perpetual state of this yoga attained through equanimity.
The meaning is that this yoga does not persist forever, but lasts for only three or four days.
Why? Because of its restlessness.
For thus has equanimity been described: one should view the happiness and suffering of all people existing in the world as being exactly equal to one's own happiness and suffering.
In this regard, while equanimity might indeed exist toward those who are kinsmen and those who are neutral,
it can never exist toward those who are enemies, slayers, haters, and revilers;
for it is not possible for me to view the happiness and suffering of myself, Yudhiṣṭhira, and Duryodhana as equal in every respect.

Furthermore, because one cannot restrain the powerful and extremely fickle mind through discernment by thinking that the individual self, the supreme self, the vital breaths, the senses, and the physical elements are the same for oneself and for one's enemies—
and because, on the contrary, it is observed that the mind, when attached to sense objects, devours that very discernment— [therefore, one should practice yoga].
Baladeva: Arjuna spoke, beginning with "This which... (yo 'yam), while challenging what was said. He means:

"I do not perceive even a stable, constant state—the final consummation—of this yoga taught by you, the omniscient one, characterized by equanimity, that is, the equality of one's own and others' pleasure and pain;
rather, [it lasts] for only two or three days."
Why? Because of its fickleness.
This is the meaning: that equanimity might perhaps exist toward kinsmen and neutral persons;
but it never exists toward enemies and those who revile one.

If it is argued that the presiding nature of the Supreme Self is uniform everywhere and thus should be apprehended through discrimination (*viveka*), then that is not possible at all times; for the mind, being extremely restless and powerful, cannot be restrained by such discrimination. //33//
"O Kṛṣṇa, the mind is indeed restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (6.34)
Śrīdhara explains this with the word "cañcalam" (fickle):
it is fickle by its very nature, that is, restless;
furthermore, it is "pramāthi," meaning it has the quality of agitating or disturbing.
The meaning is that it causes agitation of the body and the senses.
Furthermore, it cannot be overcome even by powerful investigation.
Moreover, it is firm and difficult to break because of its persistent attachment to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sense objects.

Therefore, just as it is impossible to confine within jars or other vessels the wind that is blowing violently in the sky, so too do I consider the restraint—that is, the suppression—of that mind to be extremely difficult and altogether impossible to achieve. //34//
Madhusūdana:
He establishes that very restlessness by means of what is well-known to all the world, saying "for it is restless" (*cañcalaṃ hi*).
The mind is restless—that is, exceedingly mobile, having the inherent nature of constant movement.
For this is indeed well known:

he is called Kṛṣṇa because he ploughs away—that is, removes—the faults of his devotees, such as sins, even when they are impossible to ward off in every way; or because he draws toward himself and bestows upon them the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), even those that are impossible for them to attain in every way.

By addressing him in this manner, he indicates that you alone are capable of warding off even the most difficult-to-restrain restlessness of the mind and attaining even the most hard-to-reach bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Not only is it exceedingly restless, but it is also "agitating" (*pramāthin*), meaning its nature is to afflict and disturb both the body and the senses;
the sense is that, by virtue of its agitating quality, it is the cause of helplessness for the aggregate of the body and senses.
Furthermore, it is powerful, being impossible to turn away from its desired object by any means whatsoever;
moreover, it is firm, being interwoven with thousands of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding sense objects.
"In the Bhāṣya it is stated that it is impossible to break and cannot be cut, like a *tantu-nāga*;
*tantu-nāga* means a serpent-noose (*nāga-pāśa*)."
*Tāntanī* refers to a specific kind of creature dwelling in great lakes, well-known in regions such as Gurjara;

because of its extreme firmness, the strength of that powerful being, its capacity for destruction, and its great restlessness, I consider the restraint, confinement, and immobilization of a highly intoxicated wild elephant to be extremely difficult and impossible to accomplish in every respect.
"Like the wind":
the meaning is that just as it is impossible to achieve stillness and effect the cessation of the wind blowing violently in the sky, so it is here.
This is the underlying point.

Even when the knowledge of reality has arisen, for a person who continues to live in order to experience the fruits of karma already set in motion (*prārabdha-karma*), the mental states characterized by agency, enjoyership, pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth, constitute bondage because they are the cause of affliction (*kleśa*); this bondage persists as a "residual trace" (*bādhitānuvṛtti*).
However, its cessation through yoga in the form of the restraint of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*) is called liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
It has been stated that by the accomplishment of which that yogin is considered supreme; regarding this, it is said: Is bondage warded off from the witness, or rather from the mind?
Not the first, because bondage is already removed from the witness by the knowledge of reality itself;
nor the second, because it is impossible for its own nature to undergo a reversal,
and because of the presence of its opposite.

For indeed, it is not possible to prevent moisture from water or heat from fire; for, according to the principle that "all entities undergo transformation at every moment except for the power of consciousness," the mind is by nature subject to momentary transformation. Consequently, even the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which has set out to destroy ignorance along with its effects through the experience of *prārabdha* karma, encounters an obstruction.
Having established the body, senses, and so forth for the purpose of yielding their own respective fruits,
it is not possible for karma to bring about the experience of its own fruits— such as pleasure and pain— without the fluctuations of the mind (*citta-vṛtti*).
Therefore, even if it were somehow possible through yoga to suppress the natural transformations of the mind, [the result would still follow].

Nevertheless, because the karma whose fruit has already begun (prārabdha-karma) is more powerful than even yoga—which is like the knowledge of reality—I believe that when the flickering of the mind is inevitable, its cessation through yoga is impossible; I hold this to be so simply by my own understanding.
Therefore, Arjuna’s objection is: "Thus, the statement that 'the supreme yogi is considered one who sees equality everywhere by means of self-comparison' is untenable. //34//
Viśvanātha says: He states this very point with the words "unsteady" (cañcalam).

Now, one might object that according to such scriptural passages as, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body indeed as the chariot" (Kaṭhopaniṣad 1.3.3), [the mind is merely an instrument].

And from the Smṛti: "They say the body is the chariot, the senses are the horses, the mind is the reins, the lord of the senses is the driver, the paths are the objects of perception, and the intellect is the charioteer. (BhP 7.15.41)
If it is argued that since the mind is seen to be the controller of the intellect, the mind can indeed be brought under control by means of a discriminating intellect, to this he says: "powerful.
Just as a powerful disease disregards even a medicine that naturally pacifies it, so too does the mind, by its very nature, disregard the intellect even when that intellect possesses discrimination.

Moreover, I consider it as difficult to restrain the mind as it is to suddenly pierce solid iron even with the needle of an extremely subtle intellect, or to restrain the wind—that is, to arrest the wind blowing violently in the sky—by means of yoga through the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-yoga). //34//
Baladeva says: He states that very point with the words "for [the mind] is flickering" (*cañcalaṃ hi*).
By its very nature, the mind is flickering. Now, one might object: "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself."
Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind to be the reins.
"The senses are said to be the horses, and their objects are the paths;

the wise say that the self, joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer" (KaṭhU 1.3.4). Since this scripture states that the mind is to be restrained by the intellect, one might argue that it is possible to bring it under control through a discerning intellect. To this, he replies with the word "pramāthī" (the agitating).
It even overcomes such an intellect.
Why? Just as a powerful disease disregards even a potent medicine that naturally pacifies it, so it is here.
Furthermore, like iron pierced by a needle, it cannot be split even by such an intellect; therefore, I consider its restraint through yoga to be as extremely difficult as that of the wind.
"For it is not possible to grasp the wind with the fist; therefore, tell us the means for that. //34//
The Blessed Lord said:
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain.
But by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is mastered. //35//

Śrīdhara: Having thus acknowledged the restlessness and other qualities [of the mind], the Blessed Lord spoke of the means for restraining the mind, beginning with the words "asaṃśayam" (without doubt).
As for what you say—that the mind cannot be restrained due to its restlessness and so forth—this is indeed beyond doubt.
Nevertheless, it is mastered through practice, which consists of a mental state (*vṛtti*) whose form is the Supreme Self, and through detachment from sense objects.

The meaning is that, because dissolution is obstructed by practice (*abhyāsa*) and distraction is obstructed by dispassion (*vairāgya*), the mind remains with its fluctuations ceased, abiding in the form of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
As it is said in the Yoga-śāstra:
"The state of the mind, devoid of fluctuations, is its abiding in the form of Brahman."
This concentration is designated by the name "asamprajñāta" (the state beyond cognitive awareness). //35//
Madhusūdana, warding off this objection, the Blessed Lord said, "Without doubt.
He addresses him with satisfaction, saying: "The movement of your mind has been correctly understood; you will be able to restrain your mind."
"O mighty-armed one" (*mahābāho*): this indicates his unsurpassed excellence, as his two arms were once engaged in combat even with Mahādeva himself.
Because of the power of *prārabdha* karma, it is "difficult to restrain" (*asaṃyatātmanā durnigraham*)—meaning impossible to subdue even with great effort.
These three qualifying adjectives—"afflicting" (*pramāthi*), "powerful" (*balavat*), and "firm" (*dṛḍham*)—have been stated here in combination.

"The mind is restless and flickering by nature"—of this there is no doubt; there is indeed no doubt in this matter. The meaning is that you speak the truth. Even so, by means of the practice of *samādhi* alone, through detachment (*vairāgya*) and self-restraint, that mind is grasped—that is, it is restrained and rendered devoid of all fluctuations.
This is stated in order to highlight the distinction between one who lacks restraint and an undisciplined self, and one who possesses restraint and a disciplined self.

The word *tu* [indicates a distinction]. The word *ca* is used to indicate the conjunction of practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) for the purpose of restraining the mind. By addressing him as "O Kaunteya," He consoles him by pointing to the bond of affection, implying: "As the son of your father's sister, you must certainly be made happy by me. Here, it is stated that in the first half [of the verse], the forceful restraint of the mind is not possible, whereas in the second half, gradual restraint is indeed possible.
For the restraint of the mind is twofold: by force and by gradual means.

In this regard, the organs of cognition such as the eyes and ears, and the organs of action such as the voice and hands, are restrained by force through the mere obstruction of their physical seats (*golaka*).
By means of that analogy, a deluded person falls into the error of thinking, "I shall forcibly restrain the mind as well.
However, it cannot be restrained in such a manner, because its physical seat—the heart-lotus—cannot be blocked.
For this very reason, gradual restraint alone is appropriate; regarding this, the venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Even by sitting down again and again, one who knows the mind cannot conquer the mind repeatedly without an irreproachable method.
Just as a rutting, wicked elephant cannot be controlled without a goad,
so too [the mind cannot be tamed] without the acquisition of inner science and association with the virtuous.
The complete abandonment of latent impressions and the cessation of the movement of the vital breath— these,
indeed, are the mature methods for conquering the mind.
"Those who, despite these methods being available, restrain the mind by force, are like those who cast away a lamp and try to destroy the darkness with collyrium. Thus,
for gradual restraint, the mastery of inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) is the sole means.
For it (the Guru) awakens one to the falsity of the visible world and to the self-luminous nature of ultimate bliss and absolute reality of the object of vision.
And this being so, the mind, having understood its own objects, subsides of its own accord like a fire without fuel.
As for those who do not properly understand the truth even when it has been taught, or those who forget it, for them the only means is association with the virtuous.
For the virtuous repeatedly awaken and remind one [of the truth].

However, for one who—afflicted by the evil tendencies of pride in learning and the like—is unable to follow the virtuous, the only means is the abandonment of those tendencies through the aforementioned discernment (*viveka*).
But for one who, due to the extreme strength of these tendencies, is unable to abandon them, the only means is the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spanda*).
Since both the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and latent dispositions (*vāsanā*) are the motivators of the mind, when these two are restrained, the pacification of the mind is established.
This very point was stated by that same [author]: "The two seeds of the tree of the mind are the vibration of the vital breath and latent dispositions."
And when one of those two is exhausted, both quickly perish.
Through firm practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), by means of the method imparted by the Guru,
and through the yoga of posture and diet, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained.
Because one acts without attachment, because one avoids the cultivation of existence,
and because one perceives the destruction of the body, latent tendencies do not arise.
Through the complete abandonment of latent impressions, the mind attains the state of non-mind;
through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, do as you wish.
O Rāghava, I consider this alone to be the nature of the mind:
that it consists of the contemplation of an object both as an internal reality and through its aesthetic flavor.
When nothing whatsoever— whether of the nature of what is to be abandoned or what is to be adopted— is cultivated,
and one remains having relinquished everything, then the mind is not born.

"When the mind, due to the absence of latent impressions (*avāsanatva*), does not think at all, then 'no-mind' (*amanastā*) arises, which bestows the state of the Supreme Self. In this regard, two means alone are established for the purpose of arresting the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spanda*): practice (*abhyāsa*).
And dispassion (*vairāgya*) is for the purpose of abandoning latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

As for association with the virtuous and the acquisition of spiritual knowledge (*adhyātma-vidyā*), they are already established as means for producing practice and dispassion; thus, they are included within those two.
For this very reason, the Blessed One spoke of only these two: "by practice and by dispassion."
Therefore, the Blessed Patañjali formulated the aphorism: "Their cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion" (Yoga Sūtra 1.12).

This refers to the cessation of all those aforementioned fluctuations—comprising five types, namely valid cognition, misconception, conceptualization, sleep, and memory—which are infinite, and which are either afflicted by being demonic in nature or unafflicted by being divine in nature; this cessation is like a fire whose fuel has been exhausted.
The transformation known as tranquility (*upaśama*) arises through the combined application of practice and dispassion.
As it is stated in the *Yoga-bhāṣya*: "The river of the mind flows in two directions; it flows toward the auspicious and it flows toward the evil.
Therein, that which is inclined toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and directed downward toward discernment (*viveka*) is the one that flows toward the auspicious."
But that stream which flows downward toward non-discrimination and slopes toward saṃsāra is the carrier of evil.

In that regard, the stream of sense objects is blocked by dispassion (*vairāgya*), and the stream of the auspicious is opened by the practice of the vision of discrimination (*viveka*). Thus, the cessation of mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*) depends upon both.
In that state, the mind is explained as being inclined toward discernment (*viveka-nimna*) and having liberation (*kaivalya*) as its downward slope (*prāg-bhāra*).

Just as the flow of a river, though possessed of intense velocity, is diverted by the construction of a dam and, through the channeling of an irrigation trench (*kulyā*), a different lateral current is produced directed toward a field; so too, by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), the flow of objects in the river of the mind is restrained.

Since the state of flowing in tranquility is accomplished through the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is indeed a combination [of means] due to the distinction between these gateways;
for if there were only a single gateway, there would be the dilemma of choosing between rice and barley (*brīhi-yava-dvikalpa*).
This is because practice, characterized by repetition, is possible for ritual actions such as the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*) and the meditation on deities (*devatā-dhyāna*).

To dispel the doubt as to what constitutes the practice (*abhyāsa*) of that samādhi which consists in the cessation of all activity, he provides the aphorism on practice: "Practice is the effort toward steadiness therein" (YS 1.13).

Here, "therein" refers to the pure conscious self (*cid-ātman*), the seer established in its own nature; "steadiness" is the state of immobility consisting in the mind's flow in a tranquilized condition, free from fluctuations. The "effort" for that purpose is mental enthusiasm, directed toward that which—due to its inherent restlessness—is by nature prone to flow outward.

The thought "I shall bring the mind to cessation in every way"—this kind of practice, when it is being cultivated, is called *abhyāsa* (practice). That [practice], however, when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with devotion, becomes firmly established (*dṛḍha-bhūmi*). It is practiced for a long time without despondency; it is practiced without interruption by means of the absence of breaks; and it is practiced with devotion (*sat-kāreṇa*).
And when practiced with an excess of faith,
that practice becomes firmly established and cannot be shaken by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sensual pleasures.
Whether for a short period or a long period, even if interrupted—

If one practices with interruptions, lacks an excess of faith, and fails to avoid lethargy (laya), distraction (vikṣepa), passion (kaṣāya), and the relishing of pleasure (sukhāsvāda), then because the latent impressions of the emergent state (vyutthāna-saṃskāra) remain powerful, the practice will not be on a firm ground and will not lead to its fruit; therefore, these three [faith, vigor, and mindfulness] are prescribed.
Detachment (vairāgya), moreover, is of two kinds: the lower (apara) and the higher (para).
This [discriminative discernment] is further divided into four types by way of the notion of self, the notion of difference, the notion of unity, and the notion of mastery.

Among these, with the intention of explaining the attainment of the higher stages through the conquest of the preceding stages, he formulated the fourth alone: "Dispassion is the notion of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard" (Yoga Sūtra 1.15).

Women, food, drink, power, and so forth are the objects perceived through the senses; heaven, disembodied liberation (*videhatā*), absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*), and so forth are the objects revealed by sacred tradition (*anuśravika*) as being Vedic. In both these types of objects, while craving still exists, the triad beginning with "endeavor" (*yatamāna*) arises according to the degree of one's discriminative discernment (*viveka*).
In this world, the exertion of one who strives with the thought, "I shall learn through the teacher and the scriptures what is essential and what is non-essential," is *yatamāna*.

The discernment, like that of a physician, by means of the discrimination being practiced, of identifying among the defects previously existing in one's own mind which have been ripened and which remain, is *vyatireka*.
[This occurs] regarding the engagement with objects seen or heard...

Through the realization of the nature of suffering, even though craving does not produce the activity of the senses, its remaining in the mind as mere longing constitutes "one-sensed" (ekendriya) detachment.

When there is a total absence of craving even in the mind, that mental state which opposes craving and consists of the clarity of knowledge is called "the notion of mastery" (vaśīkāra-saṃjñā); this is dispassion (*vairāgya*). It is an internal means for cognitive (*samprajñāta*) samādhi, but an external means for non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi.
However, its internal means is supreme detachment (*vairāgya*) alone.
And he [Patañjali] set this forth in a sūtra: "That [detachment] is the absence of thirst for the *guṇas*, following upon the discernment of the Puruṣa" (Yoga Sūtra 1.16).
Through proficiency in *samprajñāta-samādhi*, there arises the discernment—that is, direct realization—of the Puruṣa as distinct from the *pradhāna*, which consists of the three *guṇas*.

Furthermore, that state of being free from thirst (vaitṛṣṇya) regarding all activities pertaining to the three qualities (guṇas) is the supreme, most excellent dispassion (vairāgya), which constitutes the fruit.
And from the maturation of that [dispassion], due to the resulting maturation of the tranquility of the mind, isolation (kaivalya) occurs without delay. //35//
Viśvanātha:
Accepting the point thus stated, he confirms it with the words "without doubt":
what you have said is indeed true.

However, just as even a powerful disease is surely pacified over a long period of time by the administration of its remedial medicine— applied according to the methods of a skilled physician and practiced repeatedly—

so too the mind, though difficult to restrain, can be grasped and brought under one's own control through practice in the manner taught by a true guru, by the repeated cultivation of the yoga of meditation on the Supreme Lord, and by detachment through non-attachment to sense objects.
The meaning is "it is possible.
And thus says the Pātañjala-sūtra: "Its cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion" (Yoga Sūtra 1.12).
O Mahābāhu! In battle, even great heroes are conquered by you.
And even he who holds the Pināka bow in his hand has been brought under control by him; what then?
The sense is that only when the chief warrior named Manas—the crest-jewel of great heroes—can be conquered by the employment of the great yoga-weapon, can one truly be called "long-armed."
"O son of Kuntī"—in this regard, you should not fear;
the sense is that since you are the son of Kuntī, my father’s sister, I must provide assistance to you. //35//
Baladeva: Having accepted the point stated, the Blessed One said, "Without doubt.

Nevertheless, the mind can be restrained through the practice of being solely intent upon the self-luminous bliss [of the Self] and by turning toward the qualities of the Self; likewise, it can be restrained through dispassion (*vairāgya*) born from perceiving defects in objects external to the Self.
Thus, by the practice of tasting the bliss of the Self, *laya* (dissolution) is obstructed, and by dispassion toward sense-objects, *vikṣepa* (distraction) is obstructed.

Just as a mind that has ceased its restlessness becomes easy to grasp through the use of good medicine administered by a skilled physician and practiced repeatedly over a long period until it is indeed pacified,
so too the mind, though difficult to restrain, is [subdued] through practice in the manner taught by a true guru, by means of the yoga of meditation upon the Supreme Lord.

The meaning is that by constant practice (*anuśīlana*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and non-attachment to sense objects (*viṣayeṣv anāsaṅga*), it is "grasped," which is to say it can be brought under one's own control.
Accordingly, the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: "Its cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion" (Yoga Sūtra 1.12).
"O mighty-armed one! Since even great heroes are conquered by you in battle, and even the wielder of the Pināka bow was brought under your control— what of that?"

If the preeminent warrior named Manas, who is like a crest-jewel upon the head of a great hero, can be conquered by the employment of the great weapon of Yoga, then indeed [the enemy] will be "one with mighty arms"— this is the sense.
O Kaunteya, do not fear in this matter.
The intention is that since you are the son of Kuntī, my father’s sister, I must provide assistance to you. //35//
"Yoga is difficult to attain by one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my view.
But it can be attained through the proper means by one who strives with a self-subdued mind. (6.36)
Śrīdhara: He states "by one whose self is uncontrolled" (*asaṃyata*) to show that this is the definitive conclusion here.
Yoga is difficult to attain—that is, impossible to achieve—by one whose self, meaning the mind (*citta*), is not controlled by the aforementioned practice and dispassion (*abhyāsa-vairāgya*).

However, by a person whose self, meaning the mind, is brought under control and remains obedient through practice and dispassion, yoga can indeed be attained by exerting effort through this very same means. //36//
Madhusūdana:

As for what you said—that since karma whose fruit has already begun (prārabdha-bhoga) is more powerful than even the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna), when its own results are to be given, how can the mental modifications (vṛttis) being produced therein be restrained?—to that it is replied: "by one whose self is free from doubt" (asaṃśayātmanā).
And thus the Blessed Vasiṣṭha said:
"O descendant of Raghu, indeed everything here in this world is always obtained by everyone through human effort when it is properly applied."
Human effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is contrary to the scriptures and that which is in accordance with the scriptures.
Among these, that which is contrary to the scriptures leads to misfortune, while that which is in accordance with the scriptures leads to the ultimate goal.

That which is contrary to the scriptures (*ucchāstra*)—prohibited by the scriptures—leads to misfortune and hell. That which is ordained by the scriptures (*śāstrita*)—prescribed by the scriptures—leads to the ultimate goal through the purification of the inner organ; among the four aims of life, it leads to the supreme liberation.
Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are a river flowing along two paths: the auspicious and the inauspicious.
One should be joined to the auspicious path through human effort and exertion.
O best among the powerful, by means of human effort and strength, draw your own mind away from unwholesome things and establish it only in wholesome ones.
O crusher of enemies, know that when, through the power of immediate practice, your latent tendencies arise, then you should recognize the success of that practice.
The remaining word is "virtuous" (śubha).
Even when there is doubt, intensely cultivate only the virtuous;
O dear one, when the latent impression (vāsanā) of the virtuous increases, there is no fault whatsoever.
As long as your mind is unrefined and you have not realized that state,
practice what has been determined by the authority of the Guru and the scriptures.
"Therefore, once the impurities have been cooked away and the reality has certainly been known,
even this stream of latent impressions, though auspicious, must be abandoned by you who are intent on cessation.
Thus, although the transmigratory existence residing in the witness— which is rooted in non-discrimination— is removed through the direct realization of discrimination, [the following applies].
When the natural fluctuations of the mind— which is sustained by *prārabdha* karma— are removed through the effort of yoga practice, one is a liberated-while-living (*jīvanmukta*) and a supreme yogi.
However, it is established that in the absence of the cessation of mental fluctuations, even one who possesses knowledge of reality is not a supreme yogi.
The remainder should be investigated in detail in the *Jīvanmuktiviveka*. //36//
Viśvanātha:
To this [objection], namely that "this is mere reflection," he says: "By one whose self is not restrained through practice and dispassion"—that is, by one whose mind is not controlled by those two.

However, even for a person whose self has become subdued (*vaśyātman*), meaning one whose mind has come under control, yoga—characterized as the restraint of the mind, i.e., *samādhi*—can be attained through means (*upāyataḥ*) only by one who strives for a long time, because of the abundance of the necessary instruments (*sādhana*).
It is possible. //36//

Baladeva: "By one whose self is uncontrolled. By that person whose *ātman*—the mind—is not controlled by the two aforementioned means, namely practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), yoga—characterized by the cessation of the modifications of the mind (*citta-vṛtti-nirodha*)—is difficult to attain, being impossible to achieve even by a wise man.
[But] by that person whose *ātman*—the mind—is subdued and brought under control by those two...

Nevertheless, that yoga can be attained by one who strives—that is, by one possessing such effort—through the means characterized by my worship and through the yoga of action performed without desire; this is my conviction. (36)
BhG 6.37 Arjuna said:
One who is endowed with faith but lacks self-control, whose mind has strayed from yoga—
O Kṛṣ�ṇa, failing to attain perfection in yoga, what goal does one reach? (37)
Śrīdhara: Arjuna asked, "What fruit does one obtain who, due to the absence of practice and dispassion, somehow fails to attain right knowledge? [The Lord replies:
"One who lacks effort" (ayatir), meaning one who was initially engaged in yoga endowed with faith, and not through hypocritical conduct.
Beyond that, however, one who lacks self-restraint does not strive properly;
the meaning is that his practice has become lax.
Thus, failing to attain the perfection of yoga—the fruit of which is knowledge—due to the slackening of practice and dispassion, what state does he reach? //37//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, by the preceding text, the yogi who has produced knowledge of reality but for whom supreme liberation while living (jīvanmukti) has not yet arisen is considered [an ordinary] yogi;
however, it was stated that the one who has produced knowledge of reality and produced liberation while living is considered the supreme yogi.

Through the knowledge of both of these, even though ignorance has been destroyed, as long as the body and the aggregate of the senses persist due to the karma that has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha-bhoga*), and upon the exhaustion of that karma which bears fruit, because the current body and aggregate of senses also perish and there is no cause for further production,
there is no doubt whatsoever regarding disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*).

But he who, having attained purification of the mind culminating in the desire for liberation (*vividiṣā*) through previously performed actions, and having renounced all ritual duties because his task was accomplished, attains the state of a wandering mendicant of the highest order (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*); and having approached a Guru— who is himself a wandering mendicant of the highest order, liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) through the direct realization of the Self, and capable of awakening others— he receives from him the instruction on the great Vedāntic aphorisms (*mahāvākya*).

Having attained that [state], in order to eliminate the obstacles known as the lack of conviction (*asambhāvanā*) and contrary conceptions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*), he— though already endowed with faith— begins, through the grace of his teacher, to perform hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) by means of the four-chapter *Mīmāṃsā* beginning with "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahma-jijñāsā*, VS 1.1.1) and ending with "Non-return, on account of the Word" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*, VS 4.4.23).
Due to the brevity of life and the resulting lack of effort, one whose knowledge has not reached maturity perishes midway while still engaged in hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption.
Being devoid of the maturation of knowledge, such a person is not liberated because their ignorance remains undestroyed.
Nor does he experience the world of the gods— the fruit of ritual action accompanied by meditation— by way of the path beginning with light;
nor does he experience the world of the ancestors— the fruit of mere ritual action— by way of the path beginning with smoke,
because both rituals and meditations have been abandoned.

Therefore, one might wonder whether such a person who has fallen from yoga, being ignorant, would go to a miserable state—like one who has fallen away from the conduct of their *varṇa* and *āśrama*—because they lack connection with either the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*);
or, on the other hand, whether they would not go to a miserable state because they are devoid of actions censured by the scriptures, like Vāmadeva. Thus, the mind is agitated by doubt.

Arjuna said: "Ayati" means one who lacks effort (*ayati*); *yati* means one habituated to exertion. The negative particle *nañ* here has the sense of "little," as in the expression "rice-gruel with little salt" (*alavaṇā yavāgūḥ*). Thus, *ayati* means one of little effort.

"Endowed with faith" means being possessed of a mind characterized by trust in the words of the Guru and the Vedānta. Furthermore, "faith" is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of its concomitants, such as tranquility and the rest, according to the Śruti: "Having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and endowed with faith, one sees the Self in the very Self.

By this, [the required qualifications are] the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal objects, dispassion toward enjoyments here and hereafter, the possession of tranquility, self-control, withdrawal, patience, faith, and so forth, and the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā).
And thus, even though one endowed with the fourfold means approaches a guru and engages in hearing the Vedāntic texts and so forth,
because the supreme lifespan is short and because the senses are distracted at the time of death— rendering the performance of spiritual practices impossible—
the mind may stray from yoga; [this occurs] prior to the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra) which is born from the ripening of hearing and other practices through yoga.

He whose mind has wavered and has not attained that fruit— having failed to achieve the perfection of yoga, which consists of the cessation of ignorance and its effects through the knowledge of reality, accompanied by non-return— dies while still ignorant of reality; O Kṛṣṇa, what destination does he go to— is it a good state or a miserable one?

Because of the abandonment of [forbidden] actions, because knowledge has not arisen, because of the performance of the means to liberation taught in the scriptures, and because of being free from actions censured by the scriptures. //37//
Viśvanātha:
Now, you have stated that yoga is attained only by a person who exerts effort through both practice and dispassion;
yet, for one in whom even this triad is not observed—
He asks, "What is his destination?

The term *ayatiḥ* means one who exerts little effort; here the negative particle *nañ* is used in the sense of "little," as in the word *anavarṇa* (meaning "of little color"). Furthermore, he is "endowed with faith" (*śraddhayopetaḥ*), meaning possessed of conviction in the Yoga scriptures; that is, he is simply one who has set out to practice yoga, being endowed with faith therein.
But it is not false conduct through deceiving the world;
rather, it refers to one whose mind has deviated from yoga and become inclined toward sense objects due to the absence of practice and dispassion.

Therefore, "without attaining the perfect accomplishment (saṃsiddhi) of yoga"—meaning he has indeed attained some minor accomplishment—he [falls] from the stage of one desiring to ascend to yoga to the first stage of actually ascending to yoga.
The meaning is that he has entered the armpit. //37//

Baladeva: It has been stated more than once that the yoga of action performed without desire (niṣkāma-karma-yoga), which contains knowledge within it, is crowned by the eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga), crushes all obstacles, and serves as the means for beholding one's own Supreme Self. And regarding such [yoga], it was previously stated that "there is no loss here of the effort made" (*nehābhikrama-nāśo 'sti*). Because of that aforementioned greatness, Arjuna asks about its majesty with the words "the non-striver" (*ayatiḥ*). Through practice, dispassion, and diligent effort, a person will certainly attain yoga.

But he who is first endowed with faith— that is, with confidence in the scriptures that describe such yoga— yet is a non-exertor (*ayati*), meaning one who lacks effort in the performance of his own duty (here the negative prefix *nañ* has the sense of "small," as in the word "anudarā" for a slender young woman); because of this laxity of effort, his mind has strayed from the eight-limbed yoga and is inclined toward sense objects.
