And thus, due to the slackening of his practice of performing his own duty and his dispassion, he has not attained the perfect accomplishment of various forms of yoga— characterized by the purification of the heart and characterized by the vision of the Self—
but he has indeed attained some degree of accomplishment, being full of faith.
Having performed some portion of his own duty and having commenced yoga, but not having attained the fruit of yoga, what destination does he go to at the end of the body? O Kṛṣṇa! (37)
O mighty-armed one, I hope that he who has fallen away from both, being deluded on the path of Brahman and without support, does not perish like a scattered cloud. (6.38)
Śrīdhara explains the intention behind the question with the words "kaccit" (I hope):
because actions have been offered to the Lord and not performed [as worldly duties], one does not obtain the fruits of action such as heaven;
and because yoga has not been perfected, one does not obtain liberation.

Thus, having fallen from both, being without support and without refuge, and therefore being utterly bewildered on the path—the way that is the means for attaining Brahman—one might ask: does he perish, or does he not perish? This is the meaning.

The illustration for destruction is as follows: just as a severed cloud, having detached from the preceding cloud and not yet reached another cloud, dissolves right in the middle; such is the meaning. //38//
Madhusūdana explains this very seed of doubt with the words "kaccit" (I hope that...).
The word "kaccit" is used here in the sense of an inquiry made with desire.

O Mahābāho: "Mahat" refers to those who are capable of warding off all calamities for all devotees, or alternatively, to those who are capable of bestowing the four goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). He whose four arms possess these qualities—thus, by the term *mahābāhu*, it is indicated that there is an absence of anger caused by the question and a capacity to endure the giving of its answer. [The Lord is] "vimūḍhaḥ" (deluded/confused) regarding the path of Brahman—that is, the way to attain Brahman, which is knowledge (*jñāna*).
That is to say, one who has not attained the direct realization of the non-arisen identity of Brahman and the Self.

"Without support" means being devoid of the two supports—the practices of meditation and ritual action—which are the causes for proceeding along the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*).

Such a person, having fallen away from both—having fallen from the path of action as well as the path of knowledge—is like a scattered cloud: like a cloud severed by the wind, broken into pieces, and fallen from its former mass toward the next.

Just as a cloud that has not reached the sky, being unfit for rain, perishes in mid-air, so too one who has fallen from yoga— severed from the previous path of action and having failed to reach the subsequent path of knowledge— perishes in the interval alone, along with the fruit of his actions.
The meaning of the question is: "Is it not the case that one is incapable of attaining the fruit of knowledge?
By this, the combination of knowledge and ritual action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*) is refuted;

for according to that position, since the attainment of the fruit of ritual action would still be possible even upon attaining the fruit of knowledge, the state of being "fallen from both" would be impossible.

Nor should it be argued that the statement regarding the loss of the fruit is untenable because, even though the action occurs for him, he has abandoned the desire for its fruit; for it has been demonstrated many times, by citing the words of Āpastamba as an example, that actions performed even by those free from desire possess the existence of a fruit.
Therefore, this question is directed specifically at one who has renounced all ritual actions, for it is only in that case that the apprehension of attaining an undesirable result is possible. //38//
Viśvanātha:
"Kaccit" (perhaps) is used here as an interrogative particle.
"Fallen from both" means he has fallen away from the path of action and has not properly attained the path of yoga.

"Like a severed cloud" means that just as a severed cloud— a mass of water— having detached from the preceding cloud and not yet reached another cloud, dissolves in mid-air; so too, for this person, there is the suffering of a desire to abandon the enjoyment of sense objects due to entering the path of yoga in this world, while simultaneously having a desire for the enjoyment of sense objects due to the absence of perfect dispassion (*samyag-vairāgya*).

And because in the next world there is an absence of karma that achieves heaven, and because yoga—which is the means to liberation—is also unripened, neither heaven nor liberation is attained; thus it is indicated that his destruction occurs in both worlds.

Therefore, being utterly deluded on the path—the way leading to the attainment of Brahman—and being "without support," meaning having failed to reach a firm footing or a refuge, you are asked: "Does he perish? Does he not perish? //38//
Baladeva clarifies the intent of the question with the word "kaccit" (I hope).
Because he performed action without desire for results, he did not obtain fruits such as heaven; yet, because of his lack of success in yoga, he did not attain self-realization.
Thus, having fallen from both and being without support or refuge, does he perish or does he not perish? This is the meaning.
"Like a severed cloud": just as one cloud (megha), having been separated from a preceding cloud and not yet reached the next cloud, dissolves in the interval—this is the illustration for destruction.
How does such a doubt arise?
Regarding that, he says: "On the path of Brahman, which is the means of attainment, he is utterly deluded. (38)
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to dispel this doubt of mine entirely; for indeed, no one other than you is capable of being the remover of this doubt. (6.39)
Śrīdhara: "This doubt of mine must be dispelled by you alone, the omniscient one;
there is no one other than you who can remove this doubt," he says with the words "this" (etad) and "him" (enam).
Having cut it away, [you] are the remover; the rest is clear. //39//
Madhusūdana:
In order to dispel the doubt as it has been shown, Pārtha requests the Blessed One, the Inner Controller, saying "this of mine.
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever—meaning to remove—this very doubt of mine previously shown, entirely by uprooting the unrighteousness and other factors that are the root of doubt.
Fearing that some other seer or god might dispel this doubt of yours, he says "other than you":
other than you— the Supreme Lord, the omniscient author of the scriptures, the supreme teacher, and the compassionate one— there is no other,
whether seer or god, who is not the Lord and thus not omniscient, [capable of resolving] this doubt concerning the destination of the world beyond for one who has fallen from yoga.

Since he is indeed the cutter—that is, the destroyer—by means of providing the correct answer, and since [this doubt] does not arise and is not possible, therefore you alone, as the direct witness and supreme teacher of all, ought to cut through this doubt of mine; such is the meaning. //39//
Viśvanātha: This is that very thing. //39//
Baladeva: The neuter gender in "etat" is an archaic usage (ārṣa).
Regarding "tvat": other than you, the Lord of all and the Omniscient, there is some other non-sovereign, limited-knowledge seer (ṛṣi). //39//
The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, for him there is no destruction either here or hereafter.
For no one who performs good deeds, my dear, goes to a state of misery. //40//
Śrīdhara: To that, the Blessed Lord replied with four and a half verses beginning with "O Pārtha":
in this world, ruin consists of falling away from both [dharma and artha], resulting in degradation; in the next world, ruin consists of attaining hell.
Neither of those two states exists for him at all;
for no one who performs good deeds and acts auspiciously ever goes to an evil destiny,
and this person is a doer of good because he has engaged in yoga with faith.
Addressing him as "Father," he awakens him by consoling him according to worldly custom. //40//
Madhusūdana:
Thus, dispelling Arjuna’s apprehension regarding the destruction of the yogi, the Blessed Lord spoke the reply beginning with "O Pārtha.
What is the meaning of the statement that "the yogi who has fallen away from both perishes"?
What is it that makes one censurable by the learned in this world through the abandonment of actions prescribed by the Vedas— namely,
becoming like some unrestrained person—
or what is it that causes one to attain an inferior state in the hereafter?
As it is stated in the Śruti: "Now, those who belong to neither of these two paths become worms, moths, and the like, or biting insects.
And likewise it was said by Manu: "A Brahmin who has fallen from his own duty becomes a *preta* (ghost) who eats vomit and has a mouth like a firebrand," and so forth.
To both of these [objections], He says: "O Pārtha, O Pārtha, for him there is no destruction either here or hereafter, provided he acts according to the scriptures."

For one who has renounced all actions, who is detached from everything, and who, having approached a guru, is engaged in hearing the Vedānta and so forth, there exists [no destruction] even if he dies in the interim—that is, for the one fallen from yoga.

He states the reason why there is no destruction for him in either case: because (hi) any person who performs auspicious deeds—that is, one who acts according to what is ordained by the scriptures—does not meet with misfortune (durgati), whether in this world as ill-repute or in the next as the state of being a worm and so forth.
He does not go [to a lower realm];
however, since he is already the most excellent of all, what need is there to say that he does not go to an evil destiny? This is the meaning.
He is called "father" (pitā) because he extends himself (tanoti) in the form of a son.
The suffix *aṇ* here is used in its own sense (*svārthika*), as in the words *tāta*, *rākṣasa*, and *vāyasa*.
Just as a father himself assumes the form of a son, he addresses the disciple—who occupies the position of a son—as "Father" (*tāta*) to indicate his extraordinary compassion.

As it has been said: one who falls from yoga goes to a miserable state if they lack knowledge, because, like one who has fallen away from their own duty (*svadharma*), they are connected with neither the path of the gods (*devayāna*) nor the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*).

That is incorrect, because the reason—that this [passage] is connected to the path of the gods—is unestablished (*asiddha*). For in the *pañcāgni-vidyā*, there is no distinction made between those who know thus and those who, in the forest, worship faith and truth; rather, it says, "They go forth to the light," just as it does for those who possess the knowledge of the five fires. Thus, it applies equally to those who perform the *ataskratu* rites.
This is because it is stated that even those seeking liberation who possess faith and truthfulness attain the world of Brahman by way of the path of the gods;
furthermore, for one devoted to hearing [the scriptures] and so forth who has fallen from yoga, faith is already established by the phrase "having become endowed with faith";
and truthfulness, in the form of the restraint of verbal activity consisting of speaking untruths, is already obtained by the phrase "peaceful and self-controlled."
For *dama* (self-restraint) is indeed the cessation of the unrestrained activity of the external senses;
and because it is stated as a limb of yoga in the *Yogaśāstra*: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession are the *yamas*" [Yoga Sūtra 2.30].
Even if, however, by the word "truth" (*satya*) Brahman itself is meant, there is no harm [to the argument].

This is because the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth also consists in the contemplation of the true Brahman; and even if one does not have that as one's primary purpose (*atat-kratutva*), the attainment of the world of Brahman is possible—just as in the case of those who know the five fires—as the Smṛti states: "From renunciation comes the station of Brahman."

Likewise, since even the daily investigation (*vicāra*) of Vedānta texts is a means for attaining the world of Brahman (*brahma-loka*), what is surprising about the collective group of these practices being a means to that same end? For this very reason, the Taittirīyas declare that the conduct of a yogi consists of all forms of meritorious action (*sarva-sukṛta-rūpa*), beginning with the passage, "Of this sacrifice of the one who knows thus" (*tasyaivaṃ viduṣo yajñasya*).
And it is also recorded in the Smṛti:
By him all the waters of every sacred ford have been bathed in; the entire earth has been gifted away;
a thousand sacrifices have been performed; and all the gods have been fully worshipped.
His own ancestors have been delivered from the cycle of existence, and he himself is worthy of worship by the three worlds.
He whose mind may attain steadiness for even a moment in the inquiry into Brahman—thus [it is said]. //40//
Viśvanātha:
He is so called because he performs a yoga that brings about auspiciousness and leads to the attainment of auspiciousness both in this world and in the next world. //40//
Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed One said, "O Pārtha":

for that yogin who possesses the characteristics previously described, there exists no destruction—neither in this world of material nature nor in the other world of non-material nature—characterized by the loss of happiness such as heaven, nor characterized by the loss of the vision of the Supreme Self. It does not happen.
Moreover, its attainment will certainly occur hereafter;

for this reason: one who performs good deeds—that is, one who undertakes the practice of the True Dharma which serves as the means to the supreme good—does not go to an evil rebirth, which consists in the absence of both [happiness and wealth], namely, poverty.

The address "tāta" is used out of extreme affection; it is derived from the etymology "he who [manifests] himself excessively in the form of a son. From that [root *tan*], the word *pitṛ* (father) is formed by adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthika*).
Therefore, out of great compassion, the father likewise instructs his son and disciple as the eldest [brother]. //40//

Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, one who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous. (6.41)

Śrīdhara: Then, in response to the inquiry "What does he obtain?", he says "Having reached" (prāpya). Having reached the worlds of the "merit-doers"—those who perform meritorious deeds such as the Aśvamedha sacrifice—and having dwelt there for "eternal years," that is, for many years, experiencing the pleasure of residence, [he is born among] the "pure," meaning those of virtuous conduct, and the "prosperous," meaning the wealthy.
In the home, one who has fallen from yoga is born; that is, he obtains birth. //41//
Madhusūdana:

Thus, since one who has fallen from yoga, by virtue of having performed meritorious deeds, suffers no ruin in either of the two worlds, it is said what happens to him with the word "attaining" (*prāpya*).

A certain person, having set out on the path of yoga, renounced all actions, and was engaged in such practices as hearing the Vedānta, dies in the interim; due to the manifestation of previously accumulated latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment, he [is drawn] toward sense objects.
One person longs [for rebirth], while another, due to the firmness of their cultivation of detachment (*vairāgya*), does not long for it.

Of these two, the former, having reached the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), proceeds by the path beginning with light (*arcis*) to the worlds of Brahman (*brahmaloka*).
Even though it is singular, the plural number is used with respect to the distinction between various planes of enjoyment (*bhoga-bhūmi*).

Having dwelt there— that is, having experienced residence— for eternal years, which are imperishable by the measure of Brahman, at the end of that period, one who has fallen from yoga— like Ajātaśatru, Janaka, and others— is born into the household or family of the pure, the stainless, the glorious, and the majestic great kings or universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), due to the continued presence of the drying up of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment.
"He is born again" means that, due to the intensity of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment,
he becomes a great king at the limit of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), unfit for the renunciation of all actions (*sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa*). //41//
Viśvanātha:

To the question, "In that case, what destination does he attain?", he says, "Having reached... [the worlds] of those who perform meritorious deeds, such as those who sacrifice with the Aśvamedha and other rites. Thus, the fruit of yoga consists of both liberation and enjoyment.
In that regard, when there is a desire for enjoyment, for an unripened yogin, there is only enjoyment upon the lapse of yoga;
however, for a fully ripened yogin, because a desire for enjoyment is impossible, there is only liberation.
Some, however, say that even for a fully ripened yogin, if by chance a desire for enjoyment arises—as seen in the cases of Kardama, Saubhari, and others—there is indeed enjoyment.
Of those who are pure, of good conduct, and prosperous—such as wealthy merchants and the like, or kings. //41//
Baladeva: He first describes the abundance of happiness pertaining to this world with the word "having attained.

Having attained those very objects for which he was previously slack in his own duty (*svadharma*) due to longing for sense-objects and fallen away from yoga—those same objects—he enjoys them by virtue of the greatness of having commenced his own desireless duty and yoga directed toward the Self. While enjoying them, he remains until there is a cessation of the thirst for such enjoyment through as many [lives] as are required.

Having dwelt for that many numerous and eternal years—many autumns—in those worlds, becoming free from thirst for those enjoyments, he is born in the home of the pure, those devoted to the true Dharma, those fit for yoga, and the illustrious wealthy, due to the greatness of the yoga previously undertaken; thus is shown this destiny for one who has fallen from yoga begun for a short time. //41//
Or else he is born into a family of wise yogis; for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in this world. (6.42)
Śrīdhara: This destination has been described for one who falls from yoga after practicing it for a short time.
However, he states an alternative case for one who falls from yoga after long practice with the words "or else" (athavā):
such a person is born into a family of the wise, those established in yoga, who are indeed possessors of knowledge.

But he does not praise this birth within the family of those previously mentioned who have ascended to yoga; for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to attain in the world, because it is the cause of liberation. //42//
Madhusūdana:
Regarding the second [alternative], he states another position with the words "Or else" (*athavā*).

However, when there is an abundance of auspicious qualities such as faith and dispassion, because of the absence of the latent impressions of enjoyment (*bhoga-vāsanā*), one does not reach the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds at all.
That birth of one fallen from yoga occurs only in the homes of poor Brahmins who are practitioners of yoga, and not in the houses of wealthy kings;
moreover, such a birth is difficult to obtain because it must be accomplished through manifold meritorious deeds and because it culminates in liberation.
As for that birth in the family of pure, poor Brahmins who possess the knowledge of Brahman—

For this is well known, like that of Śuka and others: "In this world, such a birth as this—one devoid of all causes for negligence—is rarer than even the rare. Thus, Viśvanātha praises the second [type of person], because of being devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment, he is fit for the renunciation of all actions (*sarva-karma-saṃnyāsa*).
This course of destiny has been described for one who falls away from yoga practiced for a short period of time.
However, regarding the fall from yoga practiced over a long period of time, he states an alternative view with the words "or else" (athavā).
This refers to yogins such as Nimi and others. //42//
Baladeva: With the words "Or else," he describes the destination of one who has fallen from yoga after practicing it for a long time.
He is born into a family of wise yogis who are practitioners of yoga and teachers of yoga.
He praises this twofold birth with the words "This... and so forth.
For those worthy of yoga who practice it, this birth—produced by the power of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous yoga—is extremely difficult for ordinary people to attain. //42//
There he regains the mental connection belonging to his previous body, and from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even more for perfection. 6.43
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says, "Therein," in one and a half verses. "Therein" refers to both types of birth; "paurvadehika" means pertaining to the previous body.
He attains union with that very [Self] through an intellect whose object is Brahman; and from that, he exerts himself even more intensely toward the perfection of liberation. //43//
Madhusūdana: Why is such a pair of births so difficult to obtain?
Because of the phrase "therein him" (*tatra tam*).

In that regard, even though birth is of two kinds, the term *paurvadehika* refers to that which pertains to the previous body; it means the connection with the intellect whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self— equivalent to the entire collection of its means— limited precisely to the extent to which [the practices] among all renunciation of action, approaching a teacher, hearing, reflecting, and meditating have been performed.
He obtains, he attains.

Not only does he obtain, but furthermore, immediately after that attainment, for the sake of accomplishing the higher stage beyond the stage already attained— for the sake of *saṃsiddhi*, which is liberation— he strives and exerts effort.

The meaning is that one accomplishes the stages [of yoga] until liberation. O descendant of Kuru, it is indicated— by mentioning the great-souled Kuru— that even for you, born into a family of pure and illustrious people, the attainment of knowledge will occur without effort due to the power of past impressions (*pūrva-vāsanā*), because you were born from one who had fallen away from yoga.
Chanting [the Lord's names].
This meaning is evident in the words of the venerable Vasiṣṭha,
as spoken by Śrī Rāma:
O Blessed One, what is the destiny of one who has ascended to the first, second, or even the third stage, yet has then passed away?

Previously, seven stages (*bhūmi*) were explained. Among them, the first stage, called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious), consists of the longing for liberation preceded by the discernment of the eternal and the non-eternal reality, by dispassion toward the enjoyment of objects in this world and the next, and by tranquility, self-control, faith, forbearance, renunciation of all actions,
and so forth.
First, there is the "perfection of the fourfold means" (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya-sampat*).

Following that, the third stage is called *tanu-mānasā*, which consists of the state of being free from doubt regarding the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) perfected through hearing and reflection;
this is equivalent to the "perfection of profound meditation" (*nididhyāsana-sampat*).
The fourth stage, however, is indeed the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*).
As for the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, they are intermediate distinctions within *jīvanmukti*, as was previously explained in the third [chapter].
In that regard, for one who has reached the fourth stage and dies, even though there is no *jīvanmukti*, there is absolutely no doubt concerning *videha-kaivalya* (liberation after death).

But for one who has attained the three stages beyond that, being liberated even while living, what need is there to mention when they are bodiless? Thus, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding these four stages.

However, regarding the three stages that serve as the means of attainment, because of the abandonment of action and the non-attainment of knowledge, doubt arises; it is precisely with respect to those that the question is posed.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
For an embodied being whose life has departed while on a stage of yoga,
previous misdeeds are exhausted in accordance with the specific portion of that stage attained.
Then, accompanied by his beloved, he delights in the celestial chariots of the gods, in the cities of the world-protectors, and in the groves and bowers of Mount Meru’s forests.
Then, when the accumulation of merit and previously committed misdeeds are completely exhausted through the depletion of their karmic results, yogins are born upon this earth.
Having been born in the secret homes of pure, prosperous, virtuous, and saintly people, these ones, perfumed by yoga, devote themselves solely to yoga.
"In that regard, having seen the sequence of the stages of yoga previously practiced through cultivation, the wise leap up to the higher sequence of stages.

Here, due to the strength of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment accumulated in the past and the weakness of the latent impressions for detachment practiced for only a short time, the renouncer of all actions experiences a longing for enjoyment at the moment of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkrānti*).
He who has been described as such is indeed that one;
however, he who— due to the intensity of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and by virtue of the grace of the Supreme Lord manifested through preeminent merit—

has no desire for the enjoyment of objects at the time of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇotkrānti*), is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) who, without the intervention of worldly enjoyment, [attains liberation] for the sake of the Brahmins.
Thus, one born into a family devoid of all causes for negligence among those who know Brahman may attain [liberation] with ease, through the manifestation of his past latent impressions (*saṃskāra*);

therefore, there is no need to suspect that he requires the previous [method] for liberation. This was not stated by Vasiṣṭha, but rather by the Blessed One, who is supremely compassionate, after proposing an alternative view (*pakṣāntara*) beginning with the word "or" (*athavā*).
The rest is clear. //43//
Viśvanātha:
In both types of birth, there is a connection with the intellect established in the Supreme Self (paramātman) that originated in a previous body—that is, from a former life. //43//
Baladeva: In that context, he states the means—caused by prior impressions—to explain the attainment of happiness and prosperity in the next world.
"Therein," in the two-fold birth, "pertaining to the previous body" means existing in the previous body;
through the intellect (*buddhi*), one attains a "connection," that is, a relationship, with one's own duty, the individual self, and the Supreme Self.

And then, with the attainment of perfection—which consists in the vision of one's own supreme Self through the purification of the heart—acting as the cause, he strives even more intensely than when first awakened from sleep, so that he may not again be struck down by obstacles. //43//
By that very previous practice, he is drawn forward even against his will; even one who merely desires to know Yoga transcends the Word-Brahman. (6.44)
Śrīdhara: The reason for this is stated as "by previous [practice].

By that very same practice performed in a former body, even one who is helpless—though unwilling due to some obstacle—is withdrawn from sense objects; being turned back from them, he is made to abide in Brahman.

Thus, by the power of previous practice, one who exerts effort is gradually liberated. He clarifies this point through the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so") in the verse beginning with "one who desires to know," consisting of one and a half verses.
One who merely desires to know the true nature of yoga, but has not yet attained it—
such a person, even if they have only just entered yoga and have fallen away from it due to the power of past sins, transcends the Word-Brahman, that is, the Veda;
he transcends the fruits of the ritual actions prescribed in the Vedas.
The meaning is that, having obtained a fruit superior to those, one is liberated. //44//
Madhusūdana:

Now, as for one who is born into a family of Vedic-knowing Brahmins that is free from all causes of negligence— because there is no interruption by the enjoyment of sense objects in their midst, his latent impressions (saṃskāra) from a previous birth are awakened, and thus [he attains realization] once again.
Granted that the attainment of the means for knowledge may indeed occur through the prior renunciation of all actions; however,

how can there be the awakening of the latent impressions of knowledge in one born into the family of illustrious universal monarchs— who are obstructed by various enjoyments of sense-objects and for whom the causes of negligence exist due to the intensity of the tendencies toward those enjoyments?
"How can one who, by virtue of being a *kṣatriya*, is unfit for the renunciation of all actions, obtain the means for the attainment of knowledge?
To this it is said: "By previous practice.

By that very same previous practice, accumulated even though separated by a very long interval of births—namely, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge acquired earlier—one is carried away, brought under one's own control, even if unwilling and even if not exerting oneself toward the means of liberation.
One is suddenly awakened from the latent impressions of worldly enjoyment (*bhoga-vāsanā*) and directed toward the means of liberation,

because even the latent impression of knowledge (*jñāna-vāsanā*), though practiced for only a short time, is more powerful than the latent impressions of enjoyment which have unreal things as their object, precisely because it has a real thing as its object.

See how you yourself, though engaged in battle and not conscious of knowledge, suddenly became oriented toward knowledge on the battlefield due to the power of prior mental impressions (*pūrva-saṃskāra*).
Therefore, it was stated previously: "In this, there is no loss of effort" (Gītā 2.40).
The intention is that even a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge, though separated by thousands of births, certainly performs its own function by suppressing all opposing factors.
For indeed, even in the absence of the renunciation of all actions, the eligibility for knowledge remains established for a Kṣatriya.

Just as a thief, even while many guards are present, might— though unwilling himself— overcome them all through his particular skill and carry off goods such as horses, and only afterwards does reflection arise as to when they were taken;
so too, one who has fallen from yoga, though existing amidst many obstacles to knowledge, [is carried away] even while unwilling himself.

Furthermore, it is indicated by the use of the root *hṛ* (to take) that [the mind], through the powerful mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge, overcomes all obstacles solely by its own specific capacity and is brought under its own control.

For this very reason, due to the intensity of that impression, even one who desires to know— that is, one who wishes to understand— Brahman, the object of yoga which is the knowledge that is the means to liberation, [is able to do so].

This refers to one who is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) established in the first stage (bhūmikā). Even he, having died in that very stage, may experience many sense-objects in the intermediate state and be reborn in a family of great kings or universal monarchs (cakravartin);
yet, though fallen from yoga, due to the strength of the predispositions (saṃskāra) of knowledge previously accumulated, he [attains] the Word-Brahman (śabda-brahman) in that very birth.
It transcends—that is, it stands beyond—the Veda that prescribes ritual action; the meaning is that by transcending the domain of action, one becomes eligible for knowledge (*jñāna*).

By this as well, the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of knowledge and action should be understood as refuted; for in the case of conjunction, even for the possessor of knowledge, there would be no transcendence of the section on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*). //44//
Viśvanātha:
He is "carried away" (hriyate), meaning he is drawn [toward it];
he even becomes one who desires to know the yoga of yoga.
Therefore, the word-Brahman—the Vedic scripture—transcends [the former]; that is to say, it exists by going beyond the path of ritual action prescribed in the Vedas.
However, the meaning is that it abides solely in the path of Yoga. //44//
Baladeva: The reason for this is as follows:

by that very same previous practice concerning yoga, that yogi is carried away—that is, drawn along—even against his will, despite some obstacle; the meaning is that even though he does not desire it.
The word "hi" indicates that this greatness of yoga is well-known.
But even one who merely desires to know yoga, having set out to practice it, transcends the Word-Brahman—the Veda which describes desire-driven action;
the meaning is that he does not strike against the Word. //44//
But the yogi who, through diligent effort, has purified all taints and attained perfection through many births— he, from that state, attains the supreme goal. (6.45)
Śrīdhara: Regarding the phrase "by effort":

if even a yogi with such slight effort attains the supreme goal, then what need is there to mention that yogi who, through effort, strives more and more intensely in yoga, making exertion, and by yoga alone becomes purified of all taints—his sins shaken off?

The meaning is: what need is there to say that one who has become fully perfected through yoga indicated by many births, having become a possessor of right knowledge, then attains the supreme goal? //45//
Madhusūdana:

And when one who has fallen from yoga, though dead while still on the first stage, even after being separated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of manifold enjoyments, obtains birth in a great royal family— a place full of various causes for negligence— nevertheless, by the power of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge previously accumulated...

If one becomes eligible for knowledge by transcending eligibility for ritual action, then what need is there to speak of one who dies on the second or third stage? Such a person, having either obtained birth in a great royal family at the end of his enjoyment of sense objects,

or having obtained birth in a Brahmin family as a knower of Brahman without even having completed his enjoyment— being fallen from yoga yet having transcended eligibility for action— is indeed eligible for knowledge.
Having become [such], and having accomplished the means for that, one is liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra through the attainment of its fruit.
This is what is meant by the phrase "through effort":
exerting oneself more and more than even previously performed effort, the yogi, possessing the impressions (saṃskāras) accumulated in the past, applies an excess of effort.
By that very merit resulting from the effort of yoga, his defilements are completely purified; the stains of sin that obstruct knowledge have been washed away.

Consequently, through the accumulation of impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the accumulation of merit over many births, he becomes perfected—having attained his final birth by means of an abundance of impressions and an abundance of merit—and then, through the maturation of the means, he attains the supreme, most excellent goal: liberation.
The meaning is that there is indeed no doubt whatsoever in this matter. //45//
Viśvanātha:
Thus, the cause of the failure of yoga has been stated to be precisely the slackening of effort (*ayatna*), as expressed in the words "one who is endowed with faith.
And for such a person who has failed in yoga due to the slackening of effort, the attainment of yoga again in another birth has indeed been declared.
But it is not [attained] immediately;
rather, perfect accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*) is determined to occur only after as many births as are required for that yoga to reach its full maturation.
But he who never at any time makes an effort toward laxity in yoga is not to be designated by the term "fallen from yoga"; rather,
[he attains perfection] through right yogic concentration ripened over many births.

As stated by Kardama: "Ascetics strive to perceive that state in empty dwellings" (BhP 3.24.28). He further says that even this is not accomplished in a single birth; the meaning is that one strives with effort—that is, one who exerts himself through preeminent effort.
The particle *tu* indicates the distinction of this person from the previously mentioned one who has fallen away from yoga.
Having his sins completely purified and his impurities fully matured, even he does not attain perfection in a single birth; thus, he attains the supreme goal, which is liberation. //45//
Baladeva: Now, with the words "through effort" (*prayatnāt*), he describes the attainment of happiness and prosperity in the hereafter.

Striving more and more than even from previous efforts—making an intensification of effort out of fear of prior obstacles—the yogi, by means of that accumulated effort, becomes one whose taints are thoroughly purified (*saṃśuddha-kilbiṣaḥ*), meaning all other latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been washed away.

Thus, one who has attained perfection through many births and whose yoga is fully matured goes to the supreme state—liberation characterized by the vision of one's own true self—solely on account of that maturation of yoga. //45//

The yogi is superior to the ascetics; he is considered superior even to those possessed of knowledge; and the yogi is superior to those who perform ritual actions. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi. 46.
Śrīdhara: Since this is so, [the text says] "to the ascetics" (tapasvibhyaḥ). This means to those devoted to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
and also to the "knowers" (*jñānibhyaḥ*), that is, to those who possess knowledge of the scriptures.
Even compared to those performers of ritual acts—those who perform sacrifices, works of public utility, and so forth—the yogi is my preferred superior;
therefore, you should become a yogi. //46//
Madhusūdana:
Now, the yogi is praised in order to enjoin yoga upon Arjuna by first generating in him an excess of faith, beginning with the verse "tapasvibhyaḥ.

Even compared to those devoted to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, the yogi is superior and more exalted; for, immediately after the arising of the knowledge of reality, he effects the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
"By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have gone to their end;
neither those who give sacrificial fees nor those ascetics who possess only limited merit go there"—so says the Śruti.
For this very reason, the yogin is superior to the performers of rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, which are accompanied by the distribution of sacrificial fees.
Because those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*) and ascetics (*tapasvinaḥ*) are unfit for liberation due to their ignorance;
and because even among the possessors of knowledge, the yogi possessing immediate realization (*aparokṣa-jñānavān*) is considered superior to those possessing mediate knowledge (*parokṣa-jñānavant*);

and likewise, even among those possessing immediate realization, the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)—by virtue of possessing the dissolution of the mind (*mano-nāśa*) and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*)—is considered by me to be superior to those who are not yet liberated while living, as they lack the dissolution of the mind and the destruction of latent impressions.
He is self-restrained.

Because it is so, therefore—by virtue of the power of ever-increasing effort—you who have fallen from yoga are now considered the supreme yogi, as previously stated: that yogi who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), having simultaneously achieved the knowledge of reality, the dissolution of the mind, and the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*). Such is he.
Through the ripening of the means for existence, O Arjuna, O Pure One—this is the meaning of the vocative address. //46//
Viśvanātha:

In response to the inquiry as to who is the best among those possessing action, knowledge, austerity, and yoga, he says: "The yogī is superior to the ascetics"—those devoted to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances—and even to the "knowers," that is, those who worship Brahman; the sense is that "this alone is my opinion. Thus, the yogī who worships the Supreme Self is considered superior.
If he is superior even to the men of knowledge, how much more so than the men of action? To this, he says: "And [superior] to the men of action" (verse 46).

Baladeva: Having thus declared that the yoga of action performed without desire—which contains knowledge within it and is crowned by the eightfold yoga—is the cause of liberation, and that even for one who has fallen from such yoga, the fruit thereof will eventually be attained, [the Lord] now praises the yogin with the words beginning "tapasvibhyaḥ.

Compared to ascetics devoted to austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance, to men of knowledge who are experts in the treatises on worldly matters, and to performers of ritual action who perform sacrifices with desire for results such as *iṣṭāpūrta*, the yogin—who practices the yoga taught by Me—is superior.
He is considered the best.

Compared to ascetics and others who are unfit for liberation due to a lack of self-knowledge, the yogi described by me is superior because he is fit for liberation through his possession of fully developed self-knowledge. //46//
Of all yogis as well, he who, with his inner self absorbed in Me, worships Me with faith— he is deemed by Me to be the most perfectly integrated. 47.

Śrīdhara: He says "even among yogins" to show that his devotee is superior even to those who are devoted to the restraints (yamas), observances (niyamas), and so forth. "With an inner self directed toward me" means with a mind attached to me.
He who, endowed with faith, worships me as the Supreme Lord Vāsudeva— he,
among those devoted to yoga, is deemed by me to be the best.
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "Become my devotee. //47//
I bow to that Mādhava, the abode of bliss and the refuge of devotees, who has spoken of the yoga of the self as the crest-jewel of the yoga of devotion.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Meditation," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana:
Now, speaking of the yogi who is the best among all yogis, he concludes the chapter with the words "yoginām" (of yogis).
Among all yogis—including those devoted to minor deities such as the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas—it is [the one] in Me, the Blessed Lord...

One who, through a particular ripening of merit regarding Vāsudeva, has entered into Me with an inner self (mind) overcome by love and absorbed in Me; and who, due to the sharpness of impressions from previous births and association with the virtuous, possesses such faith—meaning one who believes with great intensity—in the worship of Me alone; he who constantly serves and contemplates Me, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of lords, endowed with attributes.

Or, having abandoned the delusion that "this person is devoid of qualities" or "he is common to other lords," that very devotee of mine, the yogi, is the most disciplined; he is considered— meaning determined— to be the best among all those who are concentrated in mind and disciplined, by me, the Supreme Lord, the omniscient one.

The sense is this: although the hardship of practicing yoga is equal and the exertion of devotion is equal, since one who possesses devotion to Me is superior to those devoid of devotion to Me, you—being My supreme devotee and most disciplined—will be able to attain [the goal] without effort.

Thus, by this chapter, having shown the limits of Karma-yoga as a cause for the purification of the intellect, and consequently [having shown the state] of one who has performed the renunciation of all actions...

Having explained Yoga with its constituent limbs and taught the means for restraining the mind while refuting objections, and having also mitigated the fear that one who has fallen from Yoga is devoid of human purpose—thereby showing that the ritual section (*karma-kāṇḍa*) is to be followed—the Lord Vāsudeva, the referent of that word, is now defined; thus, the subsequent group of six chapters is commenced. May there be auspiciousness! 47.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Inner Self," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā), composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha:
In that case, it would follow that there is no one superior to the yogis; to prevent this conclusion, he says: "Even among the yogis... [and so forth].
The genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative because it involves a selection (*nirdhāraṇa*);
and because of the sequence of meanings associated with the ablative—as in "superior even to ascetics and to those possessed of knowledge"—the meaning is "even compared to yogis.
It is not merely [superior] in comparison to yogis of a single kind.

Moreover, it is said "even among all yogis"—that is, among those of various kinds who have ascended to yoga, including those possessing both cognitive (samprajñāta) and non-cognitive (asamprajñāta) samādhis.

Alternatively, "yogas" refers to means such as ritual action, knowledge, austerity, yoga, and devotion; among those who possess these, he who worships Me—that is, becomes My devotee—is the most disciplined (*yuktatama*), meaning the most proficient in means.
The practitioner of action, the ascetic, the man of knowledge, and the yogi are considered [yogis];
the master of eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) is a superior yogi;
but one who possesses devotion through hearing, chanting, and so forth is the best of yogis—this is the meaning.

As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam: "O great sage, even among millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely rare."
The six subsequent chapters which describe bhakti-yoga consist of aphoristic verses that serve as an ornament for the necks of devotees.
By the first [chapter], the thread of the discourse—the crest-jewel of the Gītā-śāstra—is established;
by the second and the third, as well as the fourth, the performance of action free from desire is set forth.
Knowledge is taught by the fifth [chapter] and yoga is proclaimed by the sixth;
yet even this group of six is primarily concerned with defining action (karma).
Thus, in this *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, this sixth chapter has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. //6//

Baladeva: Thus, having first described with the initial group of six verses the means for one established in [the path], namely desireless actions (niṣkāma-karma) containing knowledge and headed by yoga, he now intends to describe with the middle group the means such as taking refuge in the Lord for one who has reached perfection and so forth;
therefore, he states that aphorism which declares its superiority: "Of the yogis... and so on.
This genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (pañcamy-arthe), because of the preceding introduction with the word "tapasvibhyaḥ" (from the ascetics).

Nor can it be argued that this is a genitive of selection (nirdhāraṇe ṣaṣṭhī), because the yogin about to be described possesses activities distinct from those of the ascetics and others, and thus is not included among them.
Although there exists a mutual relationship of inferiority and superiority among the ascetics and the rest, [the yogin remains distinct].
Nevertheless, inferiority remains the same for them compared to that [Supreme Being],
just as other mountains— whether high or low— are inferior to the Golden Mountain (Sumeru).

He who possesses faith, having firm conviction in the statements of the Vedas and other scriptures that describe My devotion, beholds Me, dark-complexioned like a blue lotus, with arms thick and reaching down to the knees, and eyes like a lotus blossomed by the rays of the sun.

[He saw] the Lord Himself, the Sovereign of All, manifest in human form, composed of supreme consciousness and bliss, suckling at the breast of Yaśodā; He who was resplendent with His own radiance— adorned with a crown, earrings, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, the Kaustubha gem, anklets, and a forest garland— dispelling the darkness from all directions, and appearing in eternal forms such as Nṛsiṃha and the foremost of the Raghus, yet designated by names such as Kṛṣṇa.

One worships— that is, serves through hearing and other means— that Being which is described as being filled with jewel-like qualities such as omniscience, universal sovereignty, the fulfillment of true resolves, compassion, beauty, sweetness, and loveliness;
"with an inner self (mind) directed toward Me" means with a mind exclusively attached to Me, the sense being that one is unable to endure even a sesame-seed’s worth of separation from Me.
The meaning is that my devotee who is devoted to me alone is the most disciplined (*yuktatama*) among all ascetics and yogis.
To this, he explains: "Now, if it be argued that there is no one superior to the yogis, he says: 'Of the yogis...

Due to the gradations in the ascent of yoga, there are many karma-yogis; compared to all of them, one who has ascended to meditation (*dhyāna*) is more disciplined (*yukta*), one who has ascended to *samādhi* is even more disciplined (*yuktatara*), and one who possesses devotion through hearing and so forth is the most disciplined (*yuktatama*).
Thus:
the word *bhakti* denotes service (*sevā*). Indeed, this verbal root *bhaj* is proclaimed to signify service.
Therefore, service is frequently expressed by the word "bhakti" by the wise, according to the traditional teaching (smṛti):
"Know this bhakti through the yoga of faith, devotion, and meditation. And:
"He who has supreme bhakti for the Lord, and for the guru as he does for the Lord..."
"For these truths are revealed to that high-souled one who has been instructed" (ŚvetU 6.23).

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the act of worshiping Him; it is the fixing of the mind upon Him through detachment from the conditions of this world and the next. This alone is "freedom from action" (*naiṣkarmya*), as stated in: "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world" (BAU 1.4.8).
And likewise, there are such passages as: "The Self, indeed, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5; 4.5.6).
Furthermore, that devotion should be understood as being composed of the nature, the power, and the functions of the Blessed Lord.
"Devotion (bhakti-yoga) abides in that which is of the singular essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, a mass of consciousness and a mass of bliss," according to scripture [GTU 2.79].

Its nature as an action such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth should be understood as being like the representation of the hair-tufts and other features of the Supreme Lord, who is the embodiment of Consciousness and Bliss.

Furthermore, the state of Consciousness and Bliss inherent in devotion in the form of hearing and so forth is to be experienced through its continuous practice, just as the sweetness of sugar is experienced when bile is neutralized by the consumption of sugar. //47//
In the first [chapter], he spoke the thread of the discourse on action; in the second and subsequent [chapters], that which is devoid of desire;
and in the fifth, he declared that which has realization as its core.
But in the sixth [chapter], Mukunda [describes] that which is ignited by yoga.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad. //6//
